#2859. The little things are adding up to something bigger for the Suns

Games in November count just as much toward the standings as games in March, and what we saw from the Phoenix Suns in their overtime win over the New Orleans Pelicans is something we might look back on in March and appreciate, both for how it unfolded and the result it produced.

Going into any opposing team's arena isn't easy, and we know the Pelicans have the positional archetypes that can trouble Phoenix. They have size and length defensively, with the ability to jam up Devin Booker and effectively close out on shooters.

So what if they entered the game 5-13? All it takes is one of their players getting on a roll, feeding off the Smoothie King Center crowd, and suddenly the possibility of losing to them becomes very real.

Monday night's game was a physical one, defined by both teams exchanging runs. Ultimately, the team that made the final run was going to walk away victorious, and to the Suns' credit, it took a collective effort to ensure that was them. Five players scored in double figures, four of whom came from the starting five. Everybody contributed, and when you take care of the little things, the big things tend to take care of themselves.

That big thing was a fourth consecutive victory on this road trip for Phoenix, further reinforcing that the Suns are figuring out how to play team basketball this season. 16 games in, there's still plenty of room for growth. Playing perfect basketball is impossible, but that doesn't mean you shouldn't chase perfection. The one thing potentially keeping this team from going from a good basketball team, which is what they currently are, to a great one is their ability to rebound. From a connectivity and cohesion standpoint, you're beginning to see a consistent level of play from this group. It's another solid win.

What I appreciate most about this stretch of basketball is that the Suns are finding different ways to win. They're learning how to navigate adversity, respond to opposing runs, and trust one another when possessions become increasingly valuable. The rebounding deficiencies remain a legitimate concern, but the collective identity of this team is beginning to take shape. And banking these victories while they're still figuring things out? That's something we might be especially thankful for come March.

#2857. Top Wall Street analysts like these 3 dividend stocks for steady income

Stock markets remain volatile as investors weigh uncertainty in the Middle East, rising interest rates and concerns about the artificial intelligence (AI) trade.

Given this volatile backdrop, investors seeking a stable income stream can enhance their portfolios with the addition of dividend stocks. In this regard, tracking recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend stocks that are backed by strong financials.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Integrated oil and gas giant Chevron (CVX) is the first dividend pick. Earlier this month, the company paid a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share. At an annualized dividend of $7.12 per share, CVX offers a dividend yield of about 3.5%.

After a meeting with senior leadership, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on CVX and raised his price target to $240 from $225. Among the key takeaways Mehta emphasized was that Chevron is building a solid pipeline of promising international exploration projects across Latin America, the Middle East, West Africa and the Eastern Mediterranean. In particular, he mentioned the focus on Venezuela, where Chevron expects to more than double gross production to 600 kbd from about 280 kbd by 2031, using three joint ventures.

Mehta also noted Chevron's efforts to deploy new technologies, especially in shale and tight-oil operations. CVX is focused on boosting productivity and efficiency to maximize free cash flow, he added.

Initiatives such as artificial lift optimization, AI and machine learning, and advanced chemical treatments are expected to improve recovery by about 10% in new wells. Consequently, capital spending per barrel in U.S. shale is projected to fall 25% in 2026, with total Permian spending dropping below $3.5 billion.

Mehta also said that Chevron sees power as a growth opportunity and is using its U.S. natural gas portfolio, key equipment and partnerships to meet rising demand. Notably, Chevron recently signed a 20-year power purchase deal with Microsoft (MSFT) to supply 2.67 GW of behind-the-meter capacity. This project, called Kilby, is expected to see its first power delivery in 2028 and generate mid-teens returns and long-term cash flows.

Mehta ranks No. 536 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 61% of the time, delivering an average return of 11.3%. See Chevron Statistics on TipRanks.

Enterprise Products Partners (EPD) is a master limited partnership (MLP) that provides midstream energy services to producers and consumers of natural gas, natural gas liquids (NGLs), crude oil, refined products and petrochemicals. With a quarterly cash distribution of 56 cents per common unit ($2.24 per common unit annualized), EPD offers a yield of about 6%.

Following a recent call with the company, RBC Capital analyst Elvira Scotto reiterated a buy rating on EPD with a price target of $42. The analyst slightly lowered her estimates for the second half of 2026, citing margin and volume normalization, though demand dynamics remain strong.

While the 5-star analyst expects a sequential decline due to normal seasonality and normalization following high spreads in the first half of the year, she still expects EPD to report another solid quarter (Q3 2026) and enter 2027 with a favorable setup. Ahead of Q3 earnings, Scotto expects investors to focus on export demand durability, EPD's ability to profit from spot cargo sales and growth in Permian volumes.

Scotto continues to expect $150 million of common unit buybacks per quarter in the second half of 2026. She expects buybacks to increase to $200 million per quarter in 2027, as capex spending declines and free cash flow improves.

In total, Scotto is bullish on EPD and views it as a core MLP holding that has both offensive and defensive characteristics. The analyst praised EPD's diverse asset base as ensuring stable cash flows. "Furthermore, the partnership's multi-year organic growth backlog helps provide visibility on long-term distribution growth," Scotto said.

Scotto ranks No. 199 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 67% of the time, delivering an average return of 15.9%. See Enterprise Products Partners Financials on TipRanks.

Brookfield Infrastructure Partners (BIP) operates a diversified portfolio of high-quality utilities, transport, midstream and data assets. The company declared a quarterly distribution of 45.5 cents per unit, payable on September 29. At an annualized distribution of $1.82, BIP offers a yield of 5.2%.

Recently, BMO Capital analyst Devin Dodge reaffirmed a buy rating on Brookfield Infrastructure with a price target of $47. The analyst cited improved visibility into BIP's growth and views its corporate simplification as a potential catalyst.

"Layering in the benefits from the proposed corporate simplification, a multiple well below historical levels and an attractive yield, we believe BIP offers a compelling risk/reward and it remains a preferred idea," said Dodge.

With more organic growth projects in the pipeline and new partnership investment opportunities, Dodge believes that BIP has clearer visibility into where it will deploy capital. That should support continued double-digit growth in funds from operations (FFO) per unit.

Dodge said the semiconductor foundries that BIP is developing with Intel (INTC) are expected to be fully commissioned by the end of 2026, with returns improving through Q4 2026. Dodge expects the joint venture to boost FFO by 300-400 basis points.

Dodge ranks No. 476 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 68% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.5%. See Brookfield Infrastructure Partners KPIs on TipRanks.

#2851. Why Draymond Green's NBA ‘loser' comments rubbed Baron Davis the wrong way

Why Draymond Green's NBA 'loser' comments rubbed Baron Davis the wrong way originally appeared on NBC Sports Bay Area

Another off-court Draymond Green statement is buzzing around the NBA, and a Warriors icon chipped in to give his perspective on the matter.

Baron Davis, the centerpiece of the 2006-07 Warriors "We Believe" team, was asked about Green calling Phoenix Suns commentator Eddie Johnson, among other critics, "losers" for debating Green's Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame case.

Speaking on the "Gil's Arena" podcast, Davis explained to hosts Josiah Johnson and Gilbert Arenas why those comments bothered him.

"I just don't like the loser thing, man," Davis said. "We've all played. It takes greatness to get into this league. It takes some hard work. Not everybody's gonna win. There's only one champion, so I just don't like the loser thing, because if Michael Jordan called us a loser, I can deal with that. If Kobe [Bryant] called me a loser, I can deal with that. But I think that we move the goalposts."

Davis went on to say that "everybody has their way of judging" players, emphasizing accolades or individual statistics, and gave props to both Green and Johnson, the 1989 Sixth Man of the Year.

While Davis differentiated between winners and NBA champions, he stated the conversation between the two "goes both ways."

"You learn to appreciate everybody because everybody is winners," Davis said. "They are champions, and so if you don't win a championship, that don't mean you can't talk to champions in a certain fashion. I don't agree with that."

The discussion began with a post by Johnson on Nov. 21 questioning whether Green's statistics were impressive enough to make the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame.

Green responded to Johnson's comments before Golden State's 88-87 win on Sunday and was asked about the comments after the game as well.

There is really no player who embodies the debate more than Green, whose Basketball Hall of Fame case is built on intangibles and generational defense despite a lack of elite offensive production.

Green, a nine-time All-Defensive team selection and the 2017 Defensive Player of the Year, never was the best player on the Warriors but played a vital role alongside superstar Steph Curry.

Despite declining at 36 years old, Green was the best playoff defender of his generation and an All-NBA Second Team selection at his peak.

The outspoken veteran's Olympic and college basketball resume at Michigan State strengthens his case for the Basketball Hall of Fame, being named the NABC National Player of the Year in 2012 and holding two Olympic gold medals.

The two Warriors legends might be cemented in franchise history for their impact. but this certainly appears to be a topic they don't agree on.

For release at 1:30 p.m. EST Share

The Federal Reserve Board on Thursday announced pricing, effective January 1, 2027, for payment services the Federal Reserve Banks provide to banks and credit unions, such as the clearing of checks, automated clearing house (ACH) transactions, instant payments, and wholesale payment and settlement services.

By law, the Federal Reserve must establish fees to recover the costs, including imputed costs, of providing payment services over the long run. The Federal Reserve expects to recover 101.5 percent of actual and imputed expenses in 2027, including the return on equity that would have been earned if a private-sector firm provided the services. Overall, price changes for 2027 will result in an estimated 1.4 percent average price increase for established, mature services.

In addition, the Federal Reserve Banks announced changes to streamline and adjust their check services. As described in the request for information on check services issued last year, the volume of checks processed by the Federal Reserve Banks is declining, but checks remain an important payment instrument for many consumers and businesses. The changes were informed by public feedback and ensure that the Federal Reserve Banks continue to provide check services efficiently. The adjustments include optimizing check processing windows during low-volume periods, increasing fees that banks and credit unions pay to process checks, and other operational updates. These changes do not impact consumers' and businesses' ability to pay with or receive checks and only impact how banks and credit unions process checks with Federal Reserve Banks.

The entire 2027 fee schedule for all of the Federal Reserve's payment services is published on FRBservices.org®. Additional information on the Federal Reserve's payments services, including service usage statistics, is available on the Board's website.

#2847. Chiefs sign tackle Fred Johnson to active roster

Early on Tuesday, NFL Network's Ian Rapoport reported that the Kansas City Chiefs would be signing tackle Fred Johnson — who joined their practice squad last week — to the active roster. Johnson had previously been with the Philadelphia Eagles before being waived on November 13 after seven appearances with the team in 2026.

The player himself appeared to confirm Rapoport's scoop later in the morning.

Later in the afternoon, the Chiefs made the move official. To create a spot for Johnson on the active roster, fullback Ben VanSumeren was placed on the Reserve/Injured list. VanSumeren left Kansas City's Week 11 win over the Arizona Cardinals with a knee injury.

The Chiefs have navigated uncertainty at the tackle position all season in the absence of 2025 first round selection Josh Simmons. The team also appears set to play on Thursday against the Buffalo Bills without right tackle Jaylon Moore, who is recovering from an ankle injury. Moore has missed the Chiefs' last two games and has not practiced this week.

Kansas City was fortunate to be able to add a veteran lineman with positional versatility who has played in 86 NFL games. Whether Johnson will see playing time against Buffalo after being with the team such a short time remains to be seen.

"Fred, he's had time," head coach Andy Reid said before Tuesday's practice. "Enough time? We'll have to see on that. He seems like a sharp kid. He has a ton of experience. He's got skills. We'll see how all that goes as we roll."

Johnson's short time with the Chiefs has made an impression on their most famous player.

"Obviously, he's played football for a number of years — and played really good football," observed quarterback Patrick Mahomes. "He can play guard and tackle, so that versatility is going to help out a ton. We'll continue to try to get him more and more work within our offense and within our scheme. I know one thing — he's a big guy, and he's athletic. You see why he's had success in this league. It's about getting him more and more accustomed to how we do things here."

With Tuesday's transactions, the Chiefs will have an opening on their practice squad.

#2846. Walker Kessler thankful for big stage with Lakers after beating former team

Walker Kessler has a lot to be thankful for as the Los Angeles Lakers earned a 109-94 victory over the Utah Jazz at Crypto.com Arena on Monday, Nov. 23.

The Lakers clinched the season series against the center's former team, giving Los Angeles some momentum ahead of Thanksgiving and a showdown against the San Antonio Spurs on Friday, Nov. 27.

While the Lakers may only go as far as Luka Doncic and Austin Reaves can take them, Kessler is viewed as the third piece to a potential championship puzzle.

Los Angeles invested a lot to acquire Kessler before signing him four-year, $130 million deal during the offseason. In order to secure the big man, the Lakers sent unprotected first-round picks in 2031 and 2033 and first-round swaps in 2028 and 2030 to the Jazz.

All eyes will be on Kessler as he will be tasked with defending Victor Wembanyama of the Spurs on Friday.

The center finished with 10 points and 12 rebounds against Utah for his 10th double-double of the season on Monday.

Kessler had impressed Los Angeles in the season opener with a 26-point performance, having made all 12 of his shots against the Golden State Warriors. He had another high-efficiency night against the Atlanta Hawks, posting 21 points on 8-of-12 shooting and making five of his six free throw attempts.

"I'm thankful for this opportunity to play on such a big stage," Kessler said during his postgame press conference on Monday. "Sometimes you get so tied down in your individual performance and stats and all this stuff, but to be a professional basketball player like as a kid, you look at that, it's like, oh my gosh. That's the dream."

Kessler will be on the big stage later this week with a formidable opponent in Wembanyama.

Wembanyama and the Spurs are the standard in the conference, having won the 2025-26 conference finals and making an appearance in the NBA Finals.

Wembanyama is one of the league's top young stars while Kessler is looking to have a breakout season on a winning team.

Kessler did not play a lot of meaningful basketball during his first four seasons in the NBA, as the Jazz never finished with a record above .500.

Kessler and Wembanyama have an even 3-3 record when their respective teams have played against one another. Considering the differences in the roles those players may have had on those respective teams over the years, it's not surprising that Wembanyama has averaged more points, rebounds, blocks and minutes per game.

Kessler will have to find a balance during the game, having admitted that his emotions have factored into his play at least once this season.

Kessler had a strong start to the season, but an early matchup in Utah led to a two-point performance in a 132-123 victory for the Lakers on Oct. 25.

"I think going into the game I let my emotions get the best of me," Kessler said at the time. "But you have to learn in those moments and move on. I'm just glad we got the win tonight … even though it wasn't my best night, I really appreciate (my teammates)."

Kessler has averaged 14.3 points and 10.7 rebounds per game in 16 games played this season.

The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the Federal Reserve Board, the National Credit Union Administration, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency today announced that they will extend, until December 16, the comment period for proposed guidance on managing risks associated with third-party relationships. Comments on the proposal were originally due November 16.

The proposed guidance reflects the agencies' supervisory experience and lessons learned from examining financial institutions' third-party risk management practices. It is intended to help banks and credit unions tailor their risk management practices to the risks associated with individual third-party relationships. The proposed guidance takes a principles-based approach and, like all supervisory guidance, is non-binding.

When finalized, the federal bank regulatory agencies plan to rescind existing third-party risk management guidance and replace it with the finalized guidance to promote consistency and prudent innovation in the banking industry. NCUA also plans to rescind its existing third-party risk management guidance and will conduct its own reviews to update related guidance as needed.

Also today, the Federal Reserve Board separately announced that it will extend, until December 16, the comment period on a proposed third-party risk management guide specifically for Federal Reserve-supervised traditional community banks.

Philadelphia signed Milton off Dallas' practice squad in October, and he is now getting an opportunity to lead the Eagles' offense. It's an unusual twist in an already important NFC East matchup, especially considering the Cowboys handed Philadelphia a 38-21 loss the last time these teams met. The Eagles are still trying to find consistency, but Sunday's win showed that they shouldn't be taken lightly.

The biggest storyline for the Eagles heading into Thursday is undoubtedly Milton. The former Cowboys practice-squad quarterback is now preparing to make his third NFL start, and his first against his former team. Philadelphia turned to Milton after Jalen Hurts was shut down and they struggled to find consistency at quarterback. The move has given the Eagles a different look under center.

Milton's performance against Pittsburgh was far from perfect. He completed 10 of 20 passes before his final completion, and he missed several opportunities downfield, including an overthrown pass to DeVonta Smith that could have resulted in a 68-yard touchdown. He did, however, make the most important throw of the afternoon.

With just over a minute remaining and Philadelphia facing third-and-six, Milton connected with Smith for a seven-yard gain to move the chains and effectively seal the victory. It was a meaningful moment for a young quarterback who has struggled with consistency, and it showed that head coach Nick Sirianni is willing to put the game in his hands.

Milton has a powerful arm and the athleticism to make plays outside the pocket. Through his first two appearances this season, he has completed 29 of 55 passes for 310 yards, with no touchdowns or interceptions. He has also rushed 14 times for 71 yards.

The Cowboys should know better than anyone that Milton has the arm strength to push the ball downfield. The challenge will be making him prove he can consistently deliver accurate throws and make good decisions. Dallas needs to pressure him, keep him contained in the pocket and avoid giving him easy opportunities to extend plays.

Regardless of who's playing quarterback, Philadelphia's offense still revolves around Saquon Barkley. The running back has dealt with injuries and inconsistent production throughout the season, but he remains one of the most dangerous players on the Eagles' roster. Through 10 games, Barkley has rushed for 371 yards and four touchdowns on 86 carries, averaging 4.3 yards per attempt.

He showed signs of life against Pittsburgh, finishing with 75 yards on 17 carries and a 38-yard touchdown run. Unfortunately for Philadelphia, Barkley left the game after getting shaken up late, and his status heading into Thanksgiving will be worth monitoring.

The Eagles have other backfield options, including Dameon Pierce, Tank Bigsby and Will Shipley. However, none brings the same combination of explosiveness and big-play potential as Barkley. The first meeting between these teams reminded everyone what Philadelphia can do on the ground. A hobbling Barkley rushed for 62 yards on seven carries, averaging nearly nine yards per attempt.

Dallas ultimately controlled the game by establishing its own running attack and finished with 204 rushing yards. That will be an important matchup again, particularly with the Cowboys' defense still trying to find consistency against the run. If Barkley is healthy, Dallas cannot afford to let him get comfortable. The Eagles need their running game to take pressure off Milton, and the Cowboys need to make Philadelphia one-dimensional.

Milton's biggest challenge will be getting the ball to Philadelphia's playmakers consistently. DeVonta Smith is back in the lineup after missing significant time with a hamstring injury. He returned against Pittsburgh and finished with five receptions for 41 yards on 12 targets. The numbers weren't spectacular, but his presence gives Milton a reliable receiver who can create separation and make plays downfield. Smith has 31 receptions for 351 yards and two touchdowns this season.

Tight end Dallas Goedert has also been a productive target, recording 32 receptions for 346 yards and two touchdowns. He remains an important part of the passing game, particularly when Philadelphia needs a dependable option underneath.

Rookie Makai Lemon has emerged as another contributor, leading the team with 38 receptions for 315 yards. Dontayvion Wicks has added 284 receiving yards, while Darius Cooper has 259 yards and four touchdowns. Dallas' secondary has struggled this season, especially in preventing explosive plays. The Cowboys cannot afford to give Smith and the rest of Philadelphia's receivers free access downfield. Making Milton work through his progressions and forcing him to be accurate will be essential.

The Eagles' defense has had its share of problems this season, including a difficult performance against Dallas in October. The Cowboys finished with 416 total yards, rushed for 204 yards and scored 38 points in the 38-21 victory. Philadelphia failed to record a sack, tackle for loss or quarterback hit in that game. Javonte Williams ran through the defense for 155 yards, and Prescott threw three touchdown passes without an interception.

That performance should give Dallas confidence heading into the rematch, but the Eagles looked much better against Pittsburgh. Philadelphia recorded five sacks, held the Steelers to 255 total yards and limited them to just 73 rushing yards on 20 carries. The defense also held Pittsburgh to five conversions on 17 third-down attempts and kept the Steelers out of the end zone on two red-zone opportunities.

Nolan Smith has been one of the team's most productive pass rushers, leading Philadelphia with six sacks. Defensive tackle Jalen Carter has added five sacks, while Byron Young recorded two against Pittsburgh.

The Eagles still have a talented secondary led by cornerbacks Quinyon Mitchell and Cooper DeJean. Mitchell left Sunday's game with a hamstring injury, so his availability is uncertain. Still, significant personnel questions remain. Linebacker Zack Baun is on injured reserve, and Philadelphia traded defensive tackle Jordan Davis. Those are meaningful losses for a defense that will need to find a way to slow down a Dallas offense that has scored 91 points over its last two games.

The biggest question is whether the Eagles can replicate Sunday's defensive performance. If they can generate pressure and limit Dallas' rushing attack, they have a chance to make this game interesting. If they allow the Cowboys to control the line of scrimmage again, it could be a long afternoon.

The first meeting between these teams offered a pretty clear blueprint for how Dallas can beat Philadelphia. The Cowboys rushed for 204 yards on 38 carries, averaging 5.4 yards per attempt. Williams led the way with a career-high 155 rushing yards and a touchdown. Prescott added three passing touchdowns, and Dallas scored on seven of its nine offensive possessions.

Philadelphia simply couldn't stop the run.

That needs to be the starting point again. Dallas has found more balance offensively over the last several weeks, and the running game has become an important part of its success. Against an Eagles defense that just held Pittsburgh to 73 rushing yards, the Cowboys will need to establish that physical identity early.

Defensively, the game plan should be centered on making Milton uncomfortable. He has the arm strength to make big plays, but his accuracy and decision-making remain question marks. Dallas should pressure him without losing its discipline, particularly when he tries to escape the pocket. Easier said than done for this bunch.

The Cowboys also need to keep Barkley from taking over the game if he plays. If Philadelphia can establish its running attack, it can protect Milton and control the tempo. Dallas has struggled to consistently stop opposing offenses this season, and it cannot afford to let the Eagles dictate the terms of the matchup.

There is also a little extra motivation on the other sideline. Milton knows the Cowboys' organization, and he will undoubtedly want to make a statement against his former team. But Dallas has the more established offense and already showed it can take advantage of Philadelphia's defensive weaknesses.

The Eagles are coming off a win, and the rivalry always brings a different level of intensity. Still, the Cowboys have an opportunity to make another statement in the NFC East. If they can run the football like they did in October and force Milton to win through the air, they should have a good chance of leaving Thanksgiving with another division win.

#2837. Karl-Anthony Towns is so much more than the Knicks’ best player

In New York, it is customary for an athlete to have distractions. How do you hide in a city that adores you? How do you hide in a city full of people counting on your performance to get them from the capitalistic ills of living in New York? So many of our great athletes — everyone from Ruth, Clyde Frazier, Reggie Jackson, Sugar Ray Richardson, Derek Jeter, Alex Rodriguez, Carmelo Anthony — have had off-the-court news show up in Page Six, on TMZ, on the internet, those times when the fame and notoriety in New York becomes too showy, causing discomfort for even the most New York of New York fans. I remember when Stephon Marbury was in the paper constantly, diminishing the goodwill that came from being raised in Coney Island, blending a conflicting cocktail of bitterness towards the press with a heroic sense of duty to working class New Yorkers. Sometimes it was because of his arguments with Isiah Thomas, on the team plane, cursing him out for his lack of loyalty; sometimes it was his inappropriate liaisons with interns. If you are a New York athlete and you don't end up in the newspaper or the gossip columns for merely existing in a way that would not anoint you into a private club of sainthood, then I rebuke your non-existent personality.

The glory of this New York Knicks team, the absolute greatness that exists within the halls of Tarrytown and Madison Square Garden, is that for the first time in my lifetime, we're cheering for a Knicks team that isn't dramatic. It's led by Jalen Brunson, of course, who is a businessman with a sharp crossover, sophisticated at blocking out chatter from elsewhere until he is a champion, in front of a microphone at City Hall about to finally speak about his haters. That deadly professionalism is what the team has become since the fateful day we first signed him from Dallas in free agency. Yet, and this is something that I don't think I realized until the start of the season, the player that I am most proud of for embodying these virtues is Karl-Anthony Towns. Towns, 31, has been the team's best player, by far, and considering that I saw Brunson put the team on his back in the game-clinching game, I don't say that fact lightly. KAT, however, has been the best big man in the world so far. Right now, he is averaging 21.3 points per game and 14 rebounds. Those are terrific numbers, but it is the fact that he leads the Knicks in plus minus (+/-) that is the most surprising part of the season so far. Plus, he's been silencing any critics.

Before the season started, the Knicks and Towns were in talks for a contract extension. The two sides were apart on the numbers and because the Knicks have a rule where they don't negotiate during the beginning of the season, the season started before Towns was able to re-sign for more money. I'm not too concerned. It feels like it'd be a depressing longshot if the Knicks didn't re-up with Towns. In the wake of the championship that the Knicks won, Towns took a point forward role that was completely different from the role that he started the season playing. Controlling the ball at the top of the key, waiting for the offense to set, waiting for those sequences where players grunt and grind off of screens, Towns would be steady, attacking as soon as he saw someone open or he saw a lane to gallop into. Towns became an example of why the bullishness about the Knicks turned out to be a real, tangible thing. Their ace was Brunson but the force, the light saber, was Towns, emboldened to play a style of basketball it would have seemed like a no-brainer to have always allowed him to play.

The games from that run are firmly indelible. The game four against the Hawks, the first time this new offense was employed, when he had a triple double; the first game against the Spurs, where he took it to Wemby, supplying Brunson's thirty points with eighteen points. However, maybe a little less important, but still quite necessary, Towns's personality — unabashedly emotionally intelligent, gentle, and strong — won people over. One of the more meaningful parts of the title celebration was seeing Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani connect with Towns, two ethnic New York men, one in politics, the other in sports, connecting with whimsy and joy. Somehow, all of the disses, the fake macho act that his opponents tried to do to him, went out the window. He won, and his way of being won. He's not alone. He's all of us. Why did it ever become popular to pretend like greatness meant being an asshole? Why did it ever become common for folks to be angry while being great? Towns, as a player, is so unique for his emotional gifts, for his understanding of the game. It isn't like he is a soft player, he is rarely getting pushed off the block by anyone. The performance of masculinity, one that is popular for big men of the previous generation, do not apply to Towns.

Last year, I wrote about this. "Towns is an earnest star. His instincts lead him to show emotion on the court, emotion that allows for the most traditional kinds of men to question his mental toughness", I wrote. This piece has aged well, thank you to Towns's overall play and spirit during the Knicks playoffs. His championship has given him newfound respect that I wonder if he would have if we had failed to defeat the Spurs. What if part of the reason that Towns is as universally accepted as he has ever been is because he won the championship? Ring culture, despite the fact that I often dabble in that practice, can be deceiving. Luckily with Towns, it is earned. He won playing a role that Draymond Green hasn't played in years; he won before Jimmy Butler did.

This year has been more of the same. A lesser player and person than Towns would have sulked about the dissolution of the contract talks, but Towns hasn't let it get to his head. He was fantastic against the Pistons three weeks ago with a 20 and 20 double-double, against the Wolves on Thursday night, and against the Raptors, extending his streak of double-doubles to fourteen games. You haven't heard a whisper of discontent out of Towns. Nothing about the lack of respect from the contract, nothing about the fact that he has been the Knicks's best player so far this season, nothing about himself. No one would blame him if he did that. Instead, he has been excellent on the court, adding to his already great legacy with the Knicks, busting lesser big men off the dribble, finishing through hard contact. Malika Andrews said Towns has been the best player in the Eastern Conference and I think she is right. His new trick is his slim body: knowing that he is getting older, Towns lost weight, cutting down on his carbs in the offseason. His body is built to last, all the way through the postseason. Right now, the Knicks are still 9-1 to win the championship, the fourth best odds in the league. When April rolls around, I'd gamble on everyone else catching up to Towns's energy. Until then, we'll rely on him to carry us to the postseason, relying on his steadiness and smile to ground us during a grueling title defense.

Soon, in ten years, we'll be talking about Towns being one of NBA's history's most underrated players, Dirk Nowitzki with somehow less adoration, and a player who helped bring a title back to New York — victory mixed with tears of joy, glory mixed with urban swagger. For this season, a parade down Chambers Street and its surrounding FiDi blocks could happen again. Karl-Anthony Towns is a champion, and when there is will, there is a way.

#2836. Top Wall Street analysts are upbeat about the prospects for these 3 stocks

September ended on a mixed note, with the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average falling 0.5% and 4.3%, respectively, while the Nasdaq Composite climbed 1.9%. Markets remained on edge with higher oil prices and Treasury yields weighing on investor sentiment and triggering fears of additional interest rate hikes.

In this climate, investors with a long-term horizon can track recommendations from top Wall Street analysts to find stocks with solid growth prospects.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Neocloud company CoreWeave (CRWV) is benefiting from robust AI-driven demand for cloud computing.

Recently, JPMorgan analyst Samik Chatterjee upgraded CoreWeave to buy from hold, raising his price target to $125 from $120. The analyst cited favorable pricing, driven by solid demand, for the upgrade.

Chatterjee said CoreWeave is now more willing to sign premium priced, shorter-term contracts, which lift his revenue and margin estimates. CRWV stock performance has been underwhelming as investors worry about high capital spending, the analyst noted. That said, he believes that higher prices and increased margins will more than offset the rise in debt to fund capital spending, improving the stock's valuation.

Chatterjee noted the 25% price hike in July across CoreWeave's product offerings and frequent price increases by rivals like Nebius (NBIS), adding that some peers are charging nearly three times more for short-term compute contracts than what CoreWeave charges on longer-term deals.

"CoreWeave's leverage of the opportunity [is] evident in its recent press release highlighting contracts signed in F3Q at ~$40M/MW," said Chatterjee. JPMorgan said higher pricing is already contributing 5-10 percentage points to contract margins versus earlier deals.

Chatterjee ranks No. 4 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 75% of the time, delivering an average return of 55.3%. See CoreWeave Statistics on TipRanks.

Palo Alto Networks (PANW) is a provider of cybersecurity solutions across network, cloud, security operations, AI and identity. Following a discussion with management, BTIG analyst Gray Powell reiterated a buy rating on PANW and raised his price target to $425 from $404.

After a review of Palo Alto's product-level growth catalysts, Powell sees clear upside to both revenue and next-generation security (NGS) annual recurring revenue (ARR) in fiscal 2027. He expects PANW to deliver pro forma revenue growth of more than 17%, above the consensus estimate of 14.6%, and NGS ARR growth of more than 26% versus the Street's expectation of 24.5%.

Over the past five years, the Palo Alto business mix, has moved to higher-growth product areas and new markets. from what was earlier viewed as a hardware-centric network security company, Powell said. The 5-star analyst estimates that hardware firewalls and attached subscriptions now account for less than 50% of revenue.

Meanwhile, high-growth solutions, including Prisma SASE, software firewalls, Cortex XSIAM, Chronosphere and Idira now represent more than 35% of PANW's revenue. "Investors may not fully realize the growth potential within PANW's platform story," Powell said.

BTIG is optimistic about the prospects of Chronosphere in observability, CyberArk in identity and software firewalls and Prisma AIRS in the network and AI security business.

Powell ranks No. 320 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 61% of the time, delivering an average return of 17.3%. See Palo Alto Networks KPIs on TipRanks.

In a research note on September 30, Rosenblatt analyst Scott Devitt reiterated a buy rating on e-commerce and cloud computing platform Amazon (AMZN), raising his price target to $360 from $335. Fears that agentic commerce poses a major threat to Amazon's advertising business seem "overstated," he said.

Devitt noted that the growing adoption of personal agents and AI shopping assistants has sparked concern about displacement of Amazon's retail media business. But the 5-star analyst remains bullish, given Amazon's ability to adapt to changing consumer behavior, as it's done in the past.

Additionally, Devitt argues that even if an AI agent helps a shopper discover a product, Amazon can still handle the purchase and delivery, keeping much of the transaction value. He highlighted that management believes that existing Amazon shoppers will likely continue to start their shopping journey on the platform because it has better personalization, accurate pricing and inventory information that third-party agents still lack.

Overall, Devitt expects Amazon's retail business to prove a net beneficiary of agentic commerce. Fewer clicks would not hurt the company if the value of each remaining click and overall volumes keep rising, he said. The argument is that even if Amazon loses some sponsored ad revenue over the next few years, it would likely be only a small part of the company's total business and could be offset by growth in other areas.

"Consistent with our AI framework, we continue to view Amazon as one of the most resilient leaders in our coverage, combining owned compute infrastructure with a physical fulfillment moat," said Devitt. His bullish view is supported, Devitt said, by expectations that Amazon Web Services (AWS) will exit the year at a more than 45% growth rate with continued margin improvement.

Devitt ranks No. 765 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 49% of the time, delivering an average return of 12%. See Amazon Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

#2830. Fernando Mendoza draws praise in Week 12 NFL Power Rankings for Las Vegas Raiders

Fernando Mendoza is two games into his tenure as the Las Vegas Raiders' starting quarterback. While he's 0-2 in those outings, there have been a handful of promising moments, and he's coming off a three-touchdown performance against a strong Denver Broncos defense. As a result, Mendoza has drawn plenty of praise in the Week 12 NFL Power Rankings across the league's media.

The Las Vegas Raiders have lost both games in which Fernando Mendoza started. Yet, the resiliency seen from this year's No. 1 overall draft pick has been impressive. The Denver Broncos built a 17-0 lead Sunday. Mendoza is going to have his ups and downs, of course. At the same time, the rookie signal-caller led his team to 17 straight points before everything started to fall apart again. In doing so, he opened some eyes among the Raiders' division rival.

"There certainly was a lot of respect for Fernando Mendoza in the Broncos locker room," James Palmer reported. "What stood out was how calm he was in the pocket and his feel in the pocket, as well as how unpredictable he is when he starts to move. Most young players have something they do and go to it over and over again. Mendoza scrambles out a variety of ways and scans the field well while doing it." — Brent Sobleski

To be fair, the No. 1 pick did play a role in everything falling apart for the Raiders. After tying the game, he missed Jalen Nailor on an open fourth-down conversion and had the pick-six that sealed the team's fate. However, the defense was undoubtedly the bigger issue. Denver scored touchdowns on its two possessions after the contest was knotted up at 17 with about five minutes left in the third quarter.

Also, it's hard to win when the other team's offense scores 31 points and has 350 yards from scrimmage. Granted, the Raiders outgained the Broncos by 19 yards despite running four fewer plays and losing the time of possession battle by about 7.5 minutes. Mendoza has to avoid the big mistake, but he's far from the biggest reason the Silver and Black lost on Sunday.

I'm fascinated to see what the Raiders can do to improve their defense this offseason because I know this offense can put up points. Fernando Mendoza produced the first strong game of his career, and the Silver and Black delivered an entertaining contest against a superior Broncos squad in Denver, which is a good sign about where Las Vegas is headed in the bigger, multiyear picture. — Nick Shook

This picks up right where the section above left off. Las Vegas ranks third-to-last in yards allowed (382.0) and dead last in points allowed (29.7) per game, signalling big changes are needed on defense in the offseason.

Defensive tackle should be the starting point, and it will be interesting to see how the young corners — Jermod McCoy, Hezekiah Masses and Darien Porter — finish the season. Adding another edge-rusher wouldn't hurt either, but the Raiders will get Keyron Crawford back from injury next season to give the position group a young talent to turn to.

Something to be thankful for: Fernando Mendoza's learning curve

After making his first two starts against Seattle and Denver, the rookie quarterback is a predictable 0-2. The good news is he threw for 267 yards and three touchdowns against the Broncos, and the road gets easier from here. "I was really impressed with (Mendoza's) off-schedule stuff," Broncos coach Sean Payton said. "I was more impressed with his size and his escapability than maybe I saw on tape." — Josh Kendall, Chad Graff

It's funny, being able to make out of structure plays was viewed as one of the Indiana product's weaknesses coming out of college. But something that stood out about his game during the Mendoza Mania series this summer was his ability to make defenders wrong when scrambling; either using his legs to move the ball or dumping it to receivers when defenders don't plaster. We've seen that pop up a few times in the last two weeks, and, as Payton mentioned, Mendoza's escapability was much better from start one to start two.

Bowers will be eligible for an extension in the offseason, and Las Vegas shouldn't waste time locking down a franchise cornerstone. Despite battling knee and ankle injuries this season, he still has been productive, with 50 catches for 676 receiving yards and six touchdowns. Having Bowers around for the early stages of quarterback Fernando Mendoza's career will be essential for the No. 1 pick's development. Negotiations between Bowers and the Raiders could get interesting, given the number of times he has lined up on the outside this season. — Ryan McFadden

McFadden brings up a point that helps add some context/encouragement about Mendoza's first two starts: Bowers has only been on the field for 11 snaps in the last two weeks, per Pro Football Focus. That leaves the rookie quarterback with an underwhelming crew of pass-catchers, and he's still managed to turn heads. The problem is that's music to Bowers' agent's ears, as he's about to get paid like a 'WR1' when the time comes.

Luckily, the Raiders can buy themselves some time in the negotiation by picking up his fifth-year option this spring. According to Over The Cap, that will cost $17.35 million for 2028, which would make him the fifth-highest-paid tight end in terms of dollars per year. Seeing as the two-time Pro Bowler will undoubtedly make more than that when his contract is up, exercising the option is a no-brainer.

Some coaches spend minutes saying absolutely nothing. Klint Kubiak is the polar opposite in terms of meaningful words per second in pre-halftime interviews. — Conor Orr

We're veering away from the main topic here; Orr is referencing Kubiak's halftime interview where he said the refs need to call the game both ways when asked about the penalty discrepancy between the two teams last Sunday. The Raiders were flagged nine times for 63 yards, while the Broncos had just two penalties for 10 yards in the contest.

Even more interesting, Vegas averages the third-fewest penalties per game (5.7) this season while Denver is tied for 16th (7.1), according to TeamRankings. The one that stood out to me the most was Cody White getting called for offensive pass interference, which wiped away a touchdown, while the play below by Courtland Sutton wasn't penalized. Then again, this is nothing new for Raider Nation.

The University of California, Los Angeles won the 23rd Annual National College Fed Challenge.

The University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) won the 23rd annual national College Fed Challenge on Friday, a team competition that encourages undergraduate students to learn about the U.S. economy, monetary policymaking, and the role of the Federal Reserve System. Teams analyze economic and financial conditions and formulate a monetary policy recommendation, modeling the Federal Open Market Committee. The team, from Los Angeles, California, represented the San Francisco District and included Aarushi Maheshwari, Annika Chan, Atul Prasanth, Caitlyn Cox, Finn Karish, Eli Brooks (alternate), Kennedy Yang (alternate), Manasi Vartak (alternate), Ronojoy Borpujari (alternate), and Sahil Sudani (alternate). The team's advisers were Chris Surro and Ali Haider Ismail.

"I am very happy to congratulate the students who competed in this year's College Fed Challenge, especially the winners and finalists," said Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh. "They took on the same big questions we policymakers face. I'm impressed by their talent, their rigor, and their eagerness to think hard about monetary policy and the economy."

This year's College Fed Challenge included 141 schools from 34 states across the nation, the most in the competition's history. Teams submitted video presentations or participated in local competitions last month. Twenty-one semi-finalist teams then participated in question-and-answer sessions held earlier this month, and seven finalists were invited to the Federal Reserve Board for the national finals. The other national finalists were the University of Chicago in second place and the University of Maryland, College Park in third place. #2822. Junk bonds are 'flashing yellow.' Watch these warning signs

Cracks are forming in the junk bond market as investors demand higher payouts for owning the market's riskiest debt. It isn't time to ditch high-yield bonds, but investors should pay attention to the warning signs.

High-yield bonds now yield 8.1%, up from 7.22% a month ago. The increase reflects a jump in yields across the curve as investors bake in more inflation from high energy prices and other pressures, including concern about the deficit — hitting nearly $2 trillion in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30.

The high-yield market is also showing stress on the credit side with spreads recently widening to levels not seen since April, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Credit spreads are the difference in yield between the bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. Wider spreads mean investors are demanding higher yields for holding corporate debt, viewing it as riskier.

Spreads are at 315 basis points in the overall high-yield market, higher than a year ago but still below levels in March when they reached 346 bps. One basis point equals one one-hundredth of a percent, or 0.01%.

The high-yield market consists of bonds rated BB+ by S&P and Fitch and Ba1 and under by Moody's. The lowest-rated cohort, CCC and below, has seen the most movement with spreads climbing dramatically over the past year to roughly 1,250 bps.

Right now, the high-yield market is "flashing yellow" but is "far from red," said Michael Arone, chief investment strategist at State Street Investment Management.

It makes sense that investors are demanding more compensation for taking on additional credit risk as borrowing costs rise, he said.

Yields are elevated across the board with the 10-year Treasury reaching its highest level since 2002 earlier in the week.

"The bigger question is whether this is simply a repricing of interest rate risk, or the beginning of a more fundamental reassessment of credit quality," Arone said.

He's in a wait-and-see mode since earnings are still growing, interest-coverage ratios remain good, and while default rates have ticked up some, he believes it is not concerning.

That said, the starting point in spreads is likely weighing on investors' psyche, since they are still low by historical standards.

"There's a small margin of error here, which I also think raises the anxiety level," Arone explained. "The compensation that investors are receiving for taking on this credit risk isn't overwhelming relative to history, and therefore subtle changes in credit spreads can be concerning."

While there may be concerns about part of the lower-rated market, the overall high-yield market is in good fundamental shape.

In fact, credit quality is at a record high, with BB bonds making up over 60% of the market compared with 38% prior to the global financial crisis, said Kelley Gerrity, a fixed income strategist at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

"We've had higher-quality companies coming in, and with higher rates now, you also have more discipline from companies that are more indebted ... just because of the higher cost of capital, so that actually is creating a bit of a healthier picture as well," she said.

The lowest tier of high yield has always been more speculative, since the bonds have a higher default risk. Therefore, it's no surprise that they are the ones seeing the most widening in spreads, said Collin Martin, head of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research.

The overall move in high-yield spreads have been "orderly," he said. "Are there cracks forming? I think the cracks are logical cracks with the lowest-rated bonds and it's too early to say that it's spreading to the broad credit market."

In addition, fluctuations within the CCC-rated and lower spreads have been idiosyncratic, Gerrity added. Morgan Stanley recently broke down the spreads in the lowest cohort into two buckets: performing assets and non-performing assets, which are defined as spreads above 1,000 bps.

The non-performing spread to worst is 2,818 bps, while the performing bucket — the biggest piece of the CCC market — is 461 bps, she said.

"It is isolated," she said. "I'm not necessarily sure that that will go away anytime soon, but it doesn't tell the story of overall concern and flashing caution for credit markets right now."

For now, investors should remain selective within higher yield, Gerrity advised.

"We're looking for the best relative value opportunities, and we think that exists within that single-B cohort, and so we're leaning into that," she said.

Investors should be concerned if there is a steep widening in the broader high-yield market.

But there's scant evidence of stress in the BB cohort. Spreads in that group are at 194 bps, up from 179 bps a year ago — although the move hasn't been in a straight line.

"We're going to be focusing our attention on what are considered some stronger businesses," Martin said. "If we start to see the markets demand higher spreads there also, that's what we'll be looking at to see if risks are really rising."

It's also important to understand that the Federal Reserve is raising rates in a strong economic environment, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. The central bank is concerned about an inflation problem amid high fossil fuel prices due to the Iran war, while growth has been stronger than expected, he noted.

"With growth being good as the reason that the Fed is hiking, then you wouldn't expect high yield to blow out because growth means revenues stay up, means cash flow and profitability stays up," he explained.

High yield becomes a disaster when the economy is heading into a sharp economic downturn, Gallo said.

"That's when spreads really widen out," he said. "But a recession is not the odds-on bet. Now, talk to me in six months if the Fed keeps hiking over and over, if oil prices stay high for longer, well, then maybe we will start to wonder."

#2820. Ravens cut WR LaJohntay Wester after 2 muffed punts in Carolina

The Baltimore Ravens are waiving second-year wide receiver/returner LaJohntay Wester after two muffed punts in Sunday's loss to the Carolina Panthers, per Jeff Zrebiec of The Athletic.

Wester, 24, let his first punt return go into the end zone for a touchback on Sunday, but could not handle the second and third balls from Sam Martin, both in the second quarter. On the first, he signaled for a fair catch but never settled under the ball, instead attempting a diving grab and letting the ball fall through his arms. The Panthers took over at the Ravens' 23-yard line and scored a go-ahead touchdown two plays later.

The second was significantly worse. Wester had ample time and space to make a clean catch, but the ball ricocheted off his helmet and rolled toward Baltimore's end zone. Ravens cornerback Keyon Martin managed to corral it at the 1, forcing the offense to battle out of their own end zone with a minute left in the half instead of pushing for another score.

Wester did not play another snap for the rest of the game and could be seen on the sidelines being consoled by team chaplain Rev. Johnny Shelton. Carolina only punted one more time with Ravens safety Malaki Starks back to return. He let the ball roll to the 1, where it was downed by a Panther whose heel was on the goal line, resulting in a touchback.

This is a breaking story that will be updated with more information.

#2818. Quitting can actually be the key to success, says expert: It's one of the 'most courageous moves you can make'

Lindsay Crouse wants people to stop treating "quitter" like a bad word.

In fact, the former New York Times journalist believes that knowing when to quit is a crucial component to a successful, healthy life.

But Crouse didn't always feel that way. In her recent book "The Case for Quitting: The Surprising Benefits of Opting Out," published in September, Crouse shared that she used to push herself to the point of exhaustion at work and as a distance runner and marathoner.

"I'd achieved things I'd never dreamed were in reach, yet it didn't feel like enough. I was doing too much, and somehow it amounted to less than before," she wrote.

Now, Crouse wants to challenge the popular narrative around quitting. She spoke to psychologists, endurance athletes and fellow recovering workaholics about what they gained when they decided to let go.

"We're conditioned to see perseverance and quitting in these very binary ways," she tells CNBC Make It. "We think of people who never give up as people who succeed, and people who quit as people who fail."

But in Crouse's view, quitting can actually be a strategic move that allows us to focus on what's important.

"If we're going to succeed and do our very best, we need to learn to walk away," she says. "We need to learn to abandon paths that aren't working in order to find paths that might succeed."

When you're already struggling with something, "it's really natural to want to escalate your commitment to achieving your goal," Crouse says.

That could mean putting even more hours into a job that you know deep down isn't a good fit for you, or pushing yourself harder during marathon training because you're frustrated by an injury slowing you down.

But what many people don't realize is that investing more energy into a failing cause "actually only creates more failure," she says.

In those cases, doggedly persevering only "increases the amount that you lose, whether that's energy, whether it's money, whether it's time, or whether it's just your happiness," she says. "If you don't cut your losses, those losses are only going to grow."

To determine whether your approach to a task is becoming "a little unhealthy," Crouse recommends asking yourself these questions:

"How are you talking about achieving your goal? Are you getting more and more desperate? Are you constantly telling yourself that success is just one beat away, even as evidence might be telling you otherwise?"

If the answer is "yes" to the latter two questions, it might be a sign that you need to take a step back and reevaluate whether it makes sense to keep pushing — or whether it's time to pivot, Crouse says.

It can also be helpful to ask your friends whether they think you're on the right track, she says: "A lot of times, our friends will tell us the truth that we don't want to hear."

If you still feel like quitting is a sign of failure, Crouse recommends looking at it from a different angle.

Quitting is "one of the most courageous moves you can make," she says, because it "inherently involves risk, and being brave enough to do it means that you have confidence that you can look at something uncertain, take it on and make it work out."

#2816. NBA Cup 2026 Update: Standings, clinching scenarios, with critical Cup games on NBC and Peacock Tuesday

This is the deciding week for the NBA Cup group stage.

Games on Tuesday (on NBC and Peacock), Wednesday (on ESPN), and Friday (on Prime) will determine the six group-stage winners and two wild cards that will advance to the knockout rounds. The two Tuesday night games on NBC and Peacock — Boston at Washington at 8 p.m. ET, then Dallas at Denver at 10 p.m. — are both critical games in their groups.

Let's break down the group standings, with a reminder that the winner of each group advances, plus one wildcard from each conference, and after head-to-head, the next tiebreaker is point differential — it can be good to run up the score.

1. Dallas (2-0, +17 point differential) 2. Denver (2-0, +16) 3. Phoenix (1-1, +3) 4. Houston (1-2, -7) 5. Utah (0-3, -29)

Analysis: Denver hosts Dallas Tuesday night in a game that will essentially decide this group, and you can watch it at 10 p.m. ET on NBC and stream it on Peacock. If Denver wins, they are in as the Group A winners. If Dallas picks up the victory, it still needs Phoenix to lose to Houston Wednesday night, or Dallas can beat Phoenix on Friday, but either way Dallas very likely would advance.

1. Minnesota (2-0, +32) 2. Oklahoma City (2-1, +36) 3. Memphis (1-1, 0) 4. LA Clippers (1-1, -25) 5. New Orleans (0-3, -43)

Analysis: Minnesota travels to Oklahoma City on Wednesday night in the key game for this group. If Minnesota wins, it is in the driver's seat but still needs a Memphis loss in its last two games to clinch the group (and the Grizzlies are now without Cameron Boozer for a month). The Thunder lost to the Clippers in group play, so OKC still needs LA to lose another game to secure the division even if they beat Minnesota.

1. San Antonio (2-0, +53) 2. Los Angeles Lakers (2-1, -9) 3. Portland (1-1, +7) 4. Golden State (1-1, -21) 5. Sacramento (0-3, -30)

Analysis: Los Angeles at San Antonio Friday night is an epic early-season clash between the two top teams in Group C and the top two teams in this week's NBC Sports NBA Power Rankings. San Antonio also plays Portland on Wednesday in a game with key implications for the group.

1. Orlando (3-0, +17) 2. Toronto (2-1, +10) 3. Detroit (1-1, +13) 4. Brooklyn (0-2, -18) 5. Milwaukee (0-2, -22)

Analysis: Orlando hosts Detroit on Tuesday night and if the Magic win then they win the group. If the Pistons win on Tuesday, the door is thrown wide open, and things get complicated between Detroit, Toronto and Orlando (the Nets and Bucks are not going to advance).

1. Miami (2-0, +32) 2. Cleveland (2-1, +21) 3. Philadelphia (1-1, -19) 4. Indiana (1-2, -27) 5. New York (0-2, -7)

Analysis: We will not have a repeat NBA Cup champion as the Knicks are all but officially eliminated. For Miami, it's simple: Beat Philadelphia Wednesday and they win the group. If the 76ers win, they would take the group with a win over struggling Indiana on Friday.

1. Boston (2-0, +53) 2. Atlanta (2-1, +21) 3. Washington (2-1, +13) 4. Chicago (1-2, -18) 5. Charlotte (0-3, -69)

Analysis: If Boston can beat Washington Tuesday night in a game you can watch on NBC and Peacock (8 p.m. ET), they will be in the driver's seat heading into Friday's game against Atlanta. If the Wizards win we get chaos, because Washington lost to Atlanta, giving the Hawks the head-to-head tiebreaker.

One thing that has remained steady over the four years of the NBA Cup is the format. The only real change this season is that the NBA Cup semifinals will take place on a team's home court (the higher East and West seed remaining), and the NBA Cup Final will be played at the Hinkle Fieldhouse in Indianapolis, home to the Butler Bulldogs — and the place where the real-life game the movie "Hoosiers" was based on was played.

All 30 teams were drawn into one of six groups (five teams in each group, three East groups and three West groups). Each team plays the other teams in its group once — four games total — and those games count double as both regular season games and NBA Cup games.

The six group winners plus a wild card from each conference — determined by record and point differential — go into an eight-team knockout round bracket (East vs. East, West vs. West). The knockout round games are single-elimination.

The Final two teams, one East and one West, will head to Indianapolis for the Dec. 11 championship game.

NBA Cup games are played on specially designed courts with the home team wearing their Statement Edition uniforms.

Money. And make no mistake, that is the biggest motivation. Players talk openly about it. How much money? Here's the breakdown:

Player on championship team: $604,985 Player on runner-up: $241,994 Player on semifinals losing team: $120,997 Player on quarterfinal losing team: $60,499

While even the championship money is comparable to another game check for a star like Giannis Antetokounmpo or Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, it can be a meaningful bump for players on minimum salaries at the end of the bench. The stars realize who they are playing for when things get serious. The winning team gets a trophy, and teams will hang a banner. Even the Knicks. Eventually.

The New York Knicks, behind stellar play from NBA Cup MVP Jalen Brunson, knocked off Victor Wembanyama and the San Antonio Spurs — a Cup Final loss that would be echoed come June and the NBA Finals.

In 2024, Milwaukee bounced back from an ugly 2-8 start to the season, found its footing in NBA Cup games, and went on a run behind Giannis Antetokounmpo, reaching the Cup Finals against Oklahoma City. Once there, Antetokounmpo had a 26-point triple-double, completely controlling the game on both sides of the ball. LeBron James and the Los Angeles Lakers won the inaugural 2023 NBA In-Season Tournament (before it was officially branded as the NBA Cup).

The NBA is moving the NBA Cup Final to Indianapolis's iconic Hinkle Fieldhouse, the home of Butler University.

Famously, Hinkle Fieldhouse hosted the 1954 Indiana high school state championship game that inspired the 1986 movie "Hoosiers," and climactic scenes from the film were shot there.

San Francisco 49ers' Christian McCaffrey #23 is congratulated by Vederian Lowe #76 after scoring a touchdown Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026, in Mexico City, Mexico. Getty Images

San Francisco 49ers offensive tackle Colton McKivitz (68) goes down with an injury during the first half of an NFL football game in Mexico City, Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026. (AP Photo/Eduardo Verdugo) AP Photo/Eduardo Verdugo

Lowe has big shoes to fill and has another difficult matchup on Sunday against the Seattle Seahawks, who are coming off a bye and would love revenge after losing to the 49ers on their home field Oct. 11.

#2808. Bucks vs. Raptors Player Grades: Herro and Turner lead the way in slide-ending victory

After losing 13 consecutive games, the Milwaukee Bucks finally tasted victory, defeating the Toronto Raptors 116-111 in a nail-biter. The Bucks had been building toward this—having deserved to beat the 76ers in their last game—and finally put it all together in The Six. Most encouragingly, Milwaukee got key contributions from a struggling veteran in Myles Turner, while both rookies played very well and closed the game. Hopefully this carries into the rest of the season, and the Bucks can stack more wins. Read our full summary of the game here and catch a six-minute audio recap on the Bucks+ podcast, Bucks In Six Minutes, below.

37 minutes, 32 points, 6 rebounds, 8 assists, 1 steal, 1 block, 3 turnovers, 10/16 FG, 4/5 3P, 8/8 FT, +10

What a funny game for Herro, who scored just three points on 1/5 shooting in the first half (granted, he did have four assists), and then 29 in the second half on 9/11 from the field and 8/8 from the charity stripe. Herro mentioned this in his postgame interview, but aside from some nonchalant moments dribbling the ball up the court, I didn't think he played badly in the first half; the Raptors gave him a lot of attention, and so he gave the ball up early. Then in the second half, the vet got more opportunities and found a rhythm, especially at the free-throw line. Herro's composure throughout the second half, to shepherd the young Bucks to victory, was great to watch.

22 minutes, 6 points, 3 assists, 1 block, 3 turnovers, 3/8 FG, 0/2 3P, -16

I don't know what others thought, but it almost felt like Rollins looked a little small out there against the likes of Shead and Walter. He just struggled to make much of an impact on either side of the ball.

32 minutes, 18 points, 5 rebounds, 3 assists, 0 turnovers, 8/15 FG, 2/3 3P, +4

Aside from his customary contested three with 18 on the shot clock, Kuzma was pretty damn solid. He was Scottie Barnes' primary defender, and although Barnes made a bunch of shots over him, most felt well contested. Kuzma's two-to-three-point ratio was much better in this one too; 2-4 attempts per game seems like a much better balance than 6-8. I also love that he didn't turn it over.

24 minutes, 3 points, 4 rebounds, 2 assists, 1/7 FG, 1/5 3P, -4

Again, zero impact from Jaquez. When he starts alongside Kuzma, one of them will get open threes; you can't go 1/5.

28 minutes, 27 points, 11 rebounds, 2 blocks, 4 turnovers, 6 PF, 9/12 FG, 5/6 3P, 4/5 FT, -12

What a game from Turner—best of the season by a long way. When he looks for his shot the way he did last night, the Bucks look so much more lethal, and so does he; Turner had 11 points in the first quarter. Turner made two huge plays down the stretch, and the emotion he showed after both of them was great to see. Also, a solid second audition for the Raptors' front office, just quietly, after Turner bungled the first one. I know you liked what you saw, Bobby Webster.

23 minutes, 9 points, 3 rebounds, 3 blocks, 0 turnovers, 4/6 FG, 1/2 3P, +22

Despite his modest stat line, I thought Ware was great. One triple and three lobs; I love how he's been rolling with purpose and intent lately. How he caught that lob from Ament is beyond me; ridiculous athlete. That said, the most impressive part of Ware's game to me was his defence; for all the (fair) criticism you can level at him, his timing blocking shots is easily one of his best features. Figuring it out.

29 minutes, 14 points, 10 rebounds, 4 assists, 3 steals, 4 turnovers, 4/7 FG, 1/2 3P, 5/6 FT, +20

Impact. Impact. Impact. Burries made four shots and was still easily one of the best players. His poise down the stretch on both ends was amazing. That smooth crossover to get to the cup in crunch time wasn't even his best late play; his steal/wrench on Barnes took that spot. I don't know if I've ever seen a play like that; it reminded me of a former Buck who used to make those sorts of plays late in games… The kid's a maniac in the best way possible.

25 minutes, 7 points, 4 rebounds, 1 assist, 1 block, 1 turnover, 2/5 FG, 3/4 FT, +7

Ament's immense impact in this game will not show up on the stat sheet, and that may be the most pleasing part. I've wanted to feel his impact more and more, and this game felt like his best yet at impacting winning at a high level regardless of his stats. The main part of that was how well he guarded Scottie Barnes. Ament moved with him in space and forced tough shots; he was so good at it that Jenkins closed with him because they needed the length and foot speed he provided to win the game. Also, the Raptors tried to hide their worst defender, Jamison Battle, on Ament, which meant he had to play as a screener to get Battle into the action. I liked the rookie's ability to play out of those actions; he missed Ware on a lob once out of the short roll, but that will serve him well in the long run. Finally, just filing the play where Ament came hard off the Ware screen and threw the lob over Poeltl; I'm not sure he has had a play like that this season. If the rook can add that string to his bow…

I'll get the negative out of the way first: I still don't love starting Juquez and Kuzma, and the stats back that up—starters had a -32.8 net rating in 13 minutes. Other than that, Jenkins pressed many of the right buttons; the call to close with Ament was gutsy, and it paid off in spades. I also thought his overall game management was solid. Going at Poeltl relentlessly allowed 1) the Bucks to get in the bonus early in the fourth, which allowed them to keep the scoreboard ticking over as they went on that field-goal drought, and 2) to foul Poeltl out and thus open up the rim to score with no shot blocker present. Called some well-timed timeouts too when the team was frazzled trying to nurse the lead.

Limited Minutes: Caris LeVert, Kasparas Jakucionis, AJ Green, Gary Trent Jr.

Inactive: Pete Nance, Cormac Ryan, Kam Jones, Bogoljub Markovic

The Bucks could have played much better in many areas, yet they still won. I swear, this team can compete with more teams than people think.

Postgame, Jenkins praised the group's ability to stick to it, saying that eventually, the breakthrough would happen, and it happened.

Myles Turner reached 10,000 career points last night. His reaction: "Man, there are really no words for it. It's a testament to a lot of hard work and a lot of patience… There's no question that I've been struggling a little bit to start the season, but to have a breakthrough like tonight was really big for my confidence and just a reminder of who I am in this league."

The Bucks avoid "beating" the franchise-record 15 consecutive losses. I'm sure it would have felt good for the players to get that monkey off their backs.

The Bucks had 11 first-half turnovers (and 17 overall). I couldn't find the Raptors' points off turnovers in the first half, but they beat the Bucks 15-6 in fast break points for the game. Of course, that would have been 15-10 if Milwaukee converted on either of those easy opportunities in the fourth.

Tyler Herro's averages over the last two games: 41 PPG, 8.5 RPG, and 7.5 APG shooting 64% from the field, 65% from three, and 100% from the free throw line.

The Bucks beat the Raptors 52-44 in the paint battle.

Jenkins cut his rotation to about eight guys after previously using nine or 10.

I do want to recognise how valuable those end-of-game reps will be for Ament and Burries. You can train for those situations all you want, but nothing can replicate the real thing.

In the fourth, the Bucks had a stretch where they had all three of Kuzma, Jaquez, and Ament in the game.
