#2804. Top Wall Street analysts prefer these 3 dividend stocks for stable income

Uncertainty in the Middle East, elevated Treasury yields and fears about an AI bubble continue to keep global markets on edge. Given this volatile backdrop, investors seeking stable income can consider enhancing their portfolios by adding dividend-paying stocks.

However, the vast universe of dividend stocks can make selection challenging. Tracking the ratings of top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend stocks, as their recommendations are backed by in-depth research.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Chord Energy is an independent exploration and production company with long-lived assets primarily in the Williston Basin. With a quarterly base dividend of $1.30 per share, CHRD offers a dividend yield of 3.67%.

In a research note on third-quarter expectations, RBC Capital analyst Scott Hanold reiterated a buy rating on CHRD stock with a price target of $175. "We model production near the top of guidance and continue to see strong performance from new wells and base production," said Hanold.

Specifically, the five-star analyst expects Q3 2026 production at 283 thousand barrels of oil equivalent per day, or Mboe/d, in line with the Street's consensus and near the high end of the 278 to 284 Mboe/d guidance. Hanold said his Q3 2026 earnings per share estimate increased to $5.29 due to lower non-cash depreciation, depletion and amortization.

Meanwhile, cash flow per share estimate moved lower to $13.59 to reflect Hanold's update based on the current backdrop and commodity mark-to-market. He expects Chord Energy to report capital spending of $375 million for Q3 2026, slightly above the Street's estimate of $369 million.

Overall, Hanold remains bullish on CHRD, given its best-in-class balance sheet. He expects a free cash flow payout of 80% in the third quarter, with the possibility of an upside. Hanold expects investors to focus on management commentary on 2027 capital plans, Williston M&A opportunities, and long-term performance of 4-mile wells.

Hanold ranks No. 310 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of 14.9%. See Chord Energy KPIs on TipRanks.

Williams, an energy infrastructure company that delivers natural gas, is the next dividend pick. The company recently completed the $5.5 billion acquisition of Momentum Midstream, which will expand its natural gas infrastructure in the Haynesville to meet growing Gulf Coast LNG, power and industrial demand. At a quarterly dividend of $0.5250 per share, Williams offers a yield of 2.89%.

In her latest research note, RBC Capital analyst Elvira Scotto reiterated a buy rating on Williams stock with a price target of $87. Ahead of Q3 2026 earnings, the analyst said that she expects WMB to announce strong quarterly performance.

Scotto raised her estimates to reflect insights from the quarterly catch-up call, the completion of the Momentum Midstream acquisition, and mark-to-market quarter-to-date commodity prices. She expects WMB to report Q3 2026 adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of $2,036 million, which is modestly above the Street's consensus estimate.

Furthermore, Scotto expects Williams' Transmission, Power & Gulf segment to increase quarter-over-quarter, driven by the startup of the Socrates power project and favorable natural gas liquids, or NGL, margins.

Scotto noted that WMB stock has underperformed due to backlash related to data centers and investor anticipation of another Power Innovation project. She expects the company to announce at least one more project before the end of this year, potentially with a new customer and a contract duration of 15 to 20 years, which would be a positive catalyst for the stock.

Scotto ranks No. 175 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been profitable 67% of the time, delivering an average return of 16.2%. See Williams Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

EOG Resources, a crude oil and natural gas exploration and production company, will hold its third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 6. At a quarterly dividend of $1.02 per share, EOG offers a dividend yield of 2.75%.

Heading into Q3 earnings, Jefferies analyst Lloyd Byrne reiterated a buy rating on EOG Resources stock and increased his price target to $185 from $175. The analyst expects the company's Q3 cash flow per share to exceed the Street's consensus by 13%, driven by better-than-expected production.

Byrne expects crude oil production, excluding the UAE, to reach 551 Mboe/d, which is at the high end of guidance (546-551 Mboe/d) and above the Street's projection of 548 Mboe/d, driven by continued growth in the Utica.

Furthermore, Byrne expects cash operating expenses to come in at $10.27 per barrel of oil equivalent, below the midpoint of guidance of $10.05 to $11.35, helped by lower lease operating expenses. Overall, the analyst expects EOG to deliver free cash flow of $2.65 billion, supporting another quarter of buybacks near the minimum 70% shareholder return threshold and implying about $1.5 billion in share repurchases.

"As a first indication of the '27 plan, we expect EOG will message another year of mid-single-digit (~3.5%) growth on a flat capital budget (~$6.55bn), which is above the Street modeling 1% oil growth at $6.6bn," said Byrne.

Byrne ranks No. 303 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 58% of the time, delivering an average return of 18.5%. See EOG Resources Statistics on TipRanks.

#2799. Game Preview: Knicks vs. Cavaliers, November 25, 2026

Writing a preview for a Cleveland Cavaliers game can be an interesting task these days. Not because the upcoming Knicks-Cavs matchup on Wednesday is another NBA Cup game (sorry, Mr. Silver), but rather because it can get a bit dicey with your deadline. After meandering through stats and stories, recaps and rosters, you inevitably stumble upon some post on social media. Just a short video clip of a guy with an extensive beard not trying to play defense. As is common with train wrecks, you can't look away and click on it. Oh, the algorithm shows you another one?! Bang! One more, maybe?? You try to restrain your hand, but it still clicks on it. It could go on like that forever.

Watching James Harden play something that supposedly passes for NBA defense in 2026 from afar is almost like a guilty pleasure. Only for a moment, of course, until you realize that you're seeing one of the great scorers of this generation making a mockery of the game you dearly love. Then you breathe a sigh of relief that he isn't on your team, even if you've seen him score 51 points the other night against the Indiana Pacers. But it's all right; his own coach seems to be more than happy with the bearded fellow:

Analytically, he may be, but Lil' Coach K still seems a bit delusional here. Better said, he seems to have skipped the last few sessions of media training. You can't say stuff like that and then watch Harden in a game getting blown by like he is Andrea Bargnani after too many glasses of limoncello. Yes, he might, just might, be a top-ten scorer of all time (I certainly think he isn't), but you have to point that out specifically. By phrasing it the way he did, he opens himself up to major criticism, which is exactly what you don't need when your basketball team is in a funk. Or when some of your own players see what we're seeing.

If you want to know why things aren't really clicking for the Cleveland Cavaliers (9-9), you only have to connect the dots between these two clips. Your coach is praising one of your big-name players as if he is the second coming of Julius Erving, and then your big offseason acquisition is saying that the effort of said star player, among other things, is the reason why your team can't play a lick of defense. Now, he didn't say the name James Harden out loud, but you don't need the guys from "Mindhunter" to know where Watson is going here. He might just as well be talking about Donovan Mitchell, who is nowhere to be found as a leader these days. Either way, the Cavs are in a world of trouble.

You could argue they were before the last game against the Knicks, too, a contest they won and that figured to get them going a little bit. But in the six games since, it has been more of the inconsistent same for Cleveland. Missing Evan Mobley with a toe injury has been a major problem for their defense, as they now start three subpar defenders in Harden, Mitchell, and sharpshooter Sam Merrill. Their point-of-attack D has been nonexistent and looks even worse without Mobley behind it to at least erase a few mistakes by the matadors on the perimeter. Peyton Watson is working as hard as he can on that end (1.8 blocks per game as a wing), but ultimately, it's not enough.

It can't be that bad, can it? Well, without Mobley in their last six games, the Cavs have been 26th in defensive rating in the NBA. In their most recent outing, they allowed 45 second-quarter points to a Chicago Bulls team playing without Caleb Wilson and Norman Powell. If that wasn't embarrassing enough, they topped it off by giving up 63 points to the Windy City's bench mob, a group highlighted by the infamous star power of Jordan Hawkins, Noa Essengue, and Jaylin Sellers—no offense, in more ways than one.

There is a reason, of course, why the Cavs are still at .500, even if they'd make Tom Thibodeau rip out his last Homer Simpson hairs if he had to watch them play defense every night. That reason is their offense, their firepower. Cleveland has a top-five scoring group in the entire NBA; they've got two guys who can explode for half a hundred on any given night and plenty of role players who know how to put the ball in the basket, as the Knicks saw in their last meeting. If the Cavs win, they do it by outscoring teams, mostly in the half-court (Cleveland and New York are the two slowest teams in terms of pace right now), and by letting their individual talent create favorable situations. That can be enough on a lot of nights in the NBA regular season; it sure doesn't look like a recipe tasty enough for a team that went to the conference finals last year and would love to go a step further this time around.

New York isn't sure yet about the status of the wounded OG Anunoby, Deuce McBride, and Jordan Clarkson, which might be a problem in a game where you will need to score some points to keep up. We also know that big stars want to perform on the big MSG stage, so there is that. In the end, though, I'd say the Knicks will surely feel they owe Cleveland one after that last home defeat. Maybe they can even manage to get into one of those clips with the bearded guy. Who knows?

Who: Cleveland Cavaliers (9-9) at New York Knicks (11-6)Date: Wednesday, November 25, 2026Time: 7:30 PM ETPlace: Madison Square Garden, New York, NYTV: MSG, DAZN, NBA TVFollow: @ptknicksblog and bsky

#2797. Fed's John Williams indicates higher interest rates likely 'over time' to address inflation

New York Federal Reserve President John Williams said Monday that policymakers have more work to do to bring inflation under control, though he indicated that further action can unfold over time as the economy continues to grow.

In remarks consistent with previous statements, the influential central banker expressed confidence that inflation will get closer to the Fed's 2% target in 2027 before hitting the goal the following year. He also said that while artificial intelligence is pressuring prices, there's "little evidence" it will be the source of more persistent inflation.

"But getting inflation back to 2% is 100% essential," he said in remarks at the University of Mount Saint Vincent in New York. "We must take actions over time that will ensure that we get inflation back to our 2% goal in a timely manner and on a sustained basis. There is still work to do to get that done."

The comments come at a delicate moment for monetary policy, as the economy continues to grow and inflation stays well above the Fed's goal.

Fed officials have differed over how quickly to raise rates, with some advocating more aggressive action while others, including Williams, have emphasized a measured approach.

Williams ascribed the current inflation pressures to the conflict in Iran, demand for goods associated with the AI build-out and tariffs, the effects of which he said "have largely abated" as a source of pressure. Nevertheless, he expressed confidence that inflation will subside substantially in 2027 even as economic growth remains robust and unemployment edges lower.

The Federal Open Market Committee next meets on Dec. 8-9, with markets fully pricing in a quarter percentage point interest rate increase from the current target range of 3.75%-4%. The remarks from Williams are expected to be the last major policy statement from any Fed official before the December decision.

"Monetary policy cannot move ships or reopen pipelines and refineries, but it can — and must — ensure that these shocks do not lead to broader or persistent inflationary dynamics or erode well-anchored inflation expectations," Williams said, according to his prepared remarks.

Williams did not explicitly address the December meeting expectations, instead pointing to the statement released after the prior FOMC meeting in late October that said the "accumulation of more information" will help decide the future policy path.

"The data that we have received since then show that the economy has remained strong and that inflation has continued to run too high," he said.

#2795. Commanders, Giants and Cowboys – this team will win the NFC East

The NFC East is one of the NFL's wilder divisions. Every team has had a wild ride this season and dealt with monumental momentum shifts.

The New York Giants lead the division at 6-3-1 and have started three different quarterbacks. The Dallas Cowboys are 5-6, but their defense has been horrible all year. It got really interesting after the Washington Commanders' Monday Night Football victory, which moved their record to 4-5-1. The Philadelphia Eagles are 3-7 and have been plagued by injuries all year.

Who will win this historic division? Here's who will come out on top once this regular season is over.

MORE: NFC power rankings Week 12 spotlight Bears-Lions as NFC North Thanksgiving headliner

Nov 1, 2026; Arlington, Texas, USA; Dallas Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott (4) takes the field before the game between the Cowboys and the Arizona Cardinals at AT&T Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Jerome Miron-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)

The Dallas Cowboys have an elite offense, and that will carry them to a Division title. They're ranked 3rd in the NFL, averaging 30.6 points per game. Dak Prescott is the best QB in the NFC East. He has CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens, both elite wideouts. I trust Prescott more than any other QB in the Division because the other teams have too much uncertainty.

Jerry Jones' squad has a very leaky defense, and it is their biggest weakness. They're allowing 28.4 PPG, ranking 28th in the league. I think they're offence will overcome their defense.

It can be tough to put faith in this Cowboys roster but they're the best team in this Division and will get some clutch wins along the way.

The New York Giants' quarterback situation is too shaky to trust, and you never know when Cam Skattebo will have a back-breaking fumble. They do currently lead the NFC East, but I'm putting no faith in J.J. McCarthy.

Jayden Daniels looked good for the Commanders in their MNF win over the Cincinnati Bengals, but his health/elbow is always a concern. There's no reason to trust Dan Quinn's time management or decision-making either. They do have the easiest strength of schedule in the Division.

Eagles fans did get to see their squad beat Aaron Rodgers and the Pittsburgh Steelers in Week 11. It would be popsterous to trust Joe Milton as their QB1, and Philly seems to get a new injury every week. This could be the last year we see Jalen Hurts, Nick Sirianni, and Saquon Barkley on the Eagles roster.

#2794. NFL Week 12 Injury Report: Drake Maye's updated timeline, Dalton Kincaid returns to practice, and more

Staying up to date on NFL injury news is of the utmost importance for fantasy football success. The article below tracks all fantasy-relevant players currently listed on their team's injury report and provides fantasy managers with actionable recommendations as new information rolls in.

Check back for updates from Tuesday through Saturday.

**UPDATED AS OF TUESDAY, NOVEMBER 24 AT 4 PM ET**

Kincaid missed Week 11 with multiple ailments but returned to a limited session Tuesday.

Impact: Kincaid's absence against the Dolphins could have been a ploy to get him healthy for the marquee matchup against the Chiefs on Thanksgiving. Fantasy managers will want to confirm his level of participation Wednesday, but we tentatively expect the veteran tight end to return in Week 12. Consider Kincaid a legitimate TE1, if active.

Palmer managed only seven offensive snaps in Week 8 before departing with an aggravation of the hamstring injury he has battled since Week 4. He was placed on injured reserve.

Impact: Not much, honestly. Palmer has played sparingly this season in a situational role, although his absence could leave room for Skyler Bell to be active for the third time this season. The Bills also activated Tyrell Shavers (knee) from the reserve/physically unable to perform list. He could join the wide receiver rotation but does not need to be rostered in 12-team leagues.

Achane suffered a torn ACL in the team's Week 3 loss to the Chiefs, ending his season.

Impact: Achane's unfortunate season-ending injury creates opportunity for Ollie Gordon and Jaylen Wright. The timing of the injury makes it likely that Achane is able to fully recover before the start of the 2027 regular season.

The Dolphins placed Willis on injured reserve in Week 10. He will be eligible to return in Week 14, but Willis is seeking a second opinion after the injury progressed into his abdomen. Season-ending surgery is possible, although the team has yet to decide if or when surgery would take place.

Impact: Kyle McCord's installation as the team's starter hurts all involved. Until we see how McCord fares in this system, only Ollie Gordon is a safe FLEX starter.

Maye will reportedly be sidelined for at least six weeks, giving him the slimmest of chances to return for a playoff run, should the team make it.Impact: The team is reportedly reaching out to quarterbacks as they look to right a sinking ship following consecutive losses for the first time in head coach Mike Vrabel's tenure, although they also said Monday that Tommy DeVito is their starter. More to come on this developing story. Suffice to say, the fantasy value of the primary skill position players in New England takes a significant hit for as long as Maye remains sidelined.

Doubs was placed on injured reserve following a shoulder injury sustained in Week 6. He will miss the next four games, at minimum.

Impact: The Patriots have now played only 33 offensive snaps with both Doubs and A.J. Brown on the field together this season after Doubs was injured on his second offensive snap in Week 6. Brown returned from injured reserve in Week 6 and should have the runway to return WR1 numbers while Doubs remains sidelined.

Brown missed Week 8 and Week 9 with ankle and knee issues before returning for Week 10 against the Lions, only to pick up a hamstring injury. He is expected to miss multiple weeks with his most recent ailment.

Impact: DeMario Douglas, Kyle Williams, Mack Hollins, and Kyle Williams led the team in snaps and routes in the absence of Brown in Week 9, with none of the bunch consistent fantasy producers. Fantasy managers are likely forced to wait until more information is released to gauge Brown's expected status in Week 12.

Henderson was placed on injured reserve ahead of Week 10 and will miss the next four games, at minimum.

Impact: Rhamondre Stevenson and Corey Kiner are likely to form a one-two punch in the absence of Henderson, with Stevenson the favorite to lead the team in opportunities and snaps. Stevenson can be viewed as a volume-backed RB2 for the time being.

Cooper aggravated the same ankle injury he has been dealing with for multiple weeks in Week 10. The rookie receiver missed Week 11 and his status for Week 12 appears to be in doubt.

Impact: Target volume would likely concentrate further on Garrett Wilson and Adonai Mitchell should Cooper be unable to play in Week 12. Isaiah Williams (ribs) is also hurt and did not play in Week 11. Rookie tight end Kenyon Sadiq could find his way into an increased role out of the slate considering the absence of both slot options.

Jackson returned from an ankle injury in Week 8 and made it all of one offensive snap before suffering a thumb injury that is likely to sideline him for the remainder of the regular season.

Impact: Jackson's absence is the biggest hit to the fantasy value of alpha receiver Zay Flowers, who falls to a mid-range WR2 in rest of season rankings. Recent signee Jacoby Brissett is expected to start under center in Week 10.

Huntley suffered a season-ending turf toe injury in the team's Week 8 loss to the Bills.

Smythe suffered a torn Achilles in the team's Week 4 win over the Titans. His season is done.

Impact: It was Matt Hibner who saw the largest increase in snaps following Smythe's departure in Week 4, making it unlikely we see veteran Mark Andrews in a more robust role.

Lane suffered a dislocated ankle and fracture in Week 4 and is likely done for the season.

Impact: Minimal. Lane was primarily a special teams contributor.

McNichols suffered a foot injury in Week 8 and was placed on injured reserve in Week 9.

Impact: Rachaad White and veteran Austin Ekeler are suddenly the only two healthy backs on the Washington roster, neither of whom is an overly exciting fantasy option on a struggling offense. White is the preferred option and could be started as a viable FLEX, should McNichols miss time.

Kmet suffered a season-ending knee injury in the team's Thursday Night Football win over the Patriots.

Impact: Expect Sam Roush to serve as the team's TE2 for the remainder of the season, while second-year tight end Colston Loveland should continue his recent ascension back into TE1 territory.

Pacheco was placed on injured reserve to start the season. General Manager Brad Holmes said he "hopes Pacheco returns this season."

Impact: Well, that doesn't sound great. There appears to be something more insidious going on with Pacheco's back than initially thought. Lions coach Dan Campbell said running backs Jacob Saylors and Sione Vaki could split touches behind Jahmyr Gibbs. Saylors appears to be the first player up. Gibbs handled an absurd 34 opportunities, of 37 total running back opportunities, in the team's Week 1, overtime win over the Saints

Jacobs suffered a fractured finger in the team's Week 9 win over the Patriots. He will miss two-to-three weeks after undergoing surgery. He is listed as questionable for Week 12 against the Rams.

Impact: Kaleb Johnson is reportedly the first in line for lead back duties in his absence. Jacobs would be a viable Flex, should he return for Week 12.

Reed suffered a scary-looking neck injury that required stabilization in the team's Week 2 win over the Jets. Packers head coach Matt LaFleur said on Tuesday that it is "way too early" to determine whether Reed will play again in 2026. That said, he was not placed on injured reserve ahead of their Week 3 contest. He will reportedly undergo surgery.

Impact: Beyond the football implications, it is good to hear Reed avoided any life-altering injuries in Week 2. Skyy Moore and Bo Melton are likely to soak up additional snaps, although volume is most likely to concentrate on Christian Watson, Matthew Golden, and Tucker Kraft.

Impact: Murray can be dropped. Carson Wentz (ankle) is also ailing.

Addison will undergo surgery to address a thumb injury sustained in practice and will miss multiple weeks, although he avoided injured reserve. Head coach Kevin O'Connell said Monday that he doesn't expect Addison to play in Week 12.

Impact: Tai Felton will serve as the starting wide receiver opposite Justin Jefferson for as long as Addison remains sidelined.

Robinson was placed on injured reserve on Saturday.

Impact: In a shocking development, Robinson went from limited showings in practice with a questionable designation for Week 9 to injured reserve, with the potential that the veteran backup aggravated his ailment sometime during practice to end the week. He will miss the next four games, at minimum. Khalil Herbert should continue as the top change-of-pace option behind Bijan Robinson, the former of whom is not fantasy-viable.

Branch was ruled out for Week 9 against the Bengals early in the week. He remains sidelined in Week 10.

Impact: Drake London, Bijan Robinson and Kyle Pitts should continue dominating targets.

Brooks aggravated the groin injury that forced him to miss the end of camp. The Panthers placed him on injured reserve in Week 3. The Panthers designated him to return in Week 10. Head coach Dave Canales said Monday that it is "difficult" to find room for Brooks on the active roster, meaning the team could allow his 21-day practice window to expire, losing him for the remainder of the season.

Impact: Chuba Hubbard remains in the volume-driven RB1 tier. Brooks is a moderately worthwhile stash.

McMillan suffered a sprained PCL in his first game action of the season in Week 3. The team placed him on injured reserve Monday, with an expected absence of 6-8 weeks.

Impact: Not much change considering he made his season debut in Week 3, although rookie Ted Hurst should remain in the starting lineup.

The team placed Love on injured reserve after yet another ankle injury sustained in Week 8.

Impact: Bam Knight (concussion) resumed practicing in Week 10. Tyler Allgeier likely returns to a receiving/rotational rushing role.

Brooks had emergency surgery on his wrist and will miss the remainder of the regular season.

Impact: The team signed veteran Zay Jones Tuesday in an associated move. Expect volume to continue to remain heavily concentrated on Michael Wilson and Trey McBride. Elijah Higgins is notable for DFS purposes.

Minshew is feared to have torn his UCL in the team's Week 9 loss to the Seahawks.

Impact: Minshew appears likely to be placed on injured reserve in the coming days, leaving rookie Carson Beck to start under center for the remainder of the season.

Wilson suffered a neck injury in Week 9 that will end his 2026 season.

Impact: The Cardinals are now without their starting quarterback, second-string quarterback, alpha wide receiver, secondary and tertiary wide receiver, and starting running back as they head into the second half of a lost season. Trey McBride should soak up all the volume he can handle, with that volume now coming from rookie Carson Beck.

Beck was ruled out for Week 11 Saturday with a back injury.

Impact: Veteran journeyman Josh Johnson will draw the start for the Cardinals after being added to the team less than two weeks. It's a significant downgrade to all primary skill position players in Arizona.

Ferguson appeared to be on track to be activated from injured reserve after logging a full practice to end the week, but was ruled out for Week 9 with a new hamstring injury. He will miss multiple games.

Impact: Fantasy managers will have to continue to wait for the return of Ferguson.

Impact: The Rams will employ run-heavy game plans in the coming weeks.

Nacua suffered PCL and MCL sprains, plus a turf toe injury, on the final play from scrimmage in the team's Week 9 win over the Commanders. Nacua was placed on injured reserve Friday.

Kirk was limited on Wednesday. He was ruled out for Week 9 on Friday and placed on injured reserve on Saturday.

Stribling suffered an ankle injury in the team's Week 1 win over the Rams. The 49ers placed him on injured reserve in Week 2 after he underwent surgery to repair a deltoid ligament tear. He is expected to return in 10 weeks. Stribling worked with trainers, for the first time, off to the side early in Week 11.

Impact: The Athletic's Matt Barrows believes Demarcus Robinson will be the primary beneficiary.George

Pearsall was placed on season-ending injured reserve.

Impact: Pearsall will miss the entirety of the 2026 season.

Darnold returned to the practice field Monday but head coach Mike Macdonald would not comment on whether he would start in Week 12.

Impact: Fantasy managers will want to track his status throughout the week ahead of a divisional tilt against the 49ers.

Holani is week-to-week with an MCL sprain as of Week 11.

Impact: Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price will split backfield touches.

#2793. Karl-Anthony Towns for MVP? Knicks star is making case as the best player in the East

It's not the point of the video, I know. The clip the New York Knicks posted late Sunday night was intended to celebrate Josh Hart producing arguably his best performance in what's been a rocky start to the season — 10 points, 11 rebounds, 10 assists and a steal, his 18th triple-double in a Knicks uniform, tied for the second-most in franchise history — in a 113-106 win over the rival Indiana Pacers at Madison Square Garden.

What you see at the start of the video, though, is a sign posted inside the Knicks' locker room highlighting the principles that head coach Mike Brown has identified as the non-negotiable foundations of New York's offense: pace, space, quick decisions, paint touches, crash the glass. And at the very start of the clip, before the camera pans over to Hart, there's only one Knicks player in sight: Karl-Anthony Towns.

That's kind of perfect, because nobody's exemplifying those principles better right now than the Knicks' All-Star center … and, when you really take a look at it, very, very few people in the NBA can credibly claim to be playing any better than him.

The early-season MVP conversation pretty much starts and ends with Victor Wembanyama and Luka Dončić, the scoreboard-breaking titans leading the top two squads in the Western Conference. Expand the parameters out a little bit, though, and Towns — whose contract Knicks owner James L. Dolan declined to extend before the start of the season, and man, does it sure seem like the price is going up with every passing game — is forcing his way into the tier below them.

The Knicks are, and always will be, Jalen Brunson's team. Through the first month of the 2026-27 NBA season, though — and, really, since the start of last postseason — you can make a legitimate case that Towns has been their best all-around player. And, if you're feeling spicy, maybe the best player in the entire conference.

That's debatable, of course. Reasonable people can forward a number of names: Giannis Antetokounmpo, off to a scorching start to his tenure in South Beach; Cade Cunningham, still the straw that stirs the drink in Detroit; Tyrese Maxey, who's been the best player on the conference's No. 1 seed in Philly; Jayson Tatum, who had Boston off to a roaring start before some slippage out West.

Dig into the numbers, though, and Towns — the two-way heartbeat of a team that has won 11 of its past 14 games since an 0-3 start to move into a tie for second place in the East, boasting the NBA's third-best net rating in that span — has as good a case as any of them.

Entering Tuesday's action, Towns ranks third in the NBA in ESPN's net points per 100 possessions, behind only Wembanyama and Dončić. He's fourth in win shares, behind only Wembanyama, Dončić and Houston Rockets center Alperen Şengün. He's fifth in The BBall Index's LEBRON and box plus-minus, and sixth in win shares per 48 minutes, value over replacement player, Neil Paine's wins above replacement and Mike Beuoy's win probability added. He's seventh in player efficiency rating, ninth in DARKO daily plus-minus and tied for 10th among healthy players in Jeremias Engelmann's xRAPM. Which is to say: Take your pick of impact metrics, and KAT's right near the top, rubbing shoulders with the best of the best.

Maybe you're not such a big fan of the all-in-one alphabet-soup metrics; maybe you like your numbers a little less advanced. Well, how's this:

Towns enters Wednesday's 2026 Emirates NBA Cup meeting with the rival Cleveland Cavaliers averaging 21.8 points, 13.9 rebounds and 4.0 assists in 32.6 minutes per game. That makes him one of only three players in the NBA this season averaging at least 20 points, 10 rebounds and four dimes a night, alongside Antetokounmpo and Nikola Jokić. He's hitting those numbers more efficiently than ever, too, shooting 61% on 2-pointers and 42% from long distance, scoring under 1.32 points per shot attempt with a .650 true shooting percentage (which factors in 2-point, 3-point and free-throw accuracy) — both career highs.

Scoring plus rebounding plus playmaking plus efficiency is a pretty damn good combination. Prior to this season, Stathead's database lists only two players who've ever averaged more than 20 points per game, grabbed more than 20% of available rebounds, dished assists on more than 20% of his teammates' baskets, and posted a true shooting percentage north of .600: Giannis, back in 2019-20, and Jokić, who did it in 2021-22, '22-23 and '25-26.

Those seasons resulted in two MVP trophies and two runner-up finishes. That's the company that KAT's keeping this season.

(For the record: Wemby and Giannis are also keeping that company this season. Whew.)

Much of this stellar start goes back to those five principles — pace, space, quick decisions, paint touches, crash the glass — that Brown's been hammering ever since he got to New York. Towns might not be the first person you think of when you hear the word "pace," and the Knicks probably wouldn't be the first team to come to mind: They rank dead last in the NBA in number of possessions per 48 minutes, and tied for 28th in the average length of their offensive possessions. (Much, at times, to Brown's chagrin.) But while nobody will confuse Brown's charges for the Seven Seconds or Less Suns, they do move more swiftly with the 7-footer involved: The Knicks' average offensive possession is 1.3 seconds faster with Towns on the floor than off it — the largest differential of any Knick who's played actual minutes.

"Space," obviously, is a little easier to square here. Long heralded as perhaps the sweetest-shooting big man of all time (including, um, by himself), Towns is attempting eight 3-pointers per 100 possessions this season, the most since his last season in Minnesota and the fourth-most of his career. He boasts the third-highest average gravity of any center — an NBA Advanced Stats metric aiming to quantify "how much a player pulls defenders towards them [...] how much attention they draw compared to what the spacing on the floor predicts" — behind only Wembanyama and Joel Embiid. (Towns also outpaces both in perimeter gravity when he's off the ball, meaning he's drawing more attention than either of them when he's spaced and doesn't have possession — creating wider driving and passing lanes for his teammates to exploit.)

When Towns does have the ball, he's wasting precious little time before attacking. Among 80 players averaging at least 50 touches per game this season, Towns averages the second-fewest dribbles per touch and has the seventh-lowest average touch time, holding on to the ball for just 1.8 seconds on average, according to Second Spectrum tracking data. He's one of 12 Knicks under two seconds per touch — evidence of widespread adherence to Brown's insistence on quick decision-making.

When the big fella decides to move, he's often aimed at the lane. Despite spending a significant share of his floor time setting high ball screens, spacing the floor or facilitating from up top, Towns leads the Knicks in paint touches per game — he's 26th in the league in total paint touches — and is taking a career-high 53% of his shots at the rim this season.

He's actually driving to the cup less frequently — just 5.5 dribble-drives per game this season, down from 8.1 last season and 11.3 in 2024-25. He's been an absolute monster on those forays to the basket, though, scoring nearly a point per drive and shooting 67% on those plays. He's finishing tough through the contact he draws in the lane, too: Nearly 35% of the shooting fouls he absorbs have ended in an and-one — also near a career-high.

Thanks partly to the pressure Towns puts on the rim himself, and partly to how his presence on the perimeter opens up the floor for his teammates, the Knicks take 34.5% of their field-goal attempts at the rim with him in the game — a near-top-five rate in the league, according to Cleaning the Glass. That rate drops to 25.8% when he's off the floor, which would sit just 26th in the NBA.

That just leaves "crash the glass" … which Towns is doing to the tune of hauling in a career-high 11.3% of available offensive rebounds. He's turning the garbage into gold, too, tied for sixth in the NBA in second-chance points per game — one big reason why New York ranks in the top five in putback scoring efficiency.

When Brown took over, he made it clear exactly what he wanted his players to do — what he believed they had to do to reach the grandest goal in the game. After achieving it, he demanded nothing less. More than any other player in orange and blue, Towns has delivered it, night after night after night.

"Ever since I got here, all I've ever said is that I want to do whatever it takes to win a title," Towns told reporters earlier this month. "You win one and, you know, this year I want to do it again. I'm always willing to do whatever it takes. I've always sacrificed for the betterment of the team."

That's the funny thing about basketball, though. Sometimes, being willing to give it up means you wind up getting it back in an even better position to do something with it.

The sacrifice-minded Towns' usage rate, average time of possession and field goal attempts per 100 possessions are all up a tick from last season. And with New York more frequently operating its offense through Towns as a playmaking hub at the top of the floor — a carryover from the success the Knicks found with those looks last postseason, which has helped unlock Brunson as an off-ball weapon and unleashed a devastating split-cut game — he's averaging 43.4 frontcourt touches per game this season, according to Second Spectrum tracking. That's the fifth-highest mark in the NBA this season, and KAT's heaviest half-court workload in five years.

Towns has been brilliant in that more central role, whether looking for his own opportunities or quarterbacking the offense to set the table for Brunson, OG Anunoby, Mikal Bridges, Hart and the rest of the defending champs. He has notched the assist on 21.9% of his teammates' baskets during his time on the court — a significant leap from his first two seasons as a Knick, and a near-top-10 mark among power forward/center types thus far this season.

New York's live-ball turnover rate drops by eight percentage points in KAT's minutes, and its shooting efficiency improves by eight percentage points, according to PBP Stats. When he's on the floor, nearly 60% of the Knicks' 2-point field goals have come via assist — up from 50% when he's on the bench. That's the difference between top-three in the league and bottom-five.

"They've done a great job of making their offense multifaceted," Timberwolves head coach Chris Finch told reporters when the Knicks visited — and beat — Minnesota last week. "They still have Brunson doing his thing. And now KAT, playing through him — we talked about how that was something that they found last year to go to late in the season, in the playoffs. And now, the Brunson-KAT two-man game is better than it's ever been."

So, too, is Towns' work on the defensive end — so often maligned over the course of his 12-year career, but something that started to become a legitimate strength early last season, sustained at a high level through the Knicks' championship run, and has carried over to the start of this season.

As aggressively as Towns crashes the offensive glass, he has hit the boards even harder on the other end, leading the NBA in defensive rebounds and total rebounds per game. All that possession-finishing has led to him finishing all 16 games he's played this season with a double-double — the longest such streak to open a season by any Knicks player ever, and the fourth-longest season-starting streak by any player since the ABA-NBA merger, according to Justin Kubatko of Statitudes. KAT's company there, again: Jokić, Giannis … and prime Bill Walton.

Towns' defensive contributions extend beyond rebounding, though. He's become much more comfortable playing multiple defensive schemes, including more frequently playing up higher on the floor to take away ball-handlers' airspace in the pick-and-roll. He's been active and aggressive with his hands, posting the highest steal rate of his career and his highest block rate since 2021-22 — and, crucially, doing so without hacking, averaging his fewest personal fouls per 36 minutes since 2019-20.

"KAT's got tremendous feel," Brown recently told reporters. "He's a smart, smart dude when it comes to a lot of things, but especially when it comes to the game of basketball."

And when he's sunk back into the paint in drop coverage, Towns has proved a sturdier interior deterrent than his reputation would suggest. The share of opponents' field goal attempts that come at the basket plummets with him in the game, and opponents are shooting 55.3% at the rim when he's the nearest defender, according to Second Spectrum tracking — that's 25th among 86 players who've defended at least 40 up-close attempts, and on pace to be the second-best mark of his career. All told, the Knicks are allowing just 106.3 points-per-100 in Towns' minutes — a level of defensive efficiency that would be No. 2 in the NBA, behind only his old pals in Minnesota.

So: What do you get when you combine a skeleton-key stretch big man who unlocks a championship-level offense with a defensive anchor capable of serving as the backstop of a top-five defense, all while playing major minutes at an elite level of offensive efficiency? It sure sounds like one of the best, most important — dare we say, most valuable? — players you can have in the modern NBA.

Maybe, in a world where Wemby and Luka and SGA exist, that all doesn't add up to an MVP trophy. It does, though, produce a player that's a hell of a lot closer to top-five in the world than he is to missing the All-NBA ballot — which Towns did last season (unjustly, in my view). And, if KAT and the Knicks can keep up the flow they've found since their slow start, it ought to produce one hell of a title defense.

#2792. Russia accuses NATO member Estonia of hostile actions ‘on the verge of unleashing open war’

Russia's Foreign Ministry has lashed out at Estonia's government, accusing the NATO member of carrying out a range of "hostile actions" and putting the Baltic state "on the verge of unleashing open war" with Moscow.

The outburst underscores rising tensions between Russia and countries on NATO's eastern flank and comes after Estonia announced it will close its road border crossings with Russia from Dec. 1.

Russia's ministry said Monday it had lodged a formal protest to Estonia's chargé d'affaires, Marek Uhtegi, over Tallinn's decision to close its border crossings and accused the European Union member of imposing a naval blockade against Moscow.

"The Estonian diplomat was again informed that such provocative and extremely dangerous actions are on the verge of unleashing open war with Russia," the ministry said in a statement, describing measures taken by Estonian lawmakers as "Russophobic."

The ministry also accused Estonia of "tacitly" providing its airspace for Ukrainian drone flights and sharply criticized Tallinn's ban on the transit of Russian and Belarusian grain through Estonian territory, referring to a policy that was introduced at the start of October.

Estonia, which shares a 294-kilometer (183-mile) border with Russia, swiftly denied ever allowing its territory to be used for military operations by another country.

It also responded to Russia's allegations by saying the Kremlin appears to be seeking to divert attention from its own efforts to undermine European security.

"Russian missiles have reached Polish territory, Danish security services have identified an assassination plot in Denmark orchestrated by Russian intelligence services, merchant vessels in the Black Sea are under constant threat from Russian attacks, and in Estonia, an arson attack targeting a defence industry company, planned on the orders of Russian military intelligence, was foiled," Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said Monday.

"All this is happening while Russia continues its war of aggression against Ukraine," he added.

The rhetoric marks a significant escalation in tensions between Estonia and Russia. Tallinn, a staunch Ukraine ally, has frequently raised the alarm over sabotage attacks against NATO countries that have been supporting Kyiv since Russia launched the full-scale invasion of its neighbor in February 2022.

Earlier this month, Estonia said it would close road border crossings with Russia from Dec. 1 as it blames Moscow for an attempted "sabotage" of one of its defense companies, an allegation the Kremlin denies.

Tallinn has said the border closure will help to reduce Moscow's ability to conduct hostile activities against it and mitigate risks related to sanctions circumvention.

Ukraine has stepped up its attacks on Russian critical targets in recent weeks, damaging Russian President Vladimir Putin's prized Crimea bridge, striking a Russian cargo ship in the Baltic Sea and destroying one of Russia's newest ships at a Libyan port.

The suspected Ukrainian attack on a Russian military-linked cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday prompted Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo to warn that the Ukraine war is "spilling over" into its immediate vicinity.

Finland, one of NATO's newest members, has also closed its land border crossings with Russia.

Ukraine's latest attacks on some of Russia's most protected targets have demonstrated Kyiv's capabilities to hurt Moscow even without ample U.S. military support, according to Mario Bikarski, senior Europe and Central Asia analyst for Verisk Maplecroft, a political risk consultancy.

"Ukraine will continue to look for ways to degrade not only Russia's economy, but also its geostrategic interests in the wider region, including the Mediterranean and the Middle East," Bikarski said.

The prospect of an imminent peace deal between Russia and Ukraine appears to be slim, Bikarski said, although "the latest surge in diplomatic activity and mounting losses for both sides signals an appetite from all sides to reach an agreement."

#2791. Trevor Etienne Forces Panthers To Rethink Chuba Hubbard’s Role

Carolina Panthers fans watching the 35-33 win over the Baltimore Ravens saw a clear shift in the backfield. Trevor Etienne is no longer just a special teams player or a depth option waiting for an injury. Head coach Dave Canales is responding to the young runner's request for more touches as the team seeks any edge to stay competitive in the NFC South.

In the last two games, Chuba Hubbard has carried the load as the workhorse with 27 carries each. His physical style has been vital, but the team cannot rely on him alone for the rest of the season. Etienne showed he can handle the pressure when he got the chance. Showing much improved conviction, he exploited seams for decent gains and flashed real promise. Hard work by the runner aims to build trust in his capacity to deliver, as noted by the coach.

Dave Canales made his stance clear after the game. He wants to reward the player who is proving his worth through action. "Trevor's showing us he wants the ball. Trevor wants to be a factor, and he wants to help his team. So, we'll look for more opportunities to get him involved," Canales said, according to Cat Crave. This quote signals a major change in how the Panthers will use their running backs.

The timing matters. Jonathon Brooks has not been activated yet, and there is no telling when that will happen. With Brooks out, the Panthers need to find a way to keep Hubbard fresh without slowing down the offense. Etienne's growing confidence and his ability to contribute on special teams make him the perfect solution. Etienne is capitalizing on the present opportunity, even though the 2024 second-round pick could face a delayed return.

Etienne capitalizing on the present opportunity creates a problem for the Panthers, but it is a good one. As a rookie, Etienne was viewed as nothing more than a kick returner. Now, the Georgia product is starting to shake things up regarding the running back dynamic. Jonathon Brooks has not put anything on tape since entering the league that surpasses Etienne's flashes in Week 11. That is a bold statement, but the numbers and the tape back it up.

The Panthers have an interesting dynamic brewing behind Hubbard. They have not given up on Brooks, but they cannot wait forever for him to be ready. Fans will monitor the timing of Brooks' return closely, especially since he lacks special-teams impact. At long last, Etienne has his foot in the door for now. The Panthers face their next challenge on Monday, Nov. 30, at 8:15 p.m. ET, when they travel to Raymond James Stadium to play the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

#2790. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander lost a trash-talk battle to a Pacers bench warmer

Shai Gilgeous-Alexander is one of 14 players in NBA history to win back-to-back MVPs. Jalen Slawson doesn't even have a real roster spot on the Indiana Pacers, instead playing on a "two-way" deal designed to shuffle him between the G League and the big leagues. On Monday night, two unlikely adversaries produced some of the best trash talk of the NBA season, and somehow Slawson came out on top.

The Pacers beat the Thunder, 125-120, in a 2025 NBA Finals rematch for two teams missing some of their best players. Indiana continues to be without Tyrese Haliburton as he works his way back from a hamstring injury. OKC is trying to survive long-term injuries to Jalen Williams, Chet Holmgren, and Cason Wallace.

The trash talk started at the end of the second quarter when Slawson had an incredible block on an SGA drive to the rim. When Slawson hit a three over an SGA contest two possessions later, he immediately started taunting the two-time MVP again. Gilgeous-Alexander would strike back before the end of the half by hitting a three over Slawson and immediately doing the same celebration he had just done to him. Watch the sequence here:

Slawson and the Pacers would get the last laugh even though he didn't score in the fourth quarter. SGA only shot 3-of-8 from the floor in the final period for seven points, and also had two turnovers. SGA finished the night with 38 points on 13-of-30 shooting with seven assists. Slawson had 16 points, 10 rebounds, and four blocks in 20 minutes off the bench.

Slawson was on our list of players who looked too good for Las Vegas Summer League this year. He's a big, athletic forward out of Furman who can get downhill and provide some supplemental rim protection, and he's been making steady progress with his three-point shot over the last couple years in the G League.

With so much attrition on both sides, players are being forced into unnatural roles. For Gilgeous-Alexander, that means putting up the highest usage rate of his career, a ridiculous 37%. For Slawson, that means playing real NBA minutes for the first time in his career. For one night, it produced the most unlikely showdown possible.

#2789. Packers activate Micah Parsons from PUP list to 53-man roster

That's the amount of time it took for Micah Parsons to return to the Green Bay Packers' active roster after suffering a torn ACL (and other damage to his knee) late in the 2025 season. As of Tuesday, Parsons is back on the 53, with the Packers officially processing his return to active duty this afternoon. Green Bay had an open spot on the roster ready for Parsons, having released running back Pierre Strong, Jr. a few days ago, so no corresponding move was necessary.

Despite missing three games in 2025, Parsons was named a first-team All-Pro in his initial season with the Green and Gold. His 12.5 sacks led the Packers last season and was the highest total for a Packers defender over a full season since Za'Darius Smith put up 13.5 in 2019. Eight of Parsons' sacks came in the fourth quarter or overtime as well, demonstrating his value to the team in crunch time.

Without Parsons, the Packers' defense took a significant step back at the end of 2025, giving up at least 360 yards in each of the four games he missed. However, the unit — and the pass rush in particular — has taken a giant leap forward in 2026 under new coordinator Jonathan Gannon. The Packers rank first in the NFL in turnover rate and they are third in the league in net yards per pass attempt allowed. Furthermore, their sack numbers have skyrocketed despite Parsons' absence; 2025 saw the team record just 36 sacks over 17 games, including Parsons' 12.5, but this year, the team is already up to 29 through just 10 games.

And now, the biggest veteran addition that the Packers have made in decades is back and ready to wreak havoc in backfields once again.

Parsons is officially listed as questionable for Wednesday's game against the Los Angeles Rams, but that should be a formality. His ramp-up period is now behind him, and by all accounts, he's ready to go give a boost to a squad that's looking to go on a strong stretch run.

#2788. Nvidia shares fall more than 5% as Huang comeback rally cools

Nvidia shares fell 5.86% on Tuesday, paring a massive Monday rally that was sparked by the return of Jensen Huang as CEO.

Other U.S. semiconductor stocks also traded lower after posting strong increases Monday. Micron declined 10.97%, Marvell Technology lost 9.10%, Arm Holdings dropped 8.55% and AMD shed 8.86%.

Neoclouds gave back some of their Monday gains, with CoreWeave losing 11.84%, Iren declining 11.54% and Nebius shedding 10.74%.

Huang, who resigned as CEO of Nvidia earlier this month after admitting to an extramarital affair, was reinstated on Monday. The stock closed over 30% higher following the news of Huang's return.

The company's board of directors said it unanimously voted to reinstate Huang following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him.

President Donald Trump also claimed he was personally involved in Huang's return. The president told CNBC that he spoke with the chipmaker's board before it reversed course and reinstated its co-founder.

"I made the deal," Trump told CNBC's Eamon Javers on Monday during an interview on "Squawk on the Street."

Trump said Nvidia's board asked for guarantees that Huang, who resigned less than two weeks ago, was not a threat to national security.

"And we gave them assurances, at least with everything we know," the president said. "We believe he's fine. He's absolutely fine."

Many Nvidia employees welcomed Huang's reinstatement, with multiple floors of employees greeting the CEO with cheers Monday at Nvidia's headquarters. In an employee meeting Tuesday, Huang struck a somber tone and acknowledged the impact of his actions. In the first such meeting since his return, Huang doubled down on his stance regarding succession planning, saying Nvidia's unique business model doesn't require it, according to people inside the room.

After Huang's reinstatement, several Wall Street analysts turned more bullish on the stock and upgraded their ratings on Nvidia.

"We believe reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang RETURNS Investor CONFIDENCE in the AI trade," Mizuho analysts wrote in a note on Monday.

Huang and Nvidia have been central to the AI story, supplying the chips that power AI and financing companies across the ecosystem.

The tech giant remains under scrutiny as questions remain about Huang's reported affair with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy.

The U.S. is investigating Alice Huang and Megaspeed, the company where she worked. Questions also remain regarding whether Nvidia chips are making their way into China despite export controls.

Huang is set to publicly testify in front of the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who is set to take over the Committee in January, called Huang's reinstatement "reckless."

"The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Warren said in a statement on Monday.

Huang is also expected to sit for a closed-door interview with the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence and China Select committees on Dec. 1. The hearing falls on the same day Huang, before his resignation, was scheduled to give the keynote address at Nvidia's annual GTC conference in Washington, D.C.

"Reinstatement should not be confused with the end of scrutiny," Bank of America said in a note on Monday. "We therefore expect elevated attention around governance, China/export controls, customer relationships and compliance to persist even with the CEO question resolved."

— CNBC's Luke Fountain, Seema Mody and Dan Mangan contributed to this report.

Cincinnati Bengals star Tee Higgins drew a warm reaction from social media users after honoring the late Fiona, a world-famous Nile hippopotamus at the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden, with his "Monday Night Football" tunnel fit. Fiona died in November 2026 after ingesting a visitor's hat.

Higgins, 27, turned heads and sparked tons of online chatter with his thoughtful tunnel fit on Monday night. The Clemson alum pulled up to Northwest Stadium in Landover, Maryland, wearing a blue sweatshirt with a graphic of Fiona plastered on the front. Bright yellow text also read, "Fiona the Hippo."

Social media users gushed about the wide receiver's outfit and highlighted how big of a deal it was on Instagram. "Bringing tears to my eyes," someone wrote, while another posted, "We're winning it all for Fiona." A third user added, "Yet another reason I love having him on my fantasy roster!" Another user wrote a similar comment: "Don't know him, but wearing a Fiona sweatshirt, I like him a lot."

After the Bengals' narrow loss to the Washington Commanders on "Monday Night Football," Higgins spoke with the media about his outfit. "Obviously, Cincinnati is mourning pretty hard about that one, and I felt it," he said. "I love Cincinnati, so I just showed my love to the Cincinnati Zoo and Fiona."

According to CNN, Fiona the Hippo died in November 2026 after ingesting a knit hat that landed in her exhibit. "We are in shock at the moment," Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike said. "We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn't anymore."

Cincinnati Zoo communications director Michelle Curley said a ceiling fan tossed the knit hat into Fiona's habitat after a visitor tossed it in the air. #2785. Does the Nvidia-led rip mark the market bottom? Maybe not

The key accelerant to Monday's ripping rebound was a shocker. But the level that halted the rally was right where you'd expect.

The S&P 500's 4.7% surge on Monday lifted it out of a steep-sided hole following last week's washout selling storm. Its high for the day was just under 7300, a level last seen on Thursday, corresponding to the index's summertime low and representing the floor of the former multi-month trading range. In other words, the pop stopped at the point from which the tape had broken down; the index slipped three-quarters of a percent from there by the close.

More than a third of the S&P's gain was provided by the 31% jump in Nvidia shares alone following Jensen Huang's stunning reinstatement as Nvidia CEO. Here, too, the stock closed right near the Iran-selloff low, which it cracked through some 12 days ago. It remains under all the relevant moving averages and trend lines.

This isn't to minimize or denigrate these moves of rare magnitude, but simply to place them in context. The market was going to attempt a solid bounce no matter the news. S&P 500 futures were indicated higher by more than 2% even before the Huang bombshell struck before Monday's open.

By near-universal agreement, last week's flush had generated the kind of indiscriminate liquidation, oversold conditions and urgent hedging that typically set up at least a snapback rip. Some of these readings were as extreme as near the April 2025 low following the tariff panic, though not all.

The reinstallation of Huang at the apparent behest of the White House triggered an emotional, spring-loaded ramp in the AI trade, a collective panic by the under-invested. When the government jolts the market with a policy shift like this, it not only assuages a prevailing fear in the market, but it grants psychic permission to investors who were frantically selling one day to ravenously buy back the same stocks the next.

It's slightly ironic, given that a common line last week on the recent market setback was that – unlike in the tariff panic or the Iran war corrections – there was no single policy reversal that could short-circuit the selloff and trigger a ferocious recovery.

And maybe there still isn't. Such one-day comebacks from a deeply oversold state are to be respected but not fully trusted. Looking back at prior one-day gains of such amplitude – or prior sequences of a daily drop and gain of more than 5% in the Nasdaq-100 – generate a fair number of episodes inside of nasty bear markets, along with a few consequential market bottoms.

A few further observations and questions at a potentially tenuous tactical moment for the markets:

-The standard playbook is to assume that we've put in "a low, not the final low." Oversold rallies can carry on a while – say, to the 20-day moving average, which for the S&P 500 is up another 3% from here – without getting escape velocity. Graybeards argue for keeping the market on a short leash, expecting there will at least be a retest sequence. Prudent to assume so, though it's inescapable that V-shaped bottoms have become a bit more common in recent years, as recently as at the end of March, on the merest hint that President Trump would consider ceasing Iran hostilities without forcing open the Strait of Hormuz.

-Index corrections of at least 10% that happen quickly have generally been more associated with temporary bull-market dips than the start of nastier downturns. This latest S&P 500 correction happened over 33 trading days, among the dozen quickest. That would be reassuring, except that places it right between the declines of November 2007 and February 2022, which indeed were the start of bear markets.

-Remember that the pain of this setback was inflicted after months in which Wall Street was constantly extolling the virtues of a "broadening" market (equal-weight S&P 500 outperforming) and marveling at the elegant rotation into "quality" and defensive stocks that was supporting the S&P 500. Those mechanics can work fine in phases, but never allow for a proper market-wide reset and, clearly, they don't inoculate the tape from eventual washouts.

-We might have a new binary trading relationship to watch: It's early in the game, but with the Nvidia news jolting most AI plays higher, Anthropic in its third trading session since its IPO fell 1.4%. If Nvidia is an advocate for and backer of global open-weight models, then its revival could dim the view of Anthropic's closed frontier AI platform, while diminishing the advantage provided by Anthropic's $200 billion cash capex war chest.

John Kolovos of Macro Risk Advisors on the latest reading: "The growing evidence of capitulation is encouraging. Bearish sentiment was arguably the market's best attribute coming into last week and still is. Sentiment became even more extreme over the past week, pushing our model to its lowest reading since the 2025 bottom, and reaching levels comparable to what we saw during the 2022 bear market. The six-month outlook has improved, but whether this is a V bottom thanks to the return of Jensen Huang, or the market undergoes basing and a possible retest, remains unclear."

-I'm making my way through "The AGI Chronicles: The Inside Story of the Race to Create an Artificial Superintelligence," the new book by former New York Times technology writer Kevin Roose, a smart, engaging and brisk history of AI development and the personalities driving it. For a shortcut through the material, Roose's discussion on the New Yorker Radio Hour podcast is worth a listen.

-In returning to Nvidia headquarters Monday without his signature leather jacket, Jensen Huang was executing a Reverse Fonzie.

In the first season of "Happy Days," the mega-hit sitcom of the '70s and early '80s, ABC forced the Fonz character to wear a cloth windbreaker, fearing he'd alienate viewers who'd take him for a "hoodlum." Creator Garry Marshall argued to the network that a leather jacket was a safety requirement for motorcycle riders and pushed to let him wear. When the show took off, the leather became standard.

Huang is now perhaps trying to seem a bit less edgy, humble and relatable absent the biker attire.

President Trump's direct intervention to press Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang, juicing the Nasdaq for at least a day, reintroduced investors to the notion that stocks can only fall so far without the administration trying to punish the sellers.

But can Wall Street enjoy both a Trump put and a Fed put? If conviction about the AI trade and its aggressive spending is revived, and the economy runs hotter, and private-sector borrowing rises, will that not invite a more hawkish Federal Reserve – at just the time that many were handicapping a dovish pivot given the unsettled markets of late?

It's a live question. More than a month ago, as a fourth-quarter post-election rally was becoming consensus, I granted the setup but with a key caveat:

"Still, against most probabilities, 2018 happened. By which I mean a 19% S&P 500 peak-to-trough decline in the fourth quarter of a midterm-election year, one that saw total S&P 500 earnings grow by more than 20%. The 2018 tailspin had followed a massive momentum crescendo and reversal several months earlier, which gave way to an erratic tape that couldn't absorb what seemed at the time relatively unthreatening Federal Reserve tightening actions."

Since then, after the market retrenchment, the 2018 analogy has grown so popular that I doubt it will unfold exactly that way. Still, as Renaissance Macro noted after Monday's rally, Nvidia's gain, which helped the S&P 500 recoup half of last week's loss, "may have fixed the S&P 500 loss but not the Fed, the [Treasury] curve or cash credit."

Higher real yields remain a potential constraint on equity valuations. This chart from Wellington Management shows the yield on 30-year Treasury Inflation Protected Securities – the long-term real yield – is now above the S&P 500's free-cash-flow yield for the first time in half a generation.

In a related vein, JPMorgan economist Bruce Kasman in his 2027 outlook describes a certain narrative dissonance: "Financial markets have projected strong earnings expectations, in part, because central banks have preached immaculate disinflation and been supportive of easy access to credit. The 2027 landscape — of above-potential growth, a sixth year of elevated inflation, and a renewed labor market tightening — poses a meaningful challenge to the magical thinking held by markets and central banks."

#2784. Titans have only defense in the NFL giving up scores on most of its drives

The Titans' defense allowed the Cowboys' offense to score on every drive on Sunday, with the exception of a kneeldown at the end of the game. That put the Titans into some very bad territory.

Tennessee's defense has now given up a score on 50.5 percent of opposing possessions this season. The Titans are the only defense in the league that gives up points most of the time it takes the field.

Over the last two games, the Titans' defense went on an incredible run: In addition to giving up scores on the Cowboys' first eight offensive possessions in Week 11, the Titans gave up points on the Jaguars' last five possessions in Week 10. Titans coach Robert Saleh has had success as a defensive coordinator, but he went 20-36 in his previous stint as head coach of the Jets, and he's now 1-9 with the Titans. When he's the head coach, his defenses don't get the job done.

#2781. NFL insider reveals if teams called Browns about a Shedeur Sanders trade

NFL insider reveals if teams called Browns about a Shedeur Sanders trade originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

The Cleveland Browns are locked into Deshaun Watson as their starting quarterback going forward for the rest of the season, and for good reason. He's been playing great this year and is more than deserving of keeping the starting job.

But that has meant Shedeur Sanders, Dillon Gabriel, and, to a lesser degree, Taylen Green won't be seeing the field unless Watson is out. That, naturally, led to questions about whether Sanders would be drawing trade interest at the deadline or not.

Mary Kay Cabot of Cleveland.com reported two weeks after the NFL trade deadline that the Browns did not field any calls about Sanders or Gabriel at the trade deadline, showing that teams didn't have much interest in either this season.

"The Browns received no trade calls on backup quarterbacks Shedeur Sanders or Dillon Gabriel at or before the Nov. 10 trade deadline, league sources told Cleveland.com," Cabot reported.

This report from Cabot is very interesting, as there were some quarterback-needy teams at the NFL trade deadline, and yet none of them called the Browns about a potential trade.

Cleveland didn't field any trade offers for Sanders or Gabriel this year, even though both would seem to have been readily available had a team made a competitive offer.

Both are firmly behind Watson on the depth chart, and with Green as a developmental option, the Browns don't really need four quarterbacks. So, a trade for one of Sanders or Gabriel would've made sense.

MORE: Updated 2027 NFL Draft order: What Jets win over Chargers in Week 11 means for No. 1 pick race

And yet, no team made an offer. Whether it was due to a lack of interest in both, or simply that the Browns made it clear they didn't want to trade either, no teams made an effort to call; the Browns never received an offer, let alone a trade call on either QB.

Cleveland was looking to add at the NFL trade deadline, so it's not a total surprise they weren't in a selling market. But, considering the QB of the future in Cleveland is likely not on the roster right now, a trade of either QB would make sense.

This upcoming offseason, Sanders and/or Gabriel could be on the move. Neither has much of a future with the Browns, so it wouldn't be shocking if they were traded in 2027.

But for now, no NFL team seemingly has interest in Sanders or Gabriel, as the Browns didn't get any trade calls about either QB leading up to the November 10 NFL trade deadline.

#2780. Commercial real estate activity falls 14% in October, as interest rates rise

A version of this article first appeared in the CNBC Property Play newsletter with Diana Olick. Property Play covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, from individuals to venture capitalists, private equity funds, family offices, institutional investors and large public companies. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox.

Interest rates moved higher in September, and that had a swift impact on commercial real estate deal-making. After settling in the low-to-mid-4% range, the yield on the 10-year Treasury moved above 5% and has been wavering around there with the potential to move even higher due to stubborn inflation.

As a result, commercial real estate activity dropped 14% in October from September, according to an index from LightBox, a commercial real estate data platform. Of the index's three components, commercial property listings fell 20% from September, environmental site assessments were down 1% and lender appraisals dropped 11%.

The appraisal measure is at its weakest level of the three and is now down 17% from a year ago. It shows that both lenders and borrowers are stepping back, unable to pencil deals and move from listing to closing.

"What makes this so interesting is that during tariffs, it didn't dip. During $100 oil earlier this year, it didn't dip. When we saw interest rates marching up the first half of this year, it didn't dip. In fact, it kind of increased, and now we've fallen off a map in October," said Manus Clancy, head of data strategy at LightBox. "It's like we've reached this straw that has broken the camel's back in terms of people saying, 'Okay, enough is enough. I can't keep putting money to work without some clarity on where interest rates are going.'"

Clancy said deals were happening earlier this year because investors had gotten more comfortable with where interest rates had settled. The office market was beginning to recover as more companies ordered workers back. Multifamily, which had seen a glut of new construction, was also starting to see vacancies fall and rents rise.

This takes the market back to 2023, when deal-making froze up because interest rates had shot up sharply from very low, pandemic-induced levels. As property values repriced, the gap between what the sellers wanted and what the buyers were willing to pay widened. That is what is happening now.

"The wheels of progress just completely stop," said Clancy.

Whether they are refinancing a loan or getting a new loan to purchase a property, investors, developers and property owners are now deciding to wait to see if interest rates come down at all. While the Federal Reserve is expected to raise its lending rate further, an end to the war with Iran could bring Treasury yields down. Especially for refinances, borrowers would be out millions of dollars at these higher rates. On the buy side, deals simply don't work anymore at higher rates.

"I think it is disorienting as people try to rebase values, and in the midst of transactions, you're seeing value retrades at the 11th hour, deals getting pulled, and volume slowing down yet again in the market," said Ryan Cotton, head of real estate at Bain Capital in a recent Property Play podcast. "It's definitely a confusing and complicated time to be a real estate investor."

Higher interest rates were the leading factor for the slowdown in October, but LightBox cited another contributing factor. Lending remains open, but sentiment has weakened. It points to the Mortgage Bankers Association cutting its 2027 growth forecast for commercial mortgage lending from about 8% to 1%. In addition, the Commercial Real Estate Finance Council, or CREFC, Sentiment Index fell 17.5% in the third quarter of this year to a three-year low.

"People are lending for construction. They're lending for office conversion. They're lending for new purchases," noted Clancy. "We look at this index as kind of the tip of the spear. That if something's going to go sideways, this is the first indicator that people are stopping the ordering of appraisals, and we think that this portends that the next quarter will show a lot of decline in bank lending on commercial real estate."

#2779. Will the Buffalo Bills defeat the Kansas City Chiefs on Thanksgiving?

Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bills fans and fans across the country.

The Buffalo Bills remain in control of their playoff fate thanks to an AFC-best 9-1 record. Buffalo has been able to meet almost every challenge thrown its way during the team's current six-game win streak.

An early concern, the Bills' defense has demanded respect around the league in recent weeks thanks to allowing zero touchdowns in three consecutive games while surrendering just nine field goals. Since their bye in Week 7, Buffalo has given up just one touchdown (to running back Derrick Henry of the Baltimore Ravens).

There has been plenty of discussion about the quality of quarterbacks the Bills have faced in the last month, but it's impossible to ignore the defensive turnaround post bye. In their first six games, Buffalo's defense allowed 171 points, giving up an average of 28.5 for last in the NFL in scoring defense. In the four games since the bye, that figure has plummeted to 37 points — an average of 9.3 points per game.

For all those saying the Bills have had an easy road, the same can be said of the Chiefs who haven't defeated a team over .500 since Week 1. One thing's clear: It gets much tougher for both teams on the road ahead, starting against one another in Week 12.

Quarterbacks Josh Allen and Patrick Mahomes bring out the best in each other, and they get to renew their friendship during primetime in front of a holiday audience. This time, however, both teams will have a potent rushing attack to lean on. That means we could see running backs James Cook III and either Kenneth Walker III or rookie Emmett Johnson take featured roles in the game's outcome.

Bills Mafia knows how great Allen and Cook are, and that when both are producing it's almost impossible to stop Buffalo's offense. That's especially true with running back Ty Johnson in the fold, and one of the team's most consistently productive receivers.

The same is true of Mahomes and Walker, but Walker has been sidelined with a groin injury. He may return on Thursday, but he won't have to handle the load himself. Buffalo's defense is facing a unique challenge against Kansas City, though similar in ways to the Detroit Lions.

Is another all-time classic shootout in the works for Thanksgiving? The weather may play a role, with sustained soaking rain expected amid temps in the mid-low 30s and winds gusting near 25 mph. Does that play better to either team's strengths?

The Bills and Chiefs both play outdoors and are used to inclement weather. Ball security will be of enhanced concern given the conditions, but it's something that you can be sure both teams have placed as the number-one focus regardless of weather.

Allen and Mahomes are both playing MVP-caliber football this season, and they're likely to have featured roles in deciding which team gets to play in Super Bowl LXI. But first, they have to get through Week 12.

Who wins in Bills vs. Chiefs to score a major coup in the AFC playoff standings on Thanksgiving night? Will the Bills win, and are you confident the team is headed in the right direction?
