#2778. Bucks Reacts Survey: Are your vibes still high?

Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NBA. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bucks fans and fans across the country.

Back in September, we gauged your enthusiasm for the season ahead, asking if you were more or less excited for this season than last. As it turned out, you were much more excited for this season. Since then, however, there's been a whole lotta losing. But has that been enough to kill your vibes, or, as they have for resident commenter Boom_Shakalaka, have the young Bucks done enough to fill your cup?

As it stands, the Bucks sit 15th in the Eastern Conference with a 2-16 record. In the process, they've earned the not-so-enviable records of worst start to a season in franchise history and second-longest losing streak in franchise history (13 in a row, prior to last night's win against the Toronto Raptors). Unsurprisingly, they also have the second-worst point differential in the entire league (-11.4 PPG), ahead of only the 2-16 and seemingly always-inept Sacramento Kings (-12.5 PPG). Yet, despite Sacramento's lengthy run of failures—only twice in the last 20 years have they had a winning record—the Kings have the better average attendance, attracting an average crowd of 14,345 people this year to the Bucks' 13,296 (which ranks dead last).

On a player level, there's been plenty to gripe about too. Last night aside, Myles Turner has been okay at best and woeful at worst, while Kyle Kuzma continues his Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde play to the ire of fans. Jaime Jaquez Jr. has cooled off considerably after some hot form early, and Ryan Rollins has been a shell of the player he was last season, at least on the offensive end. For all his talent, Kel'el Ware has been similarly underwhelming.

Despite the losing, there's been plenty for Bucks fans to cheer (okay, quietly bump their fists) about. Rookies Brayden Burries and Nate Ament are playing more often and looking even better than we could have hoped for—especially at this early stage of the season. Burries, in particular, has been outstanding, playing every game (including 10 starts) and putting up 11.4 PPG, 5.7 RPG, 2.5 APG, 0.9 SPG and just 1.4 TOV on .455/.313/.741 shooting splits. Beyond the numbers, he's looked every bit the seasoned pro, consistently one of Milwaukee's better rebounders and downhill scorers, and, at times, even looking like the team's best player. Ament, while not as spectacular, has arguably been even more surprising. He's played in 16 games (two starts) and has proven to be a reliable shooter, opportunistic rim finisher, and legitimately good on-ball defender on his way to averages of 7.6 PPG and 3.1 RPG on .453/.349/.750 shooting. Beyond those two, Kasparas Jakučionis has had more than a few moments—including a Brew Hoop MVB and Defensive Belt double—while Tyler Herro has largely been good and, on occasion, unbelievable. Others have had moments too.

Recently, despite the continually fluctuating and at times infuriating rotation, the Bucks have also looked much more cohesive as a whole. They had a very real shot at winning against the Portland Trail Blazers, should have won—or at least gone into overtime—against the Philadelphia 76ers, and did put it all together in an uplifting win over the Raptors in Canada. Sweetening that win was Turner's play. Where he'd looked out of sorts earlier in the season—perhaps most noticeably against the same Raptors team—he was decisive in this one: engaged on both ends; dynamic as a spacer and finisher inside; and a defensive presence, both as a rim protector and rebounder. That this performance came against the very team that could potentially seek Turner's services in exchange for draft capital makes it even sweeter. Keep it coming, big fella!

Taking all of this into consideration—the "little wins" highs and the lower-than-Lil-Jon-can-make-you-get lows—just how much are you enjoying this season?

#2777. Robinhood shares fall as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses

Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.

Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.

Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.

Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.

Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.

Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.

Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.

—With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney

#2776. Kushner-backed OakNorth secures U.S. bank charter as global digital banks push into America

The U.K.'s OakNorth has secured a federal bank charter, saying it is the first foreign digital bank to do so, as international competitors vie for U.S. market share.

The charter clears OakNorth, which is backed by Jared Kushner's private equity firm, to acquire Michigan-based Community Unity Bank, subject to an $80 million capital injection, according to approval documents issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency on Nov. 19.

The deal, which is expected to close by the end of 2026, would allow OakNorth to provide loans, take deposits, and offer other banking services across all 50 states.

Kushner's private equity firm, Affinity Partners, took an 8% stake in OakNorth in 2025, with backing from major Gulf investors, including the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia and Qatar. SoftBank is also an OakNorth investor.

The bank reported $295 million in pretax profit for 2025 in its annual report, up from $280 million the previous year and close to three times the $100 million in profits five years prior.

It said principal losses on $20 billion in credit facilities issued over the past 10 years totaled £9 million, or less than 0.05%. Its 1.4% return on assets placed it among the top five banks in Western Europe and in the top 1% of commercial banks globally, according to The Banker's rankings.

"I would say that the level of animal spirits in the U.S. is always higher, right? So the momentum of business and the optimism is always a step up," OakNorth CEO Rishi Khosla told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Monday.

He said U.S. economic growth, investment in artificial intelligence and infrastructure spending would create opportunities for the bank.

OakNorth has focused on lending to lower mid-market businesses rather than competing for consumer customers in a crowded U.S. market.

The lender targets businesses with annual revenues of $5 million to $100 million with loans worth $5 million to $50 million. The bank entered the U.S. market in 2023 and has lent about $3.5 billion to U.S. businesses to date. The U.S. accounted for 40% of its $12.4 billion in new loans in 2025.

"These are really growth companies which are scaling up, and given that focus, you really haven't had an institution in the last decades that focus on that customer segment, and that's opened up the opportunity for us," Khosla said.

He cited commercial real estate lending as a particularly strong growth opportunity in the U.S.

Securing the charter is notoriously difficult, with many regulatory hurdles. It took OakNorth 20 months, a restructure of the bank's corporate ownership, and relocating its holding company from the island of Jersey to the U.K. to meet Federal Reserve requirements.

Other international fintechs seeking a foothold in the U.S. have struggled to gain traction. Monzo and Revolut withdrew their initial U.S. applications for a full banking charter between 2021 and 2023 after regulatory pushback.

Monzo closed its U.S. operations in April just four years after it launched, amid a crowded consumer market. "We have made a strategic decision to focus on scaling in our home market and Europe and to step away from the U.S.," the company said.

But the regulatory landscape has since shifted. Revolut and Brazil's Nubank have received conditional approval for U.S. banking charters from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.

Dutch digital bank Bunq reapplied after withdrawing its 2023 application, but its second application was denied in August.

Another U.K. digital lender, Starling, is also seeking U.S. growth. It sells its Engine banking software to mid-tier U.S. lenders and is looking to acquire a domestic bank to serve business clients.

#2775. Todd Bowles says Buccaneers must fix late-game errors

Todd Bowles knows the Tampa Bay Buccaneers are close.

The Buccaneers' record is just 3-7 following their latest loss to the Detroit Lions, falling by a score of 31-21. However, the score doesn't tell the whole story, as Tampa Bay trailed 17-14 entering the fourth quarter. Furthermore, it was the first time the Buccaneers had lost by more than one possession all season. In all six prior losses, they had been by one possession.

After a dominant two-game win streak that saw them outscore their NFC South opponents 59-13, Tampa Bay is now on a two-game losing streak to NFC North opponents, the Lions and Chicago Bears. In defense of the Buccaneers, they're arguably two of the top teams in the conference.

During his Monday press conference availability, reporters asked Bowles what it will take for the Buccaneers to start playing better in the fourth quarter. Unsurprisingly, Bowles -- who is in his fifth season as head coach -- kept it simple.

"Got to be able to finish, minimize the mistakes on both sides of the ball, all three phases, really," said Bowles. "You got to minimize the mistakes. You got to win field position, and you got to execute."

The Buccaneers are in second place in the NFC South with the Panthers at 5-5. The catch is that the Buccaneers currently hold the tiebreaker and can keep it at the end of the season by beating Carolina at home on Monday Night Football next week.

"Yeah, they're aware of it -- they understand it," Bowles said of the Buccaneers needing to have urgency this week. "They know where we stand, and you know it starts with us in this room. So we got to correct everything and turn that thing around, and we got to do it a game at a time."

With the Buccaneers having six one-possession losses this season, they'll have to learn to close out games in this final stretch. That will have to start in Week 12 when they face the division-leading Panthers.

#2772. Six key questions raised by Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia

Jensen Huang made a dramatic return as Nvidia CEO on Monday, less than a week after board Chairman Harvey Jones said directors did not intend to reinstate him. The board later voted unanimously to bring Huang back.

Nvidia shares surged as much as 36% during the session and closed 31% higher.

The reversal followed a steep decline in Nvidia shares, which closed at $125.53 on Friday even after the company reported strong third-quarter results. A petition calling for Huang's return had drawn more than 200,000 signatures, according to its organizers.

The rally spread across the broader market, with the Nasdaq Composite gaining 6.5% and the S&P 500 rising 4.7%, each posting its strongest session since April 2025.

Nvidia's board said it had received input from senior U.S. government officials and that its investigation into Huang's conduct would continue.

Still, the board's reversal, President Donald Trump's administration's role and continued scrutiny of Nvidia's China business leave major questions for both investors and lawmakers.

Sen. Jack Reed, a member of the Senate Banking Committee, urged Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Monday to appear before the committee to discuss the case.

Reed did not lay out a specific list of questions for the two officials, but his statement cited reporting that Trump had been briefed by intelligence officials led by then-National Security Adviser Marco Rubio before intervening in support of Huang's return.

Reed's call adds to mounting pressure on both Nvidia and the Trump administration to explain what they knew and when.

Rep. Gabe Amo, D-R.I., vice ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said Huang’s reinstatement could broaden congressional scrutiny rather than bring it to a close.

“I think it frankly broadens the scope of the query,” Amo told CNBC, adding that lawmakers should also examine administration officials involved in decisions affecting Nvidia and chip sales to China.

Amo said he expects the planned closed-door interview with Huang on Dec. 1 to proceed and that Congress would continue seeking answers both privately and publicly in the coming months.

“He should start purchasing his plane tickets to Washington,” he said. “It is abundantly clear that this is ripe for questioning by Congress.”

On Nvidia's third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 17, Jones said the board had accepted Huang's resignation and did not intend to reinstate him.

Less than a week later, the board reversed course, saying Monday that it had unanimously voted to bring Huang back after discussions with him and input from senior U.S. government officials.

Trump said he had spoken with board members and that his administration provided assurances based on the information available to it. But the board has not publicly detailed what it was told.

"The board decided to do what we wanted to do," Trump told CNBC, adding that he believed his intervention had been important.

"I've been speaking to the board directly and indirectly, and I felt very strongly about it," he said.

Trump also called into an Nvidia board meeting to argue for Huang's return, Semafor reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

Reed has called on Huang to disclose his communications with Trump and on Nvidia to release a transcript of the board's call with the president.

Lawmakers are still seeking answers about the alleged smuggling of Nvidia products to China, their possible diversion for military use and possible advancement of Chinese AI capabilities.

The Senate Banking Committee has scheduled Huang to testify on U.S. export controls on Dec. 3. House lawmakers have also confirmed closed-door interviews with Huang on Dec. 1 and Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter on Dec. 2.

"The Nvidia board's brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed," Reps. John Moolenaar, Rick Crawford and Brian Mast said in a joint statement.

Their inquiry may also examine what Nvidia knew about the customers and resellers involved, as well as what controls the company had in place.

Other lawmakers have also sought to preserve the paper trail. Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons had asked senior administration officials on Nov. 11 to retain records related to Nvidia exports of advanced AI chips to China and associated national security concerns.

Nvidia has promised to hire a chief compliance officer and establish a committee overseeing national security and export controls. The board's investigation into Huang's conduct also remains underway.

Josh Gilbert, eToro's lead analyst for APAC and the Middle East, said investors will be watching whether those new safeguards carry meaningful authority.

Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson, said Nvidia has a limited window to prepare for the possibility that a future president may be less supportive of Huang.

With Trump's term ending in two years, Luria argued that Nvidia needs a clearer plan for who could take over if Huang were forced to leave again.

Gilbert pointed to Nvidia's roughly 75% revenue-growth forecast for the next financial year as evidence of strong near-term demand. The longer-term question, he said, is whether customer orders and artificial intelligence investment can sustain that pace.

Luria told CNBC that concerns about the broader AI trade remain, including the cost of financing data centers, potential overbuilding by neocloud companies and obstacles to building new facilities.

Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon said worries about whether AI spending is achievable and sustainable were not caused solely by Huang's departure. UBS, meanwhile, flagged Nvidia's roughly $390 billion in supply commitments and the need to keep demand flowing through its ecosystem.

Gilbert said part of Monday's rally reflected investors recovering earlier losses rather than pricing in new growth. Bernstein restored its "Outperform" rating and kept its $200 price target, while UBS maintained its $220 target.

"For the share price, it comes down to whether Nvidia can keep delivering as it has done over recent years," said Gilbert, adding that Huang's return could ease some concerns about Nvidia's longer-term outlook.

"The real worry has been what happens beyond next year. Having Huang back at the helm goes a long way to easing those concerns, because he's the one who sits down with the biggest customers and gets those multi-year orders over the line," he said.

— CNBC's David Sucherman, Justin Papp and Eko Prasetyo contributed to the story

#2771. The Rams have no choice but to win Wednesday

If the Los Angeles Rams want to make the NFL postseason, they'd better find a way to beat the Green Bay Packers on Wednesday night.

Otherwise, we're likely barreling toward one of the biggest single-season flops in modern league history.

That's harsh, to be sure, but it's also the reality the Rams are currently facing. This was the heavy preseason favorite to win the Super Bowl, currently sitting on the outside looking in at the playoff picture as we enter Week 12. If they can't edge out a team in a similarly precarious position, and one with a devastating weakness, at that, reality will get even more grim.

This overall point is fleshed out by the math. There is massive playoff leverage on the line for whichever wins (and, subsequently, whichever one loses). According to RBSDM.com, Los Angeles currently has a 42% chance to make the playoffs. With a win on Thanksgiving Eve, the odds are bumped up to 56%. With a loss? They plummet to merely 20%.

Compared to The Athletic's playoff predictor, RBSDM's modeling is actually rosy for the Rams. That outlet gives L.A. just a 34% chance of reaching the postseason as things currently stand. It increases to 47% with a win and drops off to 16% with a loss.

The obvious storylines and narratives, and simply looking at the upcoming schedule, flesh out what the models are indicating.

Right now, the Packers are clinging to the No. 7 seed in the NFC playoffs. The Seattle Seahawks are one spot back of them, followed by the Rams and they're all 6-4 entering this week's action. The Packers and Seahawks don't play each other, so that potential tiebreaker is a little more complicated than simply head-to-head results, but Green Bay obviously is in control for the time being. Los Angeles gets at least one crack at both, however, with two meetings against Seattle. Blowing a chance to win the tiebreaker over the Packers would be devastating.

Per Tankathon, the Rams have the second-most challenging schedule left in the NFL, only behind that of the Chicago Bears. The Seahawks are fourth in that metric while the Packers are seventh. None of those home stretches are particularly easy, but it's an especially difficult road for the Rams. Throw in a lost tiebreaker and it gets scary quickly.

It isn't impossible for the Rams to make the playoffs with a loss on Wednesday night, but it becomes exceptionally difficult and it takes their fate out of their hands. Even if Los Angeles sweeps Seattle late in the season, a loss this week means it would need help to crack the top seven in the NFC.

This team has already had to battle through so much, and we're only 2/3 of the way through the season. It's only getting more difficult with each passing devastating injury.

From an objective viewpoint, that desperation is what makes this week's matchup such incredible theater, especially considering the Packers are essentially in the same boat. They're almost certainly toast for the postseason with a loss.

The Rams would love to make that their opponents' reality this week. For their own sake, they have to.

#2765. Despite everything, the Packers still have their goals within reach

I'd like to say 2026 has been a uniquely stupid year of Packers football, but I don't know if that's true. Certainly there have been uniquely stupid aspects of it; I can't think of another year where the Packers have taken such drastic steps to find someone, anyone capable of playing replacement-level football on their offensive line during the season. I can't think of another season where the Packers have had a comparable cavalcade of injuries, except for maybe 2025. Maybe that's just modern football. I don't know. I can't think of another season where so many games have been, if not just affected, seemingly outright steered toward an outcome by the officials.

But handwaving all of that, let's just say it's been a stupid year. If not uniquely so, I think we can land on that.

And yet! Here the Packers sit entering Week 12 with everything they want still within reach.

If the season ended today, the Packers would make the playoffs, occupying the seventh seed in the NFC field, a position that will surely one day be named for Matt LaFleur. The Rams and Seahawks are hot on their tails, but a win this week — certainly very achievable against an injury-diminished Rams squad — would solidify their lead over both teams. They'd widen their lead over the Seahawks by strengthening their conference record and put a serious dent in the Rams' chances by taking ownership of the head-to-head tiebreaker.

And if the Packers make the playoffs, who knows what could happen? Right now, the playoff field would see them matched up against the Detroit Lions in the wildcard round. That, too, is an eminently winnable game. The Packers had the Lions all but dead to rights in Week 7 but for their semi-permanent kicking woes. And even so, if Josh Jacobs takes the small but significant step of simply catching the ball in the end zone, there's a very good chance they beat the Lions.

I think outside of the Vikings, the Packers could at least be competitive against pretty much any team in the NFC. There are certainly some talented teams in the field, but none of them have the borderline psychopathy of Brian Flores. If that's what it takes to beat the Packers (other than a kicker meltdown), you have to at least think the Packers have a chance.

And I suppose that's the point I'm trying to make here. The Packers still have virtually everything to play for and all of it is within their control. The NFC North title might be out of reach, but the playoffs are still fully achievable. The Packers control their own destiny on every front; keep winning and they're in the playoffs. Stumble and their odds grow more remote by the week.

But it's all up to the Packers. They've shown this year that they can beat anyone — or lose to just about anyone, too. Their weaknesses are almost entirely self inflicted, but the solutions to those weaknesses are all self-driven, too.

There are a lot of different ways you could spin this Packers season, but I think the ultimate story is that this is a team that had everything within its grasp, despite whatever weirdness befell them. And that fact may end up being the biggest indictment anyone can level against the 2026 Green Bay Packers.

#2764. Op-ed: Trump’s Nvidia board intervention put a price on national security. Our adversaries will take note

To learn more about the CNBC CFO Council, visit cnbccouncils.com/cfo

President Donald J. Trump has accomplished something extraordinary. He directly inserted himself into the boardroom of one of America's most strategically important companies, Nvidia, helping to reverse a corporate leadership decision, and personally vouched for restored CEO Jensen Huang as having a clean bill of health regarding the national security investigations into his business activities with China.

On Monday, after Nvidia's board reinstated Huang following his resignation amid a counterintelligence controversy and allegations that Alice Huang, with whom he had an affair, is under suspicion of being a Chinese intelligence asset, Wall Street celebrated with a historic market bounce. But the market's enthusiasm should not obscure a far more consequential question circulating in Washington, D.C.: Does American national security have a price?

What happened at Nvidia raises the frightening possibility that it does, and it fits a recent pattern that is exactly what geopolitical rivals around the world want to see. Consider the economic pressures surrounding the Iran war. Disruptions to energy markets, shipping, supply chains, and consumer prices have complicated American strategic decision-making. These are notably different circumstances, but they raise the same troubling question about the costs of defending American national security interests, and when they become economically unpalatable to those in the Trump administration.

Beijing, Tehran, and Moscow are watching — as are our allies and partners — and they all may agree on one thing: America has an Achilles' heel that military and technological superiority cannot overcome. It is possible to impose sufficient economic pain to alter Washington's strategic calculation with friends and foes alike. Bleed American capital markets, disrupt commerce, squeeze consumers, and eventually Washington may look for an exit.

Despite the narrative that the president is weaving, there is a fundamental difference between responsibly weighing economic consequences and allowing adversaries to conclude that they can impose an economic veto over U.S. national security policy. Trump told CNBC in an extensive interview on Monday morning that when it comes to national security, "losing the brain power of somebody like Jensen ... would be a far bigger threat than anything we're talking about."

"The bigger impact was the long term. The bigger impact was you know he's got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about, including me, that nobody else understands," Trump said. "This was a big loss. This was a tremendous loss. And you saw that it affected the market. It affected even, I think it even affected the perception of our country in the world," the president said.

And that's true, but not only in the way Trump thinks it did.

This is not about whether Huang is a brilliant executive or whether Nvidia is enormously important to American competitiveness. Both are true. The question that America, particularly its government, must ask is whether Huang's economic importance justifies subordinating corporate governance, interfering with counterintelligence procedures, and stymying national security oversight.

Trump characterized the Justice Department's assessment as having exonerated Huang. Yet Nvidia's board reinstated him while its own review remained open.

The allegations involving reported contacts with Chinese intelligence assets do not establish legal wrongdoing. However, presidential personal assurances are not substitutes for independent counterintelligence assessments and investigations or congressional oversight. Monday's rising stock price might only measure what shareholders believe Huang at the helm of Nvidia is worth, while discounting or ignoring the unresolved counterintelligence risk that he may still pose to Nvidia and the entire artificial intelligence ecosystem.

The Trump administration, Silicon Valley, and Wall Street may believe the matter is closed.

"That thing's like a rocket ship going in the wrong direction. Now it's a rocket ship going in the right direction, and it's taking the whole market," Trump told CNBC about Nvidia's 31.5% Monday gains.

One glaring vulnerability still on the horizon is what Washington does not know. If Beijing possesses additional damaging information, it controls whether, when, and how that information might be weaponized in an ongoing and now reignited strategic competition between the U.S. and China. Beijing retains the capacity to reopen this matter at a time of its choosing. Chinese intelligence could drip-feed disclosures, compel repeated explanations from Huang and the president, and transform Monday's declaration of resolution of this matter into a prolonged national security vulnerability.

There is also a striking irony here. Some pundits are comparing Trump's intervention to China's state-controlled market. To be sure, the Chinese government has a very heavy hand in its economy, but one thing the Chinese Communist Party will never do is put an individual ahead of national security and political authority despite the economic impact that this person or company is perceived to have. Xi Jinping and China's Communist Party have demonstrated a willingness to make almost the opposite calculation about national security and economic growth. Under Xi, national and political security generally takes precedence over the interests of individual companies and brilliant executives.

Consider Jack Ma. In 2020, Beijing halted Ant Group's planned $37 billion initial public offering and subsequently imposed sweeping regulatory restrictions on Ma's business empire. Beijing accepted substantial economic consequences to reinforce national security and political authority. This is not an argument for importing China's authoritarian model into American corporate governance. But the strategic asymmetry is noteworthy to revisit in this latest comparative context. Beijing has demonstrated that even its most celebrated entrepreneurs are not indispensable to the party and the nation. Washington risks signaling that some of its entrepreneurs are in fact indispensable to the state, which ironically potentially makes them even bigger intelligence targets for foreign adversaries.

As an economic matter, the commercial realities of Nvidia's China business make this situation even more perplexing. China, including Hong Kong, accounted for just 9.1% of Nvidia's reported global revenue in fiscal 2026, down from 19.2% the previous year. Its latest fourth-quarter guidance assumes no Chinese data center compute revenue. Nvidia did change the way it reports geographic sales, to customer headquarter address, in late 2025. But anyone familiar with Chinese strategic documents, including the 15th Five-Year Plan, should understand that Beijing has no intention of becoming permanently "addicted" to American chips. Its objective is technological self-reliance, not expanding Nvidia's market share and by extension its dependency on them.

Whatever the exact figure, I cannot think of a number that is worth selling out U.S. national security over, but it certainly isn't  9.1%, which is also a number that will continue to shrink. Furthermore, if the AI ecosystem is critical to our economy and our national security, then selling advanced chips to China or loosening export controls is the opposite of what we should be doing because the chips are used to juice the compute of Chinese LLMs that compete with ours, and to increase the effectiveness and lethality of Chinese weapons systems. The questionable sales of Nvidia chips in Asia, which are at the heart of this story, support neither our economy nor our national security. They undermine them both.

There is also an extraordinary corporate governance precedent that extends well beyond Nvidia and Huang, one that is escalating and growing more bold at each turn. While Trump has intervened in the markets before, in cases including U.S. Steel and Intel, he has never gone to this level, making the argument that a company is so critical to the national security of the nation that at any point its decision making could require executive branch intervention and specific direction.

Based on the president's rationale, what should the boards of key national security relevant companies like Boeing, Lockheed Martin, Palantir, Anduril, SpaceX, or even Rio Tinto — whose jointly owned Resolution Copper project in Arizona could eventually supply up to 25 percent of America's copper demand — expect?  Does their strategic importance justify presidential intervention in executive appointments, succession planning, corporate strategy, or commercial relationships? A precedent established by one president becomes an idea, option, and instrument available to future presidents, including those with fundamentally different political preferences.

All of this brings us to Congress. If you take Trump at his word, that Nvidia's strategic importance justifies extraordinary executive branch intervention, it also justifies extraordinary legislative intervention and oversight. Article I grants Congress authority to regulate foreign commerce. Congress established the statutory framework governing executive export-control authority through legislation, including the Export Control Reform Act of 2018. Those authorities were delegated, not surrendered. The president may have driven this Nvidia CEO decision by telephone. Congress possesses something more enduring: the authority to establish the rules through legislation. The Senate Banking Committee's scheduled December 3 hearing on export controls provides an opportunity to begin.

Congress should do much more than demand classified briefings on the counterintelligence concerns.  Lawmakers should pass, with veto-proof majorities, requirements for stronger board-level counterintelligence responsibilities, mandatory defensive briefings to vulnerable tech executives and innovation sector leadership, much tighter export-license oversight with enforcement mechanisms that have teeth, and enforceable reporting requirements. Legislative proposals including the AI Overwatch Act, Match Act, and Remote Access Security Act must be passed as soon as possible. Nvidia and its leadership may warrant considerably tighter legal and regulatory scrutiny given its importance as the fulcrum of the AI ecosystem.

It is important for Congress to remember that the legislative branch is a co-equal branch of government, not a rubber stamp or talk shop providing us with commentary about the outcome of executive branch decisions. They have an active and constitutional role to play in our democracy. They need to get it together and get to work. If Nvidia is important enough for the president to enter its boardroom, it is important enough for Congress to exercise its constitutional authority over the rules governing this entire process.

—By Dewardic McNeal, Managing Director and Senior Policy Analyst at Longview Global, and a CNBC Contributor

Tennessee was fined $250K for their fans' conduct during the school's game against LSU

Lane Kiffin and LSU were pelted with golf balls and bottles of mustard during their game against Tennessee

Tennessee fans didn't hold the mustard — or roll out the welcome mat — for Lane Kiffin in his return to Neyland Stadium.

The LSU coach was the target of golf balls, boos and bottles of the yellow condiment, all of which resulted in the school receiving a $250,000 fine handed down from the Southeastern Conference (SEC).

The conference said in a statement on Sunday, Nov. 22 that Tennessee was assessed the fine for "interruption of its November 21 football game with Louisiana State University due to fans throwing debris onto the field." The game was stopped for several minutes and LSU moved to the center of the field to avoid getting pelted by the detritus.

Saturday's decision to throw mustard and golf balls harkens back to what students threw at Kiffin in 2021 when he returned then, as the coach at Ole Miss.

Kiffin, who is in his first year as LSU's head coach and is sporting a 6-5 record, sparked similar sentiment when he abandoned the Rebels for Baton Rouge last year.

#2762. Tokenization platform Securitize gains 10% postmarket on Q3 results, move into asset-backed finance

Tokenization platform Securitize climbed about 10% postmarket after reporting third quarter growth alongside increased operating expenses, and announcing an expansion into asset-backed finance through a strategic acquisition.

Miami-based Securitize, which made its public market debut in July, operates in the relatively new corner of the crypto equity universe involved in institutional tokenization infrastructure. Tokenized assets on the platform grew 9% in the third quarter, to $4.8 billion, from the same period a year ago. Aggregate transaction volume rose 20% from a year ago, to $4.3 billion. Revenue of $11.5 million was up 28% from last year.

The growth came as bullish sentiment around tokenization gained traction throughout the third quarter, ahead of the Security and Exchange Commission formalizing the long awaited Innovation Exemption on Sept. 17, which created a temporary pathway for trading of certain tokenized stocks and strengthened the regulatory outlook.

Profitability is still meaningfully below year-ago levels, due in part to costs associated with going public over the summer, as well as the scaling up of the tokenization business at an active time for the entire sector, Securitize CEO Carlos Domingo told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Securitize reinforced "certain areas of the company like finance, compliance, legal [and] cybersecurity," which increased corporate costs "compared to a year ago when we were privately held," Domingo said. "We're in in a very good position. The adjusted EBITDA … is improving significantly from previous quarters."

Securitize reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of $2 million, compared with positive adjusted EBITDA of $3.6 million a year ago, better than a $5.5 million loss in the second quarter. The company posted a 183% increase in operating costs and expenses.

Also on Monday, the Securitize board authorized a $50 million share buyback and announced the acquisition of River One, an institutional asset-backed financing platform developing technology to connect stablecoin capital with traditional lending markets. Terms were not disclosed.

Securitize sees an opportunity to modernize the $9 trillion market for asset backed finance by using stablecoins to finance real world assets, generate yield and tokenize investment positions and credit products, Domingo said.The acquisition also marks an expansion beyond Securitize's core niche markets at a time when tokenization's competitive landscape is growing, with traditional asset managers like BlackRock and Franklin Templeton, and established financial market infrastructure providers like DTCC and Broadridge, entering the industry.

"We have been very active in tokenized funds, treasuries [and] yield … And we've been obviously recently very active in tokenized stocks, so this adds another piece of the puzzle in the emerging tokenization space for us to capture revenue growth."

#2761. AG Blanche, FBI’s Patel dodge questions about Jensen Huang investigation

Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel on Tuesday dodged questions about the conclusions of an investigation President Donald Trump cited to push Nvidia's board to bring back Jensen Huang as CEO.

Asked by a reporter whether the Department of Justice had investigated Huang and the results of that probe, Blanche said, "What the president said is that he talked to a lot of people going into the decision that he made to encourage the board to reinstate him."

"And so I'm not going to get into communications I have with the president," Blanche said at a news conference in Washington.

Huang was reinstated as CEO of Nvidia on Monday morning, less than two weeks after resigning amid allegations he had affairs with a purported spy for China and two Nvidia employees plus concerns that advanced semiconductor chips made by his company had been diverted to China in violation of U.S. law.

In an interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump was asked what led him to personally confirm to Nvidia's board that Huang was not a national security risk.

"We've done a very thorough investigation, and the investigation showed that he did, I mean, he had bad judgment having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents, but he did nothing wrong," Trump replied.

Trump in a Truth Social post on Monday said the U.S. government had no reason to believe Huang's return to the company "poses any risk to National Security," and that Blanche had confirmed the government "does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."

Nvidia, in its statement Monday announcing Huang's return, said, "The Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk."

Blanche on Tuesday said, "Nvidia is a good corporate citizen."

"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target, or was the subject of some criminal investigation, or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people," he said.

Patel did not answer a reporter's question of whether the FBI has spoken to Huang and whether the FBI had been made aware of an assessment by U.S. intelligence agencies that Huang's reported paramour, Alice Huang, was an asset for China's spy agency.

Jensen Huang is not related to Alice Huang, who was an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia's semiconductor chips.

The DOJ and Commerce Department on Nov. 17 said they were investigating Megaspeed for potential diversion of Nvidia chips in violation of U.S. export law.

Asked how the DOJ could rule out Jensen Huang having potential criminal liability given the fact that the investigation remains ongoing, Blanche replied, "So, when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about."

"We have hundreds, if not more, export investigations going at any time at the Department of Justice," Blanche said.

#2760. JJ Redick reveals rarely-seen qualities that separate this Lakers team

One of the reasons why things are clicking so seamlessly?

Apparently none of the team's wings are keeping score of petty things, such as who starts, who gets more touches, etc.

Lakers coach JJ Redick has a theory as to why that's happening.

"I think they're all really grateful to be here, to be Lakers," Redick said after the Lakers' 109-94 win over the Jazz on Monday. "They're all really grateful to be on this team and be part of the group."

Redick pointed out that Matisse Thybulle, Ziaire Williams, Quentin Grimes and Jake LaRavia are all in the same boat even though different circumstances brought them to this moment.

In other words, they all know this is a rare opportunity.

They deeply understand that playing for a Laker team that is tied for the best record in the league at 15-3 and has a real shot at winning a championship is something worth sacrificing for.

"They've experienced adversity in their careers, in different ways, and I think that gratitude piece is like they're all in a situation [together]," Redick said. "…They're just all in a situation where they're putting the team first and they're putting their egos aside and that stuff matters and I think you know it's one of the reasons our group has had early success because we said on day one we wanted this season to be about the team and not any one individual one of us, and so far it's been that."

Los Angeles Lakers head coach JJ Redick looks on before an NBA basketball game against the Utah Jazz on Monday, Nov. 23, 2026, in Los Angeles. NBAE via Getty Images

Jake LaRavia started in 11 straight games before coming off the bench in the team's two contests prior to their win over the Jazz. He returned to the starting lineup Monday, finishing with 15 points, 10 rebounds and two steals.

"I've talked about it before, I think just everyone is willing to sacrifice for the same goal, and we just have a lot of adaptable players," LaRavia said.

"A lot of it's like lineup-based, matchup-based, so you know, whoever the coaches think should start that night is who's going to start. And I think as players we're all willing to be kind of thrown in and out of the lineup.

"And it doesn't really change much for us as players. You just, you know, keep the same mindset and keep the same goal and just go out there and play hard."

Jake LaRavia (12) of the Los Angeles Lakers dribbles during a game against the Utah Jazz on Monday, Nov. 23, 2026, at Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles. NBAE via Getty Images

As for Redick, he said this roster lends itself to experimenting with different rotations, as he did by putting Ziaire Williams in the starting lineup for LaRavia in a loss against the Jazz on Nov. 18 and a win over the Kings on Nov. 20.

"This group is like malleable to lineup changes, you know, tweaking rotations," Redick said. "They understand that we're still trying to figure out the group and what's best for the group. So I don't think [Ziaire] or Jake was affected at all by you know the two games with Z in the starting lineup. And we were really good with Jake in the starting lineup. We were going to go back to it at some point. We went back to it [Monday], and he played a great game."

Keyonte George #3 of the Utah Jazz drives against Ziaire Williams #11 of the Los Angeles Lakers on Monday, Nov. 23, 2026, in Los Angeles. Getty Images

The Lakers have won 11 of their last 12 games, including five of their last victories coming while Austin Reaves has been sidelined because of a left heel bruise.

Things are clicking. The chemistry is great. The locker room has good vibes.

And everyone seemingly is focused on the bigger picture instead of individual accolades or perceived slights.

"At the end of the day, we have a lot of guys who haven't been able to give it their all to win, and whenever we're able to, I feel like we're going to give it our heart and give it our all," Collin Sexton said.

"And I feel like [general manager] Rob [Pelinka] did a great job of bringing guys in that's ready to be selfless, but also ready to do whatever needed to win, and play whatever role that is. So, I think when you have a locker room full of guys who want to win more than themself, and no one cares about who's the hero at the end of the day, it's like we're going to give it our all."

#2759. NFL Thanksgiving week games: Ranking the 5 weekday games by what's on the line

The NFL went out of its way to schedule five compelling matchups for Thanksgiving Eve, Thanksgiving and Black Friday.

The schedule comes out in May, and things can change dramatically over six months. Yet four of the five matchups have held up very well. That's not a bad percentage, even if the Eagles and Cowboys have let us down. Everyone will watch those two marquee franchises anyway.

There's a lot on the line in terms of the playoff race during this week. We rank the most important games, in terms of what's at stake.

We could look back on this game as the one that determined where the AFC championship game is played. The Bills lead the conference at 9-1, but the 8-2 Chiefs can pull even with a win and also clinch the head-to-head tiebreaker. The 8-2 Broncos also will have a big say in the race for the No. 1 seed, as could the Jaguars and Bengals who are each 7-3. But a big part of the playoff picture will be revealed in the primetime Thanksgiving game.

The Bills are trying to win their first Super Bowl, and a No. 1 seed would help that quest. The Bills are 0-4 in the playoffs against the Chiefs in the Josh Allen/Patrick Mahomes era but three of those games came in Kansas City. A win Thursday night would probably ensure the Bills don't have to play at Arrowhead Stadium in January.

Josh Allen has consistently felt the pain from the Chiefs in big games.

The game will go a long way in determining the NFC North race. The Bears and Lions are tied for first place at 8-2, and the winner Thursday will have a one-game lead and an edge in the tiebreaker. They meet again in Week 17, but Thursday will shape the race over December.

The Vikings aren't out of the race either at 7-3, and the Packers are still lingering at 6-4. The NFC North is really good, and whoever wins it will have earned it.

The Lions keep overcoming injuries and have won six in a row. The Bears are on a roll too; they haven't trailed during a five-game winning streak. There was a long stretch in which the Lions' traditional Thanksgiving game didn't matter much because they weren't very good. Detroit has gotten a lot better and this game is one of the most important of the season in terms of division races.

The NFL practically invented a Thanksgiving Eve holiday as an excuse to put a game on Wednesday. At least it made it a good matchup.

This game is huge in a competitive NFC wild-card race. The Rams' chances of going to the playoffs would rise from 34% to 47% with a win, according to The Athletic, while the Packers' playoff odds would fall from 40% to 25%. If the Packers win they'll have a 61% chance of making it while the Rams' odds would fall all the way to 16%.

It's stunning to think that with a loss, the overwhelming preseason Super Bowl favorite would have worse than a one-in-five shot of even making the postseason field.

The teams are on opposite ends of recent injury news. The Rams found out that receiver Puka Nacua (knee) will miss the rest of the season. Meanwhile, the Packers will get edge rusher Micah Parsons back into the lineup for the first time since he tore his ACL last December. But it might not matter for Green Bay if it loses a key game in a tough NFC wild-card field.

The Broncos and Steelers are going in different directions. The Broncos improved to 8-2 and have a very easy remaining schedule after facing many top teams in the first half of the season. The Steelers were 6-2 a couple weeks ago, but then were blown out by the Bengals and took a bad loss to an Eagles team that had lost seven in a row. At 6-4, the Steelers are suddenly more vulnerable in the wild-card race, especially with a Week 13 matchup against the 4-6 Texans coming up. A loss to Denver would knock Pittsburgh closer to the glut of teams trying to stay in the mix for a playoff spot.

The Broncos' game against the Steelers is one of their toughest remaining, and a win would help them solidify their spot atop the AFC West. The Chiefs have a much tougher remaining schedule (second-toughest to only the Rams, according to DVOA), including a game at Buffalo on Thanksgiving. It's hard to imagine the Broncos running away with the division title, but there's a possibility they could find themselves with a one-game lead after Week 12 with a much easier path the rest of the way.

Of the 10 teams playing between Wednesday and Friday, nine have legitimate playoff hopes. The Eagles' chances of making it to the postseason are less than 1%, according to NFL.com. They're a very disappointing 3-7.

Still, it would be nice to ruin their division rival's playoff chances. The Cowboys have had plenty of defensive issues but still have a 22% chance to make the playoffs because the NFC East isn't very good this season. They can't, however, afford a loss to the Eagles.

There is some playoff intrigue to the middle game on Thanksgiving. Just not nearly as much as any of the other four games during this week.

#2757. What's ahead for AI financing after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang departs

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.

Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the company. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive.

Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change.

"Although we expect the company to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate new multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said in a note Thursday.

The news of Huang's resignation comes after investors were already concerned about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.

Tech bond yields have risen and spreads have widened on credit default swaps, most notably in lower-rated names. Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier.

On Friday, the yield on Nvidia's 4.5% bond due in 2031 sat at 5.717%, nearly 5% higher week to date. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

Tech stocks slumped Friday with the Nasdaq 100 closing down 1.2% as markets continued to digest the Nvidia news. Yields on hyperscaler bonds ticked slightly higher on Friday, signaling the broader concern about AI debt lingers.

It's the smaller AI companies that could ultimately see an impact if Nvidia makes any changes to its AI financing. The company had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July.

Neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are all in Nvidia's portfolio. Their shares were down sharply Thursday.

CoreWeave, which has become the poster child for AI debt fears, saw its bond yields retreat after its quarterly earnings on Tuesday eased investor concerns. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 14.79% on Friday after climbing to 16.7% last week. The spread on its five-year CDS also dropped more than 17% week to date, although it remained above 1,000 — which is generally considered a sign of distress.

It remains unclear how Nvidia's support for those companies may change, said CreditSights analyst Andy Li.

"We don't know what the ultimate strategy for Nvidia is going to be coming out the other side," he said.

"However, I think directionally, just given the fact that Jensen was so crucial in selling the Nvidia story and being a very aggressive deal maker, it's likely that a lot of this creative deal-making and circular financing and equity and credit support is going to moderate," he added.

CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC Wednesday, before Huang's departure, that Nvidia "is not one person."

"There are thousands of people over there that interface with thousands of people at my company every day. They integrate on the technology. They integrate on the physical infrastructure. They integrate on the networking," he said in an interview with "Squawk on the Street." "They have been a great partner for us for years. They will continue to be a great partner for us."

Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, doesn't see any big changes in terms of Nvidia's relevance or its ability to finance for now. As CFO, Kress was involved in the financing deals, and the search for a permanent CEO is going to take some time, he noted.

The real issue is just how much money the company will want to lend for AI financing, rather than, say using its hundreds of billions in free cash flow for other purposes, like share buybacks, capex, or acquisitions.

"Big companies like Nvidia and Meta, they're holding all the cards," he said. "When they decide that the game is over, that's it — it's going to be curtains for some of these smaller companies."

— CNBC'S Kif Leswing and Isabel O'Brien contributed reporting.

#2756. Utah drops criminal charges against Kalshi founders after company suspended operations in state

Utah on Tuesday dismissed criminal charges against Kalshi and its two co-founders following the decision by the prediction market platform on Monday to suspend operations in the state.

The state originally filed the 14 criminal charges against the company and founders Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara on Oct. 28, claiming that Kalshi operated an illegal gambling operation in the state.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the federal regulator for prediction markets which views itself as the sole body that can develop rules over the growing industry — sued Utah the day before the state announced its charges.

Mansour and Lara were slated to appear in a Utah district court on Dec. 4, according to court documents.

However, Kalshi suspended operations in Utah on Monday, citing legal uncertainty. Utah Attorney General Derek Brown celebrated the decision in a statement announcing the move to dismiss the state's charges.

"Every company in this space should take note," he said. "If they promote, support, or enable gambling, we will hold them accountable."

Brown's office noted in the statement that dismissal is without prejudice, meaning if Kalshi were to begin operations again in the state the charges could be refiled.

"Good faith jurisdictional disagreements should never be criminalized," Kalshi's general counsel Yaakov Roth said in a post on X. "We stand ready to work with State AGs on reasonable interim measures until courts resolve the dispute over who regulates prediction markets."

While Kalshi faces legal setbacks in Utah, it faced some relief in New York on Monday when a state judge denied an emergency temporary restraining order against the company to halt its operations in the jurisdiction. The court will hear arguments on the matter again in January.

Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

#2755. Colts sign Shane Buechele and Wanya Morris in flurry of roster moves, place Caden Curry on IR

The Indianapolis Colts made a series of roster moves Tuesday, signing quarterback Shane Buechele from the Buffalo Bills' practice squad, promoting defensive end Carl Lawson to the 53-man roster and placing rookie defensive end Caden Curry on injured reserve. The organization also waived offensive tackle Charlie Heck while adding tight end Sean McKeon and defensive end Cam Sample to the practice squad, according to the team's official announcement.

Indianapolis wasn't finished there, as ESPN's Adam Schefter also reported that the Colts are signing offensive tackle Wanya Morris from the Dallas Cowboys' practice squad to their active roster, providing additional help to an offensive line that has been severely affected by injuries throughout the season.

The addition of Buechele comes just days after Indianapolis released Daniel Jones and announced that Anthony Richardson would return as the starting quarterback for the remainder of the 2026 season. With Richardson now receiving another opportunity to prove himself and Riley Leonard also on the roster, Buechele provides additional depth and experience in a quarterback room that has undergone considerable changes.

Buechele entered the NFL as an undrafted free agent with the Kansas City Chiefs in 2021 after playing collegiately at Texas and SMU. He spent several seasons developing behind Patrick Mahomes before joining Buffalo in 2023, where he spent time on both the active roster and practice squad. His only regular-season appearance came with Kansas City in 2025, when he completed seven of 14 passes for 88 yards. While he is unlikely to challenge Richardson for the starting job, his familiarity with NFL systems gives Indianapolis another option as it navigates the final six games of the season.

Morris, meanwhile, represents an interesting addition given the current state of the Colts' offensive line. The 26-year-old was selected in the third round of the 2023 NFL Draft by Kansas City and appeared in 43 games, making 16 starts during his three seasons with the Chiefs. He was traded to Atlanta during the offseason before being released in August, eventually joining Dallas' practice squad.

Indianapolis has been forced to make significant adjustments at offensive tackle following injuries to Bernhard Raimann and Jalen Travis. With Raimann dealing with a concussion and Travis sidelined by a knee injury, the Colts started Luke Tenuta at left tackle and moved Matt Goncalves to right tackle against Houston. Morris provides another experienced option at a position where the team has struggled to maintain continuity, while Heck's departure ends a brief stint in Indianapolis after signing with the organization on October 29.

On the defensive side, the promotion of Lawson comes at the expense of losing another promising young contributor.

Curry, a sixth-round selection in the 2026 NFL Draft, has appeared in all 11 games this season, recording 14 tackles, one sack, two fumble recoveries and 12 special teams stops. The former Ohio State defensive end has provided useful depth along the defensive line while establishing himself as a dependable contributor on special teams. His placement on injured reserve means he will be required to miss at least four games, a disappointing development for a rookie who had begun carving out a role within the organization.

Lawson should help compensate for that absence, providing Indianapolis with an experienced pass rusher who has recorded 32 sacks across his NFL career. The former Cincinnati Bengals fourth-round pick joined the Colts' practice squad in October and was previously elevated for the team's matchup against Jacksonville, recording one tackle. Although he is no longer the player who consistently generated pressure earlier in his career, he offers additional experience to a defensive front that has already undergone considerable changes following DeForest Buckner's departure.

The Colts also added two familiar NFL veterans to their practice squad in McKeon and Sample.

McKeon returns to Indianapolis after previously spending time with the organization during the 2024 and 2025 seasons, as well as participating in this year's offseason program and training camp. His addition provides additional tight end depth following Mo Alie-Cox's placement on injured reserve earlier this month.

Sample, meanwhile, was originally selected by Cincinnati in the fourth round of the 2021 NFL Draft and has appeared in 61 career games, recording seven sacks. The veteran defensive end has spent time with the Bengals, 49ers and Falcons, and could provide another option for Indianapolis should additional injuries occur along the defensive line.

With the Colts sitting at 3-8 and preparing to face the New York Giants on Sunday, the latest moves reflect an organization attempting to manage mounting injuries while continuing to evaluate its roster for the future. Richardson's return has already brought significant changes to the offense, and the additions of Buechele and Morris provide some much-needed depth at two important positions.

While none of these transactions is likely to dramatically change the team's outlook over the final six games, they should help Indianapolis navigate the remainder of an increasingly difficult season while giving several players an opportunity to demonstrate whether they deserve a role moving forward.

#2754. Is a bottom in for the Nasdaq-100? Charts to watch

(See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.)

Is the Nasdaq-100's recent bounce a sign that the bottom is in? We're going to look at several charts to help answer that question.

First, let's remember how we got here. In September, the NDX broke out from a bullish cup-and-handle pattern, producing a 33,200-upside target. That breakout quickly failed, however, and gave way to a bearish pattern that broke down aggressively two weeks ago.

The decline brought the index relatively close to its 26,350 downside target before the current rebound began.

Zooming out, it's telling to see where the bounce originated. Three important forms of support converged in the 25,000-26,000 area:

This confluence of support helped encourage buying after a roughly 15% decline.

For perspective, we also see what larger drawdowns of 20%, 30%, 40%, and 50% would look like … a lot worse.

The following chart tracks NDX drawdowns from 52-week highs going back to just after the financial crisis. Only a handful of declines exceeded 20%, and three produced relatively quick reversals: late 2018, the Covid lows in 2020 and April 2025.

Historically, buying into declines of approximately 15%–25% has generally paid off, even when additional downside occurred first (yellow highlights).

The chart also highlights previous declines of 10%–16% in green, putting the current pullback into perspective.

The major exception was 2022, when the NDX eventually declined nearly 36% over approximately 10 months ... a much worse outcome, which many investors are concerned could happen again now.

That raises the key question: Are we experiencing another routine correction, or the early stages of a larger bear market?

One important clue will be how far this bounce progresses.

Any rally that fails to reclaim the previous highs could establish a significant lower high. Additional lower highs would provide stronger evidence of a developing, longer downtrend.

We saw this in March 2022, when that first sharp rebound effort failed to reach the previous high before a much more severe decline followed.

The bottom line: The current bounce is encouraging, particularly given where it originated and knowing how well buying prior 10-20% drawdowns has paid off.

From here, it's all about the follow through.  We don't need to see new highs right away, but any rally from here that's met with another wave of strong selling could reignite downside momentum.

Frank Cappelleri is the founder and president of CappThesis, an independent research firm that helps active investors through time-tested chart and statistical analysis. #2753. Lakers avoid another embarrassment to Jazz by turning 4th quarter tables

The Lakers' offensive malaise, if it had to happen, came at an ideal time.

Because if the quality of competition were higher, the Lakers probably would've had a worse homestand over the last week.

Luka Doncic (77) of the Los Angeles Lakers handles the ball against the Utah Jazz during a game on Monday, Nov. 23, 2026, in Los Angeles. NBAE via Getty Images

But with their 109-94 victory over the Jazz on Monday night at Crypto.com Arena in front of the soon-to-be franchise owners Josh Kushner and Bob Iger, the Lakers avoided another disaster of a loss after blowing a 16-point lead.

The Lakers improved to 15-3 with the victory, going 3-1 on the homestand that included wins over the Hornets, Kings and a loss to the Jazz last week.

Cameron Carr #43 of the Los Angeles Lakers drives to the basket against the Utah Jazz on Monday, Nov. 23, 2026, at Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles. NBAE via Getty Images

Despite struggling with their 3-point shooting for the third consecutive game, the Lakers took a 53-42 lead going into halftime after being up 51-36 earlier in the second quarter thanks to their defense.

They held the Jazz to 36.7% shooting (18 for 49) in the first two quarters, and scored 11 points off Utah's 10 turnovers.

But the Jazz chipped away at their deficit quickly, turning what was a Lakers' double-digit lead into a 57-56 lead for Utah with just over eight minutes left in the third.

The Lakers' response was what they needed it to be.

Luka Doncic (77) of the Los Angeles Lakers shoots against the Utah Jazz on Monday, Nov. 23, 2026, at Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles. NBAE via Getty Images

They outscored the Jazz 53-37 in the final 20 minutes, leaning on their defense to win in ways they haven't needed to for most of the season. That is a stark departure from how the team has played the final frame nearly all season.

The Lakers held the Jazz to 17 points on 31.6% shooting (6 for 19) in the fourth.

Collin Sexton (10) of the Los Angeles Lakers handles the ball against the Utah Jazz on Monday, Nov. 23, 2026, at Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles. NBAE via Getty Images

Luka Dončić led the Lakers with 28 points, eight assists and four rebounds, but once again struggled with his shot (8 for 24, 3 for 14 on 3s).

Jake LaRavia (15 points, 10 rebounds), Matisse Thybulle (14 points), Collin Sexton (12 points) and Walker Kessler (10 points, 12 rebounds) all scored in double figures.

#2752. Congress shreds Nvidia's 'outrageous' decision to bring back Huang: 'Failure of character'

Members of Congress from both parties on Monday expressed outrage and incredulity, and doubled down on their calls for investigations, after Nvidia announced it has reinstated Jensen Huang as its president and CEO.

The resurrection of Huang, who had resigned from the artificial intelligence behemoth just 11 days earlier, raises more questions about the company's decision-making and the Trump administration's national security assessments, on top of existing concerns about Nvidia's advanced AI chips being diverted to China, the lawmakers said.

"It's inexplicable to me why they want this guy back as CEO," Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., a China hawk who is retiring from Congress, told CNBC in a phone interview. "To me it's a failure of character."

President Donald Trump told CNBC in an extended interview later Monday morning that he personally intervened to convince Nvidia's board to bring Huang back, saying, "I made the deal."

Bacon, chairman of the House Subcommittee on Cyber, Information Technologies, and Innovation, said he wants the next Congress to conduct thorough oversight, while questioning the Trump administration's motives.

"Somebody's responsible for this, and it may be" Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose department is responsible for setting U.S. export controls on AI chips, Bacon said. "But I think we should get to the bottom of this."

Huang, who is scheduled to testify before multiple committees on Capitol Hill starting Dec. 1, is "going to get high scrutiny in a bipartisan way when he comes next week," Bacon said.

Huang's closed-door appearance before a trio of House committees is on the schedule, as the panels seek answers on the national security implications of Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, MS NOW reported. The Senate banking committee announced after Huang's reinstatement that he will appear for a public hearing Dec. 3.

John Fisher of Trident, a spokesman for Huang, declined to comment on the Nvidia CEO's scheduled appearances.

"He better be there," Rep. Gabe Amo, D-R.I., a member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, told CNBC about Huang's scheduled Dec. 1 appearance. His reinstatement will only intensify congressional probes into Nvidia and its government connections, Amo predicted.

"I think it frankly broadens the scope of the query, and it makes Howard Lutnick and his dealings — supporting his nepo children's operation at Cantor Fitzgerald — party to inquiry as well as any other administration official that has facilitated a status quo in which chips can be sold to China or Chinese operated intermediaries who don't intend good things for the American people," said Amo, referring to the financial firm run by Lutnick's sons that has business ties to Nvidia.

A Cantor spokesperson didn't comment directly when asked about Amo's comments, saying the firm "holds no material proprietary position in Nvidia" and noting its Nvidia positions "arise primarily from equity swaps executed for clients."

The Commerce Department didn't immediately respond to requests to comment on Bacon's and Amo's remarks.

Nvidia in a statement Monday said it "received input from senior levels of the United States government" and that it is confident that Huang's reinstatement "poses no national security risk."

David Rudenstine, a constitutional law professor and national security scholar at Cardozo School of Law, said the frenzy around Huang's comeback is secondary to lingering national security concerns."The real responsibility for national security is with the administration and not with the CEO of a private company," Rudenstine told CNBC."You're opposed to China getting the chips. You recognize that the intermediary companies are sending chips to China, and you don't put a stop to it. I don't get it," he said.

The CEO's reinstatement, while celebrated by the White House and in Silicon Valley, led to heightened calls on Capitol Hill to seek answers on AI chip exports to China and what the Trump administration's role has been in facilitating that.

"We are sending high-end computer chips to China, and yet we're saying we want to win the AI war. It's a contradiction, and it's a failure of leadership in the White House," Bacon told CNBC.

Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, told CNBC in an emailed statement that Huang's return "proves that under Trump, Vance, and Rubio, national security is for sale to the highest bidder."

"We will all pay the price of letting China plunder America's cutting edge technology. Democrats will be pushing for accountability for anyone in the administration that put corrupt deals over our country's security," Wyden, who is also a Senate Intelligence Committee member, said.

Trump in a Truth Social post Monday added that Attorney General Todd Blanche "has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."

Lawmakers, who have already launched multiple investigations related to Huang, Nvidia and related entities, quickly filed in to question those conclusions.

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., a close Trump ally and a former CEO, criticized the move and called for a congressional briefing "as soon as possible" on Huang's reinstatement.

"Nvidia's board is free to vote however they want, but the federal government owes the American people answers about what actually happened," Scott told CNBC in an emailed statement. "This looks terrible on its face, and it drives home the need for Congress to be informed on the full impact of Jensen Huang's actions on our national security and economy."

Rep. Scott Peters, D-Calif., a member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, told CNBC that it's still not clear to what degree Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy might have compromised national security.

"The fact that the president of the United States is involved in putting him back in there, presumably because maybe he has stock or he just cares about the stock market, it's really reached a bizarre place," Peters said. "And obviously that man has not learned anything from the election about what people think of him, or he doesn't care."

Monday's move also gave fuel to lawmakers who have already questioned Trump, his administration or Nvidia.

"The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., said in a statement via the Senate Banking Committee, where she is the top Democrat and is expected to become chair in January.

Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, more tersely questioned the official assurances that Huang poses no risks to national security.

"No national security risk? Based on what?" he wrote on X.

Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, D-Ill., who serves on the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, in an X post called Nvidia's decision to reinstate Huang "outrageous."

"We still don't know what information Chinese intelligence may have obtained from him, and neither the government nor Nvidia's own board has completed its investigation," wrote Krishnamoorthi, who is also a member of the House Oversight and Intelligence panels.

— CNBC's Dan Mangan, Garrett Downs and Luke Fountain contributed to this report.
