#2751. ESPN hints at potentially massive contract extension for Caleb Williams

Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams could be about to rewrite the contract record books this coming offseason.

At this point, it goes without saying that the third-year signal-caller will get a monster bag as Chicago's franchise quarterback when he becomes eligible for a contract extension this coming spring. ESPN's Courtney Cronin suggested as much in her latest blurb on the Bears and the top extension candidates for each team (aka Williams).

But her projection makes my preseason estimates sound tame.

"Chicago's front office has an incentive to get ahead of a rapidly inflating QB market, which will see the likes of C.J. Stroud and Lamar Jackson come to the table, along with others in Williams' draft class. Though Williams said in September that "money's not a motivating factor for me," his top-10 play on a contending team could lead to him earning around $70 million per year. Signing Williams early would allow the Bears to keep his 2027 cap hit low while prorating a massive signing bonus into future years," she wrote.

Then again, perhaps it shouldn't be surprising.

Right now, Patrick Mahomes boasts the highest average annual value among NFL quarterbacks, earning $63.09 million per year on his reworked contract, followed by Dak Prescott ($60 million) and Josh Allen ($55 million). At least four quarterbacks—Jackson, Stroud, Williams, and Drake Maye—are in line to potentially break those records this offseason as the salary cap continues to climb. (Jayden Daniels is a sneaky candidate as well, though his struggle to stay healthy could hold him back slightly.)

Of the five names listed above, only Jackson is definitively a better player than Williams. Moreover, Williams might be the only one of those players to lead their teams to the playoffs this season, which would be his second trip to the postseason in a row. Throw in his major improvement as a passer, and you have the recipe for a gargantuan payday.

What will be curious, however, is how Williams handles the contract situation in reality.

The young quarterback, who has plenty of endorsements and outside investments, isn't hurting for cash. While he shouldn't take a lowball offer simply for the sake of a hometown discount, it wouldn't be shocking to see him hold back on breaking the bank just enough to make sure the Bears can keep players in town. After all, quarterbacks are important, but they can't win Super Bowls alone.

With the race to $70 million AAV likely to be intense, maybe paying Williams that amount is inevitable for the Bears. But when you have a franchise quarterback, you pay him like one. Fortunately for the Bears, Williams seems like the kind of player who can be worth the price.

#2750. A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process

Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct. 6. The market despises uncertainty, and losing a visionary founder, particularly one without a well-telegraphed succession plan, makes it worse.

However, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive. Trading in the $160s, Nvidia's valuation has taken a big haircut, yet its underlying business fundamentals remain largely intact. While Huang was the architect of Nvidia's AI dominance, the company's moat — superior GPUs, the CUDA software ecosystem, and networking expertise — does not walk out the door with him. The company's structural advantage in the global artificial intelligence rollout persists.

Buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options.  Huang's departure guarantees that Nvidia will be operating under a cloud of transition for the foreseeable future. Executing a permanent CEO search while navigating global regulatory scrutiny takes time. Consequently, Nvidia's implied volatility (IV)—the market's pricing of expected future price swings — has spiked to highs not seen since the tariff tantrum in the first half of 2025, and this elevated IV is highly likely to persist for several months as the leadership drama slowly unfolds.

This prolonged period of high implied volatility can be a goldmine for option sellers, specifically those executing options overlays such as covered call strategies. When you buy NVDA shares at these depressed levels and simultaneously sell out-of-the-money call options against your position, the premiums you collect are directly tied to IV. Because fear and transition-related uncertainty have dramatically inflated these option prices, the income generated from selling covered calls is now significantly higher than usual.

This lowers the risk profile of holding the stock considerably over time. Consistently collecting these inflated premiums systematically lowers your overall cost basis in the underlying shares. If the stock trades sideways or recovers slowly during the CEO search, you are generating an outsized cash yield on a stagnant asset. If the stock experiences further downside turbulence, the heavy premium income acts as a substantial downside buffer, meaningfully reducing the strategy's overall risk over time.

By deploying a persistent covered call strategy, investors can leverage the exact fear driving the stock down to generate robust, risk-reducing income while maintaining exposure to the undeniable future of AI.

#2747. Berkshire breaks out to record high with fourth-quarter rally reaching 19%

(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)

Berkshire Hathaway's red-hot shares are ending a strong week with four consecutive fresh record high closes.

Since the rally began with the start of the fourth quarter on October 1, the Class A shares have closed at record highs 11 times as they soared 19.1%.

The much more widely held B shares closed at new highs just 10 times but are also up 19.1% from their near-term low.

The gains are in sharp contrast to the S&P 500's 1.2% dip as investors appear to be seeing Berkshire as a relatively safe haven amid worries about AI stocks and spending.

Both Berkshire classes were up 3.9% on the week as the S&P advanced by 2.5%, its best week since early August.

Berkshire's B shares are now 7.5 percentage points ahead of the benchmark for the year so far.

After erasing their post-Buffett CEO announcement losses three weeks ago, Berkshire shares are now up almost 10% since last year's shareholders meeting.

They've gained around 29% since last August's lows and are up around 18% year-to-date.

Berkshire Hathaway is due to disclose its quarterly equity portfolio snapshot on Monday when it files its Q3 13F with the SEC.

We won't know for sure until then, but numbers in the company's third quarter 10-Q, released last Saturday, indicate Berkshire continued to reduce its Bank of America stake.

It would be the ninth consecutive quarter of selling.

As of June 30, Berkshire reported holding 483.4 million BAC shares valued now at $24.7 billion, it's fifth largest equity position.

On June 30, 2024, before the selling began, Berkshire owned just over 1 billion shares valued at $41.1 billion.

Since then, the number of shares in the portfolio has decreased by 53.2%, not including any Q3 sales, while the stock price has increased by 28.3%.

If there had been no reductions, the position would be worth $52.7 billion.

The belief Berkshire sold more BAC shares in the third quarter is based on a $372 million reduction in the cost basis for equities categorized by the company as "banks, insurance, and finance."

The 10-Q also reports $2.2 billion of pretax gains from equity sales.

Barron's notes Bank of America and American Express are the only financial stocks in the portfolio that have a cost basis low enough to generate a gain like that. Amex is one of the four stocks new CEO Greg Abel indicated would be held for "decades" to come in his February letter to shareholders.

In any case, Berkshire's almost 23% stake in Amex would have required it to quickly disclose any sales.

Based on the numbers in the 10-Q, the warrants Berkshire received as part of a 2011 $5 billion investment in the bank that it used in 2017 to buy 700 million shares at $7.14 each, and BAC's average stock price in the quarter, Barron's estimates 30 to 40 million shares may have been sold.

That would be roughly in line with the 30.2 million shares sold in the second quarter.

The case isn't as good, but Barron's thinks Berkshire may have bought more Alphabet shares in the period. That's based on a $2.3 billion increase in the cost basis for the category that includes Google's parent.

Overall, it looks like it will be a relatively quiet quarter with $2.4 billion in equity purchases and $2.8 billion in sales.

In the first quarter, Berkshire bought $15.9 billion and sold $24.1 billion of equities. In the second quarter, it purchased $23.5 billion and sold $3.7 billion.

All those numbers exclude the company's buybacks of its own stock.

In a term sheet filed early Friday, Berkshire Hathaway says it is selling more than 182 billion yen ($1.1 billion) worth of bonds with maturities between 2029 and 2056 and annual interest rates between 2.6% and 4.6%.

Bloomberg points out the rates, compared to benchmarks, are higher than its previous sale this year.

It quotes a fund manager as saying market sentiment "has become more sensitive," forcing issuers to make their offerings more attractive.

In April, Berkshire sold 272 billion yen ($1.7 billion) of bonds.

Berkshire uses the proceeds from the yen-denominated bonds to protect its ongoing investments in Japanese stocks from currency fluctuations.

Warren Buffett recommends Benjamin Graham's book, "The Intelligent Investor," and outlines what he considers Graham's three most important ideas.

WARREN BUFFETT: On investment books, if you're asking about that, I would recommend the first two books that Phil Fisher wrote back around 1960, "Common Sense [Stocks] and Uncommon Profits" and the second one ["Paths to Wealth Through Common Stocks"]. They're very good books.

You know, I obviously recommend, first and foremost, [Benjamin Graham's] "The Intelligent Investor," with chapters eight and 20 are the ones that you really should read.

Two of the — well, all of the important ideas in investing, really, are in that book, because there's only about three ideas. And those — two of them are emphasized in those two chapters...

One is that — to think of yourself — to think of investing as owning a business and not buying something that wiggles around in price.

And the second one is your attitude, which ties in with that, the attitude toward the market, that's covered in chapter eight. And if you have the proper attitude toward market movements, it's an enormous help in securities.

And the final chapter is on the margin of safety, which means, don't try and drive a 9,800-pound truck over a bridge that says it's, you know, "Capacity: 10,000 pounds." But go down the road a little bit and find one that says, "Capacity: 15,000 pounds."

#2745. Peterson: Here’s what Bessent’s about-face on Jensen Huang reveals about Trump and China

For a minute there, it seemed like someone in the Trump administration might actually be willing to stand up to China.

For about a week and a half, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was the face of an emerging harder line on Nvidia over the potential risks its co-founder Jensen Huang's affairs posed to national security. Bessent was giving voice to China hawks who had felt sidelined by the Trump administration's willingness to sell artificial intelligence chips to  China.

They see China's AI program as a major threat, and want to restrain its growth by cutting off the supply of advanced chips to China. The resignation of Huang, who pressed the Trump Administration to allow the exports, seemed to signal that the hawks had found new influence in Washington.

By this weekend, Bessent had softened his public resistance to Huang's reinstatement. That came just in time for Nvidia's board to reappoint Huang as CEO at President Donald Trump's urging.

Whether any real damage was done to national security isn't clear. But it is safe to say that the incoming Democratic majority in Congress won't take Trump at his word when he said on CNBC Monday that the Department of Justice "did a pretty good investigation" that exonerated Huang.

Congress will look deeply into the worries Bessent himself raised about Huang's acknowledged romantic relationship with a woman The New York Times and others have reported was a Chinese intelligence asset.

Nvidia's board said it had received assurances from top U.S. officials and had concluded his return wasn't a national security risk.

A top concern is whether China was able to use the affair to help divert Nvidia's high-end artificial intelligence chips toward helping its military. Bessent in a Nov. 13 interview with CNBC outlined the stakes.

"Any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts the — it hurts our great companies and in the AI race it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.

Bessent said that his department and others had wanted to blacklist Megaspeed, the company previously run by Alice Huang, Jensen Huang's paramour. But "Commerce has the pen," Bessent said.

The Commerce Department is headed by Secretary Howard Lutnick, Bessent's rival.

Putting Huang back at Nvidia wasn't originally Bessent's preference. He said in a Fox interview on Nov. 15 that the board should "go outside the company" to find a new leader. But by this past weekend, Bessent had apparently gotten on board with Trump's wishes.

"Jensen is on the outside now," Bessent told CBS on Sunday, in trying to explain his apparent policy shift.

Commerce has since taken steps to tighten some restrictions meant to prevent U.S. chips from helping China advance in the AI race.

But there is bipartisan worry about the Nvidia episode. "I think we need to catalog the damage that's been done," Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., told The Wall Street Journal. He said Lutnick had not responded to letters he sent saying the administration should be "taking the threats of communist China more seriously."

But Trump has clearly put an upper limit on how aggressively anyone in his administration can push back on China. The president said Monday that he was swayed by the pageantry in his visit to China last week.

Xi "met me at the plane, which is something they've never done, which was a sign," Trump said.

Trump said he felt like he needed to intervene to back Huang because the stock market was plummeting in the wake of Nvidia's troubles — a development he also blamed on Democrats' midterm victory.

"I watched our country lose $5 trillion because of a bad election," he said. "If I didn't get involved, you'd probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come." Now, its stock performance will be "unbelievable."

Bessent on Sunday played down the market risks. The company "continues to be fantastically profitable, and there is near unlimited demand for their chips worldwide," he told CBS.

Lutnick has embraced Trump's transactional urges. He has backed deals in which the U.S. takes equity stakes in companies such as Intel, saying the taxpayer deserves some of the upside.

Lutnick in January said he had heard Huang pitch Trump on allowing Nvidia to sell its relatively more advanced H200 chips into China.

"There are strong — two sides. We shouldn't sell them any or we should sell them." Where does he stand? "Right in the middle," Lutnick told Bloomberg. Trump decided to go ahead with the deal.

Bessent has said he is "neither a hawk nor a dove" on China, and is simply trying to manage the ultra-sensitive relationship between the world's two biggest economies. But the upshot of the Huang affair seems to be that Bessent wasn't able to sway the president on a matter that seemed cut-and-dried just days ago.

Trump said he discussed whether Huang should return to Nvidia with Lutnick, Bessent and Vice President JD Vance. "Howard Lutnick was very good. Very, he's very professional," Trump said on CNBC Monday.

"I call them the opposites, Scott and Howard," Trump added, before declaring them "both good."

#2742. Prime Joel Embiid is a thing of the past, and that’s OK for the Sixers

For a grand majority of Joel Embiid's tenure in Philadelphia, the Sixers have only gone as far as he dragged them. His on/off splits are the stuff of legend, particularly in the playoffs.

But as his injuries piled up in recent years, the Sixers began the process of pivoting away from him as their focal point. Tyrese Maxey, whom Embiid nicknamed "The Franchise" a few years ago, started to live up to that promise following the departure of James Harden.

The additions of LeBron James and Jaylen Brown this offseason led to an onslaught of questions about "alphas" and whether the Sixers could share the ball well enough to keep all of their stars happy. One 14-4 start later, their vibes are immaculate for now.

However, one rival scout doesn't believe it'll last.

"I think it's going to be a problem, and that could railroad them," the scout told ESPN's Tim MacMahon in reference to Embiid taking more of a backseat on offense this season. "I just don't buy it right now. He's going to want the ball more. He's going to get pissed. He's going to stop playing defense. He's going to stop running."

Thus far, the exact opposite has played out.

Through his first 14 games this season, Embiid is averaging only 20.4 per outing while shooting a career-worst 40.0 percent overall and 14.3 percent from deep. That hasn't caused him to check out on defense, though. Instead, he's averaging 8.9 rebounds per game—his most since the 2023-24 campaign—and he's looking more spry defensively than he has in years.

After the Sixers' season-opening win over the New York Knicks, Embiid told reporters that he planned to vie for a spot on the All-Defense teams like he did earlier in his career because "that changes everything for our team."

That is the exact right mentality for Embiid to have this season.

For years, he's quietly bemoaned the lack of offensive support that he's had around him. Yes, the likes of Harden, Paul George, Jimmy Butler and Ben Simmons have all cycled through Philadelphia over the past decade, but more often than not, the Sixers were drawing dead without a big game from the big fella. This year is the first time where that isn't the case on a night-to-night basis.

Look no further than their NBA Cup win over the reigning-Cup-champion Knicks. Embiid finished with 10 points on 3-of-12 shooting. Prior to that game, he had finished with 10 or fewer points only 15 times across his career, many of which he left early because of injuries. (Somewhat surprisingly, the Sixers went 7-8 in those games.)

Despite his cold-shooting night, Embiid found other ways to make an impact against the Knicks. He finished with seven rebounds, seven assists (trailing only LeBron James' eight dimes on the night), one steal and one block in 33 minutes. He was a plus-eight on the game, which was tied with LeBron for the best mark among the Sixers' starters.

Embiid already had a triple-double in the third game of the season, and he nearly notched another one against the Milwaukee Bucks on Saturday. Instead, he wound up settling for a 26-17-9 night. Ho hum.

Heading into the season, it was fair to wonder whether Embiid would be willing to take a step back on offense to focus on traditional big-man tasks such as rebounding, rim protection and screening. It was also unclear whether he still had the lateral agility to switch out on the perimeter without getting roasted alive. If not, would the Sixers be forced to keep him in drop coverage? What other tactical adjustments would they have to make to account for that?

It's still far too early in the season to take a full victory lap, but so far, so good on that front. Better yet, we're still a ways away from seeing this group's ceiling on offense as they continue to work on developing chemistry with one another.

"I think we've got a long way to go offensively," Embiid told reporters after the Sixers' win over the Chicago Bulls in early November. "A lot of it is efficiency, starting with me. A lot of guys have picked up, so it's up to me to kind of pick it up."

Embiid added that the Sixers were "on the right path" because they have the "right mentality, making plays for each other." He followed up with some revealing comments about why he might be struggling with his efficiency in the early going.

"For me, it's a little bit of an adjustment," he said. "I'm such a rhythm guy. Over the years, obviously I've had a lot of opportunities to just touch the ball almost every other possession. Sometimes you can just go four or five possessions where you don't touch the ball. That's where it's kind of like an adjustment. I'm not used to catch-and-shoot as much, I'm used to more creating for myself. So I'm working on that."

But lest that anonymous scout who spoke with MacMahon feel the need to start crowing about his prophecy, Embiid quickly shot down the notion that he'd allow his own offensive struggles to impact the rest of his game.

"My mindset is really whenever I have the ball, make plays," he said. "Make the game easy for all these guys. Making the right plays over and over. Setting screens. Get Tyrese as open as much as possible. Bron. All these guys. Just kind of being the hub and trying to get these guys open and make plays for them. That's really what the focus is on.

"And then on the other side, also, working on myself. How can I get back to that level of dominance without having as much touches as I'm used to? That's a work in progress. That's where really the struggle has been because, like I said, I'm a rhythm guy. I need to feel the ball. I need to touch the ball. When you don't, it's a little different. But it's a fun process, and I'm enjoying it, trying to find ways to get over the hump. But I feel like once I do and I figure it out and I can really be dominant, then the sky's the limit for us."

The version of Embiid who averages 30-plus points per game might be gone for good, particularly with this compilation of talent around him. That's completely OK. In fact, that's the point of assembling this level of talent around him.

There will still be some nights where Embiid has it going and the Sixers need him to bully an overmatched big man in the post and/or draw a parade of trips to the free-throw line. Against the Detroit Pistons in early November, he dominated poor BBall Paul and finished with 26 points and a season-high 15 rebounds. As Liberty Ballers' own Paul Hudrick noted, he hadn't pulled down that many boards in regulation of a regular-season game in almost three years.

The Sixers will need Embiid's threes to start dropping at some point just to keep defenses honest. But they no longer need him to be the MVP version of himself on a night-in, night-out basis. Maxey, LeBron, Jaylen Brown and VJ Edgecombe are here to shoulder some of that offensive burden, not to mention snipers like Anfernee Simons and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope off the bench.

Individually, Embiid has already done everything that he could have dreamed of accomplishing in the NBA. An MVP award, five All-NBA nods and seven All-Star selections later, the only thing left to do is win it all.

As long as he remains committed to focusing on the role that the Sixers need him to play this year, he'll have his best shot yet of doing so.

#2741. Anthropic shares fall below IPO price. Traders see even more pain

Anthropic shares are back trading below the IPO price after a 13% sell-off Tuesday and a 1.5% drop Monday, despite a broad rally in most big tech artificial intelligence names. Trading under $76 on Tuesday, the stock's now 8.5% below its initial public offering level and 34% beneath its intraday high of $115.

It took just four days for ANT to fall under its offering price, compared with 21 trading days for SpaceX, which rallied out of the gate.

Options volume on the stock is picking up as the shares drop and implied volatility jumps to 96, according to ThinkOrSwim data. Almost 500,000 options traded by noon ET on Tuesday for a total premium of about $250 million, the sixth-most active single-stock options in the market, SpotGamma data shows.

Almost 300,000 puts traded versus about 200,000 calls, but the sentiment implied by the trades was not overtly bearish, and judging by the biggest single trades of the day, traders are divided on what happens next.

The biggest single option trade of the day was a $7.5 million purchase of almost 11,000 75-strike puts expiring in mid-December. The trader paid above the ask, suggesting an eagerness to get the trade done at a cost of $6.85, according to SpotGamma. With Anthropic trading at $77, the position needs Anthropic to drop 11% by expiry to pay off.

"Anthropic remains bumpy as investors add risk to other names," said noted tech analyst Dan Ives.

Only one obvious call purchase appeared among the top 10 trades: a 3,000-lot purchase of 85-strike calls expiring Jan. 15 that cost $7.10 each, for a total of $2.2 million. That trade needs Anthropic to rally 19% within the next two months to break even.

Arguably the most interesting action was a string of almost a dozen put sales, ranging from $400,000 to $1.6 million each, all within moments of each other, selling the 120-strike puts expiring Dec. 18. The puts bring in $40 each, meaning the breakeven for the trade is at $80. Selling in-the-money puts in high-volatility stocks is often a way for traders to get long stock without the capital requirements of buying the underlying equity.

#2738. How Meta is using Instagram to get an ad boost from its Muse personal AI agent

Meta's ad-free Muse personal artificial intelligence agent is already helping the social media giant boost its advertising business, and it's happening through Instagram, multiple people told CNBC.

Instagram is a major advertising revenue engine for the social media giant, and the company is leveraging existing habits on the platform by prompting users to organize their saved posts in Muse.

About 20% of daily Instagram users save at least one post to the app per day, according to a person familiar with the details, who asked not to be named because the information is not public. Many of those saved items, the person said, are either shoppable items or ads.

A senior executive told CNBC that Muse, even without ads, "is still very valuable for our ads business because it raises conversions for advertisers." It does this by reducing friction in the shopping process and allowing users to go back to items later, said the executive, who asked not to be named because the details have not been reported publicly.

"It gives advertisers a way to get more ROI for the dollars they're already spending, and that's all because Muse is helping people shop," the executive said.

Mark Zuckerberg announced in Meta's last earnings call that 25% of Muse's users shop via the agentic tool — it's the most common use case for Muse — and the average purchase price is over $200. Zuckerberg said the company plans to take a small fee from transactions made through the agentic platform.

All that information about what people are shopping for with their agent is a valuable asset to target ads more precisely within Instagram. If consumers complete purchases with their Muse, that builds Meta's new revenue stream.

Meta's efforts to drive transactions seem to be paying off, and the buzz around Muse has made it a leader in agentic shopping.

In the week ending Nov. 22, 51% of all agentic orders were done by Meta's Muse, according to transactions measured by Forter Intelligence, an e-commerce analytics and cybertechnology company.

Meta dominates agentic AI shopping market share, according to Forter, which said that SpaceX's Grok held a 24% market share in that same time period, followed by 22% to OpenAI's ChatGPT. The remaining 3% is divided between Google and startup Instinct.

Meta is expected to eventually launch ads in Muse, though multiple people said that it's not under any financial pressure to do so and tends to take its time building an audience before monetizing it.

The people said that putting ads in the Muse feed, which is more akin to a newsfeed instead of responses to specific queries, would be a natural way for Meta to test ads on the platform.

#2735. Nvidia has lost $2 trillion in value. Here's what options traders expect from earnings

Jensen Huang's forced exit from Nvidia shocked Wall Street and Washington, wiped $2 trillion off its market value, and raised serious questions about national security and regulation of the AI complex. Traders, for the moment, must content themselves with the comparatively mundane business of Tuesday's earnings, and options traders are expecting big moves.

With volatility in the stock near the highest since April 2025, options traders are now pricing a 7% reaction in the stock after its report, the biggest implied move going into an Nvidia report since February 2025, and well above the median move of 3.2% over the last eight quarters.

Implied volatility reached 68 Monday, compared to under 40 in early October, according to ThinkOrSwim data. Nvidia vol reached a multi-year high above 92 in the aftermath of President Trump's tariff Liberation day in April '25. In other words, the company that for much of the AI boom was the most reliable winner in the market, is now more volatile than all but 35 companies in the S&P 500.

"Longer term, I see significant downside risk unless Nvidia can attract an exceptional leader, someone like Tim Cook or AMD's Lisa Su," Nigam Arora, founder of the Arora report, said in a text ahead of the company's after-market report on Tuesday.

Since hitting all-time highs in October, Nvidia shares have fallen 35%, shedding $2 trillion in market capitalization along the way. Including Nvidia, there are only five companies in the S&P 500 worth more than $2 trillion. However, there is evidence that bulls have been holding out hope while bears snatch up profits: the ratio of open puts to call contracts has actually widened towards calls, according to Barchart data. The ratio is currently 0.87, down from a one-year high of 1.02 two weeks ago and the lowest since the first week of October.

The most popular contract by volume on Monday was the 155-strike put expiring at the bell Monday, but the most popular trade for later expiry was the 160-strike call expiring Thursday, and the second-most-common purchase was the 190-strike call expiring Friday, SpotGamma data show.

One catch is that most call contracts traded Monday looked like neutral to bearish positions opened by traders selling calls. Of the 5 million options traded on Monday, 3 million were calls, but more were likely opened by sellers than buyers. Of the $2.3 billion in options premium traded on Nvidia Monday, $1.2 billion was tied to puts, SpotGamma data show.

With bears taking profits in puts the past month, there's another potential snag on open interest. There are very few open put contracts at or below the $157 level at which the stock closed Monday. That suggests any bad surprise would find many traders with little downside protection.

By the same token, there's notable open interest in call contracts from the 175-strike and above, suggesting profit-taking on a bounce could limit Nvidia's recovery past levels it breached over the past week.

Either way, Tuesday's earnings could provide fireworks.

#2734. Observations after Sixers' 5-game win streak ends with blowout loss to Blazers

Observations after Sixers' 5-game win streak ends with blowout loss to Blazers originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers' five-game winning streak was snapped Monday night by the Trail Blazers.

With a 128-111 defeat at Xfinity Mobile Arena, the Sixers dropped their first game of the year against Western Conference opposition and fell to 14-4. Portland improved to 11-6.

LeBron James had a season-high 23 points and six rebounds. Tyrese Maxey scored 22 points and Jaylen Brown added 20.

Deni Avdija led the Blazers with 31 points and seven assists. Donovan Clingan posted 15 points and 18 rebounds.

The Sixers were missing Joel Embiid (illness). Ja Morant (left hamstring strain) and Shaedon Sharpe (right knee meniscus surgery) were among Portland's sidelined players.

Next on the Sixers' schedule is a Wednesday night game vs. the Heat. Here are observations on their blowout loss to the Blazers:

Jabari Walker, listed at 6-foot-7, defied conventional wisdom by winning the opening tip-off against the 7-2 Cllingan. Maxey then canned a three-pointer.

Brown scored the Sixers' next four points with a pair of free throws and a short jumper. VJ Edgecombe's layup gave the team a 9-2 lead. Brown and Dean Wade both returned Monday after sitting out the last two games with left hamstring injuries.

Avdija got hot in the first quarter. He scored 11 quick points, made his first four field goals and helped the Blazers avoid a serious early deficit.

The Sixers took a 32-30 edge with 9.3 seconds left in the first when Walker jammed in a put-back dunk. The former Portland second-round draft pick played 17 minutes in his second start of the season and continued to look deserving of a rotation spot. He posted 10 points and five rebounds.

Adem Bona was available again following an eight-game absence with a cervical spine sprain. However, Dominick Barlow checked in first to back up Walker.

Barlow had an outstanding start to his night. He scored a clever lefty push shot over Clingan and threw down a dunk in the first quarter. Barlow also made a highlight defensive play in his opening stint, defending Avdija in isolation and rejecting his layup attempt.

Bona then subbed in for Barlow with 3:23 left in the first quarter. He had a positive first possession, grabbing an offensive rebound and driving in for a dunk.

Wade later played at center, too. Barlow logged 16 minutes and had six points. Bona recorded four points and two boards in five minutes. Sixers head coach Nick Nurse ended up using a 10-man rotation and did not play rookie guard Labaron Philon Jr. until fourth-quarter garbage time.

Overall, the Sixers' defense remained considerably worse without Embiid. The team also conceded 15 offensive rebounds, including five to Clingan.

"I think your rim protection and ability to do that with some size is always a focal point of being really good defensively," Nurse said. "And then you've got to do it a little bit by committee (with Embiid out). I thought, for the most part, I was looking at possessions where I liked our help into the paint. They were doing a good job of zinging it out.

"I didn't particularly like our (defense) back out. … There were a couple of times they missed those and still got rebounds. We were compacted in the lane with everybody because we didn't get back out, and then still giving up an offensive rebound as well. That's just playing through the possession, a little bit of energy, all that kind of stuff. … We just didn't do enough pieces well."

Brown delivered tons of efficient offense for the Sixers in the first half and sure didn't appear rusty. His layup late in the second quarter tied the game at 58-all. The five-time All-Star scored 19 first-half points on 8-for-10 shooting.

Avdija exceeded Brown's production, hitting heat-check threes, leaners through contact and just about everything he put up regardless of the defender. He tallied 25 points in the first half and shot 9 for 12 from the field.

James reached 16 points when he capped a high-scoring half by nailing a corner three. The contest was even at 69 apiece heading into halftime.

Monday's game was James' first of the season with three or more made three-pointers. The four-time MVP went 4 for 5 beyond the arc. He'd gone 10 for 46 (21.7 percent) over his first 13 games and was due for a good long-range night.

James was whistled for his third foul early in the third quarter. Brown picked up his fourth with 10:15 to go in the period, forcing him to sit for an extended stretch.

"I wasn't too happy about it. … I think that affected the game," Brown said. "It also affected my rhythm a little bit in the second half. I had to sit (almost) the whole third quarter. Coming back from injury, coming back from a hamstring thing, my body didn't really feel the same after that."

Brown noted postgame that he had "a little bit of soreness and stuff like that."

"I think everything will check out," he said. "The medical staff is on top of everything. Those hamstrings are tricky, so you want to make sure you play it the right way, be safe. I also don't want to miss a lot of games, so I might be out there, but I've also got to be smart. I think I played it the right way today."

Avdija stopped lighting up the Sixers in the third period, but the team still had another unimpressive defensive quarter. Portland posted 32 points in the third and built its lead to double figures in the opening minute of the fourth.

The game devolved into a blowout. An Avdija dunk put the Blazers' advantage at 22 points with 5:15 on the clock and the Sixers didn't have a miracle comeback in store.

Even with all their wins, there's no question the Sixers have been trending downward on defense over the past couple of weeks, allowing regular dribble penetration and plenty of comfortable threes.

They'll aim to raise their level on that side of the floor and expect Embiid's presence to be a major help once he's back in action.

"I think it's just mindset," Walker said. "We're capable when we want to. You need games like this every now and then just to remind you that it's not as easy as it feels sometimes. It takes effort every game.

"I think we can learn a lot from this. It's just part of the growing pains, but I'm confident we'll get back to that (early-season) level of defense. We have what it takes."

#2733. Trump Account contributions from friends and family pass $1 billion mark, Treasury says

Families and friends have collectively contributed more than $1 billion to Trump Accounts since the July 4 launch, bringing total deposits to more than $9 billion, the U.S. Department of the Treasury said Tuesday in an announcement exclusively provided to CNBC.

The $1 billion in Trump Account deposits come from more than 3 million individuals, according to the agency. That total does not include the government's seed money or philanthropic gifts from donors such as Michael and Susan Dell.

"The American people are investing in Trump Accounts with a generosity that represents the finest instincts of our national character," U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a written statement.

"Trump Accounts are a transformative government program for American children. It is the largest government start-up in American history," Internal Revenue Service CEO Frank Bisignano said in the statement.

Also known as 530A accounts, Trump Accounts are open to any U.S. child under 18 with a Social Security number.

Parents, guardians, grandparents and others can collectively contribute up to $5,000 per child per year in after-tax dollars up until the year before the beneficiary turns 18. The annual contribution limit is indexed for inflation after 2027.

Children born from 2025 through 2028 may receive a one-time $1,000 deposit from the Treasury. Other funds may also be available, depending on certain criteria.

Most recently, Snowflake chairman Frank Slootman and his wife, Brenda, announced they would give $1,000 to every child in Montana born in 2023 and 2024.

The Treasury rolled out temporary regulations at the end of September that allow Trump Accounts to hold stock donations, a move meant to pave the way for more philanthropic gifts, according to Bisignano.

These rules make it more attractive for donors, according to Ben Henry-Moreland, a certified financial planner with advisor platform Kitces.com.

Wealthy founders and shareholders can avoid the capital gains taxes that would otherwise be triggered by selling appreciated stock and donating the cash proceeds. However, it also means some children's wealth accumulation could be tied to the performance of individual companies.

The Trump Accounts milestone comes as more billionaires and companies pledge support to the investment account for kids.

In an exclusive interview with CNBC's "Squawk on the Street," Bessent on Nov. 20 announced an Anthropic co-founder would make a "large gift" to Trump Accounts over the next few weeks.

A source briefed on the announcement confirmed that the Anthropic co-founder Bessent referred to is Tom Brown and that it is part of his broader philanthropic plan.

"This is the perfect vehicle to donate to the children of America, and they will receive 100% of the proceeds," Bessent said.

Elon Musk wrote in an X post that he plans to give every kid in America a share of SpaceX sometime in 2027, which experts say may come via Trump Accounts.

In a separate funding announcement, SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said she would donate around 2 million shares of her and her husband's SpaceX stock to the accounts.

On Monday, Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner, founder of Invest America and an architect of Trump Accounts, told CNBC's "Halftime Report" that more large-scale donations may be in the pipeline.

"I want everybody to own shares of Nvidia, in Anthropic, in OpenAI," he said. "We created 70 million stock accounts — free stock accounts — for every single citizen under the age of 18 to do just that, and we have huge announcements coming."

#2730. Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double

Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers stayed unbeaten Saturday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena, earning a 127-116 win over the Bucks and improving to 3-0 on the season.

Joel Embiid had his 10th career regular-season triple-double, tallying 28 points, 11 rebounds and 10 assists.

On his 30th birthday, Jaylen Brown posted 27 points and five assists. Tyrese Maxey had 26 points. VJ Edgecombe scored 17 and grabbed 13 boards.

The Sixers' absences on the first night of a back-to-back included LeBron James (low back/sciatica management). Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said pregame that he did not know yet who would be available for his team's matchup with the Pistons on Sunday.

Here are observations on the Sixers' victory Saturday:

Dean Wade made his Sixers debut and started in James' place. He'd missed the first two games of the regular season with a left ankle sprain.

The 3-and-D forward scored the night's first points by a sinking a corner three-pointer on the opening possession.

Embiid also had a sharp start. He moved well, made good decisions and served as the main hub of his team's offense in the early going.

The Sixers' seven-time All-Star center has often enjoyed facing Myles Turner. He entered the night with an average of 29.4 points in 18 previous games against the Bucks big man.

Embiid did a little bit of everything in the first quarter, posting eight points, four assists and four rebounds over nine minutes. After snatching an offensive board, Embiid drained a fadeaway jumper to give the Sixers a 10-1 lead.

One of Embiid's assists was quite stylish. He found Edgecombe open beyond the arc with a behind-the-back bounce pass. Edgecombe knocked down the shot and wound up going 3 for 4 from three-point range in the first quarter.

The Sixers added rookie Labaron Philon Jr. to their rotation. Jabari Walker stayed in the mix, though he didn't enter until the 7:36 mark of the second quarter.

Philon played four minutes in his NBA debut and missed his lone shot attempt, a corner three. On defense, Philon allowed a couple of blow-bys off the dribble. He generally looked like he belonged on offense, albeit without any production in his brief run.

Maxey banked in a half-court heave at the first-quarter buzzer to put the Sixers up nine points. The Sixers couldn't carry forward any momentum, however, and began the second quarter poorly.

Adem Bona had another rough stint amid a subpar start to the season. After Anfernee Simons missed a transition layup try, Ryan Rollins' three lifted the Bucks into a 40-37 lead.

The dreadful stretch for the Sixers on both sides of the ball called to mind how they'd fallen into a 29-point deficit Thursday night vs. the Cavaliers before clawing out a comeback win.

The Sixers mustered just seven points in first six minutes of the second quarter and had many stagnant possessions that concluded with contested jumpers. The team's transition defense was dismal for much of the second period. Milwaukee had the game's first 19 fast-break points.

The Sixers regained the lead late in the second quarter. Kentavious Caldwell-Pope made two three-balls in the second and nabbed three first-half steals. Embiid assisted a go-ahead, and-one Walker layup.

Brown hit a three with 11.8 seconds left in the second quarter. Unsurprisingly, his variety of shotmaking skills were useful without James in the lineup.

Even when James or Embiid sit, the Sixers should have a simple advantage in terms of volume of stars over most opponents this year. None of Brown, Embiid or Maxey had the sort of off night that would have improved the Bucks' odds of a road win. They'd all passed the 20-point mark by the end of the third quarter.

Maxey notched another final-possession bucket, this time with a more conventional make. He canned a jumper from the right elbow with 1.7 seconds left in the third to extend the Sixers' lead to 97-87.

The Bucks made a late push in the fourth quarter. Kel'el Ware's put-back, and-one layup cut the Milwaukee's deficit to 117-114.

The Sixers ultimately handled business. Embiid reached his triple-double by assisting a second-chance Brown jumper and and Caldwell-Pope soon drilled a dagger corner three. Embiid even threw down a last-minute dunk for good measure.

For the second consecutive season, the Sixers have a 3-0 start. They got to four wins last year before dropping their first game.

#2729. Connecticut football traditions, rivalries return to Thanksgiving week for eight old and new matchups

When the Bullard-Havens and Bassick football teams kick off at 6 p.m. Tuesday, it will mark the return of an old tradition. The two teams have a long history, much of which took place on Thanksgiving, dating as far back as the 1960s.

It's a history the teams are embracing for Thanksgiving week once again even in the name. The game is being dubbed "The Frank Brown Bowl" in honor of the former Bridgeport educator and Bassick coach.

"We want Thanksgiving football to always mean something to the kids," said Bullard-Havens coach Derrick Lewis, who has also coached at Bassick. "Any time you're dealing with a city type of a deal, all the kids are friends with one another, they all know each other, and they all support each other too, which is pretty cool.

The two schools had played on Thanksgiving up until 2016 and that's also the last time Bassick had a game on the holiday week until this year.

"It's great for Bridgeport to play Bridgeport on Thanksgiving week," Bassick coach Desmond Lymon said. "It's been a while since we last played and it brings a sense of pride into the city."

The Bassick vs. Bullard-Havens matchup is one of eight games during the holiday week which were not on last year's slate. They're games that are either returning, brand new, or in some cases rivalries that are joining the Thanksgiving tradition.

Bassick vs. Bullard-Havens at Kennedy Stadium, 6 p.m.

Thames River co-op at Montville/St. Bernard, 6 p.m.

Like Bassick and Bullard-Havens, the Wilton at Ridgefield match-up is a natural fit.

Wilton had been playing Trinity Catholic for Thanksgiving, but after Trinity closed after the 2019 season, the Warriors were left without a partner. They settled on a revolving series of teams such as Shelton, Xavier and Hillhouse the week before the holiday.

EJ DiNunzio was hired as Wilton's head coach in 2018 and said he had wanted to get the Ridgefield game back because of the rivalry between the schools.

However, Ridgefield had an ongoing Thanksgiving matchup with Danbury and Tigers' head coach Jamie Reed said they didn't want to leave the Hatters out in the cold.

Then in 2025, Tim Smith, a Danbury assistant coach, became the head coach at ATI, a co-op of Danbury schools Abbott Tech and Immaculate.

This season, ATI is set to play Danbury, opening the door for the Wilton-Ridgefield matchup.

"When I told the kids, they were so excited," DiNunzio said. "I'd been talking about it for a couple of years, and it was like 'yeah coach, you didn't get it again this year, we're not getting it.' So when I was finally able to tell them we finally had it secured, they went nuts."

DiNunzio added that as a traditionalist, his preference would have been to play Thursday, but he's happy having the game back during the holiday week.

"It's a great football game whenever we play it and now, it's even better because we can get the alumni back and involved," DiNunzio said.

Reed said Ridgefield athletic director Dane Street deserves a lot of credit for making the game happen.

Reed also said he got a taste of what the holiday game means while watching a junior varsity contest between the Tigers and Warriors.

"Because the Ridgefield-Wilton game has been kind of inconsistent the last few years, I was worried it might not have as much juice this season," Reed said. "But I was at the JV game this past Saturday and both sides picked up right where we left off."

Dominoes falling into place have led to other new match-ups.

Windham is facing Woodstock Academy, with the Whippets' former Thanksgiving partner, Montville, now co-opping with St. Bernard, facing the Thames River co-op.

The Gilbert/Northwestern/Housatonic co-op had played St. Paul in the past, but with St. Paul now in a co-op with Avon, GNH is playing the Nonnewaug co-op. Both teams are in the Berkshire League for other sports.

CREC and SMSA will also square off after facing other teams in recent seasons.

South Windsor and Enfield have played each other in the final game of the regular season since 2016, after Enfield and Fermi combined into one school.

It's called the Route 5 Rivalry, and the trophy is currently in the hands of South Windsor, which won the game last fall.

When Enfield hosts the game, they play during the Thanksgiving week.

Enfield coach James Lyver said he feels it's important to honor the Thanksgiving tradition in Enfield, after the Eagles had faced Fermi on the holiday for 37 years.

"It's great to bring our town together to honor our graduating senior football players, cheerleaders and band members," Lyver said. "It is also extremely important to the residents to reconnect with old friends and classmates around the Thanksgiving holiday."

The alumni factor is also something Lewis pointed to regarding the Bassick vs. Bullard-Havens game.

"It's funny, I've been coaching for so long now, I've actually coached fathers and uncles and cousins," Lewis said. "It's easy to talk about the great players and the great teams of the past. Our school doesn't have as much of a winning history as the other schools, I think we've had four All-Staters in our program, Josh Headley being one of them. We've had a chance to talk about tradition and we don't take anything lightly.

"I know they've struggled this year and we've had our struggles too but it's all thrown out during Thanksgiving."

#2728. AMD dives on short seller report of alleged China exposure

Shares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices close down 7.72% to $489.19 on Thursday after investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging that the company "has its own China problem."

Hunterbrook disclosed that it had taken a short position in AMD.

The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers."

CNBC did not independently verify this information.

Hunterbrook also said that new export rules in Washington could "tighten restrictions on AMD's foreign business," alleging that AMD "bills over 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong," and "depends on a Chinese partner to finish most of its chips."

The allegations come amid investigations of rival chipmaker Nvidia over its sales to companies in Asia with ties to China. AMD has been viewed as a beneficiary of the uncertainty surrounding Nvidia.

"The claims misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships," an AMD spokesperson said in a statement. "AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations. We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity."

Lisa Su, CEO of AMD, told investors on the company's recent earnings call that China is an "important" market and that the semiconductor giant wants to be fully compliant with U.S. export controls.

AMD continued to slide after hours, trading down 0.45% to $487 shortly after 4 p.m.

#2727. Fantasy Football Rankings: Hayden Winks' WR Blueprint for Week 12

The Blueprint is my weekly column and basically everything that I use to build out the most accurate rankings I can. There will be an RB column, this WR column and a combination column on the onesie positions. You will find film notes and endless charts. Maybe enough charts to stress test the Yahoo website. I kid.

It's impossible to get every ranking thoroughly early in the week, so be sure to keep checking in on these columns through Sunday morning. As always, my full rankings at every position will be updated here soon.

1. Ja'Marr Chase (vs. NO) - 93.5 proj. receiving yards

2. Jaxon Smith-Njigba (at SF) - 97.5 proj. receiving yards

Smith-Njigba is the WR2 in per-game half PPR scoring on WR6 expected-points usage over his past four games with Drew Lock and Sam Darnold splitting time. He has topped 100 receiving yards in three of those four contests while drawing a 44% target share in that span. What's new?

San Francisco ranks 11th in half PPR points allowed per game to opposing wideouts, having surrendered 71.2 fantasy points to the Cowboys receiver room in Week 10 when chasing points. JSN has tons of experience against this defense, most recently posting 118, 19, 84, 124 and 118 yards. Seattle travels as 3-point road underdogs with a 21.75-point team total (17th). Throwing the ball to the perimeter is the best way to move the ball against the Niners, in my opinion.

3. CeeDee Lamb (vs. PHI) - 89.5 proj. receiving yards

Lamb is the WR3 on WR2 usage this year, ranking second in targets per game (11.8) and third in yards per game (100.7). Through 11 weeks of an NFL season, Lamb's 208.2 half PPR points are 13th all-time. All-time.

The Eagles have been bad against Lamb-type receivers all year and now won't have All Pro LB Zack Baun. They've allowed the third-most points to fantasy WRs, and Lamb finished as the WR5 on WR1 overall usage against them in Week 7. Dallas carries a 28-point team total (fourth) as 8.5-point home favorites.

4. Amon-Ra St. Brown (vs. CHI) - 84.5 proj. receiving yards

St. Brown is having his usual season. He's the WR5 on WR7 usage, after going on a touchdown-less rut throughout October.

This matchup has the potential for a blowup game. The biggest factor will be if slot CB Kyler Gordon can play after he missed last week. The Bears have been pretty woeful in the secondary beyond him, while shutting down the run since Jeffery Simmons appeared. The Sun God was the WR5 and WR1 in matchups against them last year, both wins for Detroit. Jaxon Smith-Njigba hung 118-1 against them in Week 8 in a similar role, too. Detroit enters as 2.5-point home underdogs carrying a 26.5-point implied team total (sixth).

5. Tee Higgins (vs. NO) - 70.5 proj. receiving yards

6. Parker Washington (vs. TEN) - 78.5 proj. receiving yards

That really should've been a touchdown. Come on, refs! Washington still was a top-20 WR last week and is now the WR13 on WR12 usage across the season. He can be up-and-down based on the Jaguars' lopsided history, but when games are tighter, Washington catches fire, as he did last week when he racked up 16 targets while trailing.

This week, the Jaguars are expected to go crazy on offense. They have a league-high 31.0-point team total against the Titans, who have allowed 362 passing yards per game over the past month. Read that again. And again. It's one of the wildest stats of the year. It doesn't take a genius to feel good about Washington's ceiling odds here. He had 152-1 against them just two weeks ago.

7. George Pickens (vs. PHI) - 70.5 proj. receiving yards

We're so back. Pickens has 38.0 and 20.3 half PPR points, respectively, in his two games since the bye. He had one of the best grabs of the year last week along the sideline, while Dak Prescott had all day to pass behind a great Cowboys OL. It's an environment for Pickens to have monster games, even if his role and style come with some volatility. He's at his best when teams go to single high coverage, something the Eagles typically don't do.

That said, CB1 Quinyon Mitchell is dealing with a new hamstring injury, and the other star players won't be available with Jordan Davis on the Jaguars and LB Zack Baun on IR. Mitchell's status is a big deal for Pickens' matchup. Across the season, the Eagles have had far too many blown coverages, leading to the third-most fantasy points allowed to WRs (31.3). Pickens had 57-1 against them in Week 7 and 146-1 against them late last year. Dallas carries a 28-point team total (fourth) as 8.5-point home favorites.

8. Malik Nabers (at IND) - 64.5 proj. receiving yards

Nabers had a handful of underneath receptions against elite CB1 Travis Hunter last week, then teleported into the back of the end zone against Jacksonville's nickel defender to bring Nabers to a top-15 WR finish. Since Week 4, Nabers is the WR9 on WR4 usage with Puka Nacua as one of the receivers ahead. Things will always be up-and-down with J.J. McCarthy, who missed him way out of bounds for a potential back-shoulder TD, but Nabers is way too good to not be treated as a fantasy WR1 now.

The Giants have a healthy 24.0-point team total this week, and that'll easily be one of their best all year. The Colts are tanking and have allowed the 10th-most passing yards per game over their last four games. We'll see if CB1 Sauce Gardner or CB2 Charvarius Ward will return this week. Nico Collins had an awesome deep touchdown against their backups last week, and Nabers had a 171-2 game against the Colts during his rookie season, for what it's worth. Long story short, Nabers looks great this week.

9. Justin Jefferson (vs. ATL) - 84.5 proj. receiving yards

Jefferson is the WR18 on WR8 usage over the past two weeks with Kirk Cousins. The fumble on that in-cut explosion was a real bummer, but that completion had a lot of timing and anticipation from the QB, something Jefferson hasn't had since 2023. He had plenty of breaking routes against the 49ers, and Kevin O'Connell drew up two different downfield shots to him, too. A big game is long overdue. The signs of it happening soon are there.

This is a sweet matchup for just that. The Falcons don't have Pro Bowl FS Jessie Bates, and CB1 A.J. Terrell is having a down season in isolation. The Vikings getting their OL healthy again would be nice, but Jefferson should have room to operate either way. The Falcons have allowed the fifth-most passing yards per game this year and the seventh-most fantasy points to WRs. Minnesota has a strong 24.75-point team total, and Jordan Addison (finger) isn't expected to play.

10. Nico Collins (vs. BAL) - 63.5 proj. receiving yards

Collins ranks as the WR18 in half PPR points per game on WR31 expected-points usage across his last four appearances. His weekly target volume has fluctuated wildly, bottoming out at four targets in two separate contests while spiking to 15 targets in Week 10 against Cleveland. The good news is the Texans have recently ramped his snap rates up out of desperation and with Marvin Harrison Jr. and Jaylen Noel sidelined. Collins is the WR11 on WR20 usage this year. That's a fair range for him. A long dunk-on-you TD made him the WR18 last week.

Baltimore's defense has underwhelmed. We'll see if podcaster Marlon Humphrey is back this week, but he's been bad this year anyway. Collins will likely see a bunch of CB1 Nate Wiggins, who has the speed to match with Collins downfield. Opponents facing the Ravens have posted a 46% neutral pass rate, the third-lowest rate in the NFL and the Texans are 6.5-point home favorites. He likely won't have that many targets here, but a 26.5-point team total (seventh) suggests he'll be a big reason why that is.

11. Matthew Golden (at LAR) - 74.5 proj. receiving yards

Golden has produced as the WR8 in half PPR points per game on WR5 expected-points usage over his last four games. The breakout sophomore has commanded a 33% target share alongside 10.8 targets and 133 air yards per game, topping nine targets in all four contests. These are the type of metrics that make the drops livable. Golden is one of the best separators in the NFL. Full stop.

The Rams present a stingy draw on paper, ranking 30th in half PPR points allowed to WRs (21.5 per game). Opposing offenses have largely avoided testing them through the air, but have CB2 Jaylen Watson on IR right now, at least. Golden may see a handful of Trent McDuffie in this one, so he may not be as open as he usually is. The Packers simply don't have other avenues to move the ball, so Golden should still see plenty of looks. Green Bay is listed as 3-point road underdogs with a 20.75-point team total (19th).

#2726. Jensen Huang to face DC grilling the same day Nvidia releases new products at GTC

Jensen Huang is back as the CEO of Nvidia, and is now tasked with selling the company's artificial intelligence vision while also defending himself in Washington.

As Nvidia employees celebrated the return of their leader to the company's headquarters, Huang told the gathered crowd, "I'll be a better CEO the second time around."

Huang will need to be a better CEO to head off the issues surrounding Nvidia and the broader AI industry exposed by Huang's exit. The challenges include a proliferating roster of investigations and hearings from Congress, regulators and state-level officials, as well as technical and competitive questions about how long Nvidia's currently dominant graphics processing units can remain on top.

"There's nothing prohibiting him from doing what he does on his day job," said Katten chair and former federal prosecutor Gil Soffer. But investigations take significant prep time, Soffer said. "You don't just walk in cold."

At Nvidia's GTC conference in Washington, D.C., next week, the company will attempt to convince customers, partners and suppliers that it is developing the future of AI. At the same time, lawmakers will be pressing its newly reinstated CEO over what he knew and when about Megaspeed executive Alice Huang.

Huang, before his scandals, was scheduled to give the GTC DC keynote speech on Dec. 1 to discuss new Nvidia products and the trajectory of the AI ecosystem. In the past, the two-hour speech was the highlight of the event with hordes of fans full of the Huang-inspired "Jensanity."

"People will want to see that it's business as usual, which hopefully for Nvidia shareholders will mean that Jensen Huang announces some new exciting products," said Babson College associate professor Peter Cohan.

Right now, Nvidia has Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, filling the slot. A representative for Nvidia declined to answer multiple questions about whether Huang would appear at the company's event.

On the same day, Huang is scheduled to speak with three House committees — Foreign Affairs, Select Committee on the CCP, and the Select Committee on Intelligence — behind closed doors, where his interview will be transcribed.

"The NVIDIA board's brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed," the chairs said in a joint statement. They said that Huang has confirmed he will appear for the transcribed interview on Dec. 1.

Next Tuesday's interviews are just the first of a slew of investigations.

On Dec. 3, just as Nvidia's conference is wrapping up, the Senate Banking Committee will hold a hearing titled "Protecting America's AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls." Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., who chairs the committee, said Huang will publicly testify as the sole witness.

California's attorney general is also investigating Huang's remarks, and politicians from the Senate Finance, Intelligence, and Foreign Relations committees have inquired about the scandal. In the House, Energy and Commerce has requested a company briefing from Nvidia, in addition to the three committees mentioned earlier. That's not counting an investigation from the Department of Justice and a reported investigation from the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Plus, Huang still has to cooperate with an investigation from the board of directors, led by the law firm Wachtell Lipton.

Meanwhile, Nvidia needs Huang to reassure investors and the broader AI ecosystem that the company is developing new products that will be in high demand. Investors had said that while Nvidia's products for the next two years have been fully designed, they were worried that the chipmaker's pace of innovation would slow without Huang.

Nvidia is facing new competition from chips from its biggest customers, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Amazon and Microsoft. The companies have been developing their own chips to reduce reliance on Nvidia, as well as to control AI costs.

"There was already this worry that we're spending too much on it," said Stephanie Balaouras, vice president of group research at Forrester. "One of those cost management strategies is to match ... the workload requirements to the right infrastructure. You don't need to put everything on a Nvidia GPU."

Many in the AI industry see Huang as one of the staunchest defenders of "open-source" AI that is free to use for commercial purposes, as compared with "frontier models" from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, which charge users by the token.

Nvidia has also been spending heavily to develop its own open-source models called Nemotron. Currently, Nvidia Vice President Kari Briski is scheduled to present new Nemotron technology at GTC.

On Monday, Nvidia's board said that "senior levels" of the U.S. government provided input on Huang's potential national security risk. President Donald Trump told CNBC that he was central to convincing Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang and said he gave the board assurances.

Trump's help could draw even more scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers, who were already focused on probing Nvidia's chip sales.

"Today's news that Donald Trump engineered the rehiring of Jensen Huang at Nvidia is Exhibit A about the political corruption and rot at the heart of the Trump administration's big tech and AI policy," said Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland in a call with reporters Monday.

Republicans have also criticized Huang's return as the focus on the company's China sales intensifies. Still, the investigations could start to weigh on Nvidia's CEO, experts say.

"How could he possibly do the job?" Jeff Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean at the Yale School of Management, told CNBC, citing Senate investigations, House investigations and other state investigations, even before Democrats take over next year.

And the reaction in Washington to Huang's scandal could start to affect Nvidia's sales.

Last week, the Department of Commerce announced that it will prevent Chinese companies from getting around export controls by renting Nvidia's chips across borders. On Monday, Commerce also added Megaspeed to a trade blacklist.

And it's not just Nvidia that is relying on a strong performance from Huang. The company's investors, customers, partners and shareholders will also look to see if Nvidia still wants to be at the center of the AI ecosystem. Before Huang was removed, he pushed Nvidia to invest in AI startups, while selling them products, and helping finance their infrastructure.

Remarks from Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress last week while she was interim CEO suggested that Nvidia would be taking a "very strong look" at using its balance sheet to support the AI ecosystem, but it's unclear if Huang's second stint as CEO will continue with his prior showmanship or abide by a more measured approach.

#2725. Anthropic was supposed to save the AI trade. What went wrong?

Anthropic's historic IPO — the largest in U.S. history — delivered a big win for the company and its investors. But it failed at another task: reviving animal spirits in the AI trade.

The Nasdaq Composite closed down 2.25% amid a broader market pullback with the S&P 500 declining 2% to 7,175.

Investors had been looking forward to the Anthropic IPO as a "clearing event" — reviving the tech sector after months of choppy trading, the Nvidia espionage scandal, and growing concerns that AI chip sales to Asia are likely to slump as Washington cracks down on potential violations of export controls.

Some of those worries resurfaced Thursday as a short seller, Hunterbrook Media, alleged in a report that firmware sold by chipmaker AMD had turned up in U.S.-blacklisted companies. AMD stock closed down more than 7%. The chipmaker told CNBC it complies with U.S. law.

Adding to the worries, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released documents showing that a subagency of the Commerce Department approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies. That also raised the prospect of an Asia sales slowdown under stricter export controls.

Many investors and analysts continue to express confidence in the AI trade, noting that Anthropic's successful market debut — the stock closed up 17% from its IPO price and raised more than $81 billion — bodes well for capital spending across tech.

But investors acknowledged that this is a high-tension moment and said it's time to be more strategic about the trade.

Dan Niles, founder of Niles Investment Management, described himself as a "circumspect bull," making the comparison to market conditions in 2022 when the big indices tanked in the back half of the year.

"You could have still made money that year. You just needed to have the right combination of longs and shorts," he said.

Part of the challenge, Niles said, has been a price war between the two cutting-edge frontier labs, Anthropic and OpenAI. That has posed a threat to the overall revenue and profit potential of AI and the capex going into it. Fierce competition on price is producing collective losses between the two top companies, he notes.

"The combined revenue growth for OpenAI plus Anthropic went from growing 75% sequentially in Q2 to 48% in Q3," he told CNBC. "The combined losses went from $7.9 billion to about $8.4 billion from Q2 to Q3."

While uncertainty is high now, some resolution may be on the horizon if a greater degree of commercial and regulatory clarity emerges over the next few months.

Trading experts also told CNBC that the tech sector's troubles Thursday were a more serious matter than Anthropic simply siphoning capital from other parts of the market.

"There's a reset of AI in general," said JJ Kinahan, senior vice president at Cboe Global Markets.

Investors for years have profited in tech by buying the dip, he said, but "there's been an attitude change that [you] can't buy things blindly and they'll all go up." Nvidia's ongoing declines have shaken confidence in the buy-the-dip strategy, he said.

Anthropic's next few trading days will be a key gauge of the market's strength. Friday will be a "wild card," Kinahan said. It could be a "final flush out" for the market, or a bounce that leaves the market in "no man's land" while volatility remains elevated.

A better gauge may be Monday, when options on Anthropic start trading, providing insight into whether retail investors will back the company in force — providing more of a vote of confidence in the AI trade.

"If people think we're going up [on Anthropic] they'll buy stock, but retail particularly will just buy calls," he said. "There's a bigger test coming Monday."

For now, investors continue to sell AI-related stocks.

Neoclouds, the generally highly indebted AI-dedicated computing providers at the outer edges of the AI trade, were down substantially Thursday, with CoreWeave closing down more than 6%.

Hyperscalers such as Alphabet and Amazon.com, viewed as relatively defensive AI bets, also finished lower.

One bright spot: Cybersecurity stocks continued to rally, with Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike both closing up. AI is finding security holes across software infrastructure, creating a scramble to patch the vulnerabilities before hackers can exploit them.

— CNBC's Daren Fonda contributed reporting.

#2724. Anthropic closes below $83 IPO price, but analysts are still largely positive

Shares of Anthropic closed down 6.5% on Tuesday, sending the stock below the artificial intelligence company's $83 IPO price.

The AI lab's stock has been sinking steadily since opening at $111.50 on the Nasdaq on Thursday, after Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in the largest offering of all time. Investors eagerly awaited Anthropic's debut in hopes that the company would revitalize the broader AI trade, which has been volatile in recent weeks over concerns about the feasibility of a multitrillion-dollar infrastructure buildout.

Chip stocks Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and Intel, as well as neoclouds CoreWeave, IREN and Nebius, all fell during intraday trading on Tuesday. The market is still reeling after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, a dramatic reversal from his ouster earlier this month. Nvidia shares surged more than 30% on Monday, but pared those gains Tuesday.

Analysts at Canaccord Genuity said Tuesday that they're focused on Anthropic's long-term potential. They said they believe that the company is building "one of the most important enterprise technology franchises of the AI era" and that the "opportunity is considerably larger than traditional software spending."

Canaccord Genuity initiated coverage of Anthropic with a buy rating and a $135 price target.

"The risks are unusually large, particularly around infrastructure commitments and the durability of competitive differentiation, but we believe the combination of exceptional growth, emerging earnings capacity, and an attractive entry valuation support a compelling investment opportunity," the analysts wrote in a Tuesday note.

Wedbush analysts initiated coverage of Anthropic with an outperform rating and a $120 price target on Monday. They said Anthropic went public in a "tumultuous market" as debate around the AI buildout continues, but that they expect the company to navigate the competitive environment and "capture a uniquely large addressable market."

"While there's going to continue to be many ups and downs, and winners and losers as this ecosystem gets built, in our view there is no real question that it does get built over time," the analysts wrote in a Monday note. "The genie is out of the bottle. And ANT is a strong play on that theme."

Analysts at Oppenheimer initiated coverage of Anthropic with an outperform rating on Tuesday, and they set a $150 price target for the stock.

They said their "bullish stance" on the company stems from their belief that Anthropic will capture growing enterprise AI spending, that its improving compute efficiency lowers cost per task and that its multi-chip strategy optimizes price performance. The analysts added that Anthropic's focus on the enterprise also relies less on consumer subsidies, and that rising customer adoption creates "a substantial runway" for the company.

"While competition and compute commitments remain risks, we believe Anthropic can translate its leadership into durable growth and operating leverage," the analysts wrote in a Tuesday note.
