#2722. Sixers' record-setting wait for the West ends against Trail Blazers

Sixers' record-setting wait for the West ends against Trail Blazers originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Have you noticed anything different about the Sixers' season?

No, not the fact that LeBron James and Jaylen Brown are wearing red, white and blue and have helped Philadelphia build an Eastern Conference-leading 14-3 record.

The difference is hidden in their schedule. All 17 games have come against Eastern Conference opponents.

When the Sixers welcome the Portland Trail Blazers to Xfinity Mobile Arena on Monday night, it will mark the latest they have ever gone into a season before facing a Western Conference team.

Philadelphia's 18-game wait also ties the 1979-80 Atlanta Hawks for the second latest by an Eastern Conference team. Only the 1980-81 Milwaukee Bucks went longer, meeting the West for the first time in their 21st game.

The Sixers have played who has been placed in front of them and won five consecutive games. They have already beaten the Knicks twice and own victories over Cleveland and Detroit.

Their first Western Conference matchup introduces a different comparison.

The West entered Monday with 11 teams above .500. The East had seven. Western Conference teams were also 41-20 against the East through Sunday.

Portland will not answer every question about how the Sixers compare with the other conference. It begins a more varied portion of their schedule.

The Sixers will face Memphis and Denver on consecutive nights next week. Dallas and Houston visit later in December before Philadelphia travels to play the Lakers, Clippers, Kings and Suns over a six-day stretch.

Portland is 10-6 under first-year head coach Micah Nori, the father of Phillies prospect Dante Nori.

The Blazers are averaging 116.1 points while allowing 110.3 per game, with both figures ranking in the top 10. Their 15.4 made three-pointers per game rank second in the NBA.

Deni Avdija leads Portland with 23.9 points per game. Damian Lillard is averaging 20.6 points in his return to the franchise, while 7-foot-2 center Donovan Clingan has supplied size around a deep group of guards and wings.

Clingan posted 22 points and 13 rebounds Saturday night at Madison Square Garden. Portland erased a 26-point deficit and briefly took the lead before Mikal Bridges made a game-winning three-pointer at the buzzer.

The 97-96 loss dropped the Blazers to 1-3 over their last four games. Slow starts have followed them during that stretch.

"Our last three games, we haven't gotten off to great starts, and that's just something that we got to correct," Lillard said. "Our energy and our focus and our intent has to be better from the jump. We can't let this trend continue."

The Sixers know something about overcoming early deficits. Six of their 14 victories have required double-digit comebacks.

Portland will be missing two major pieces. Ja Morant is out with a left hamstring strain, while Shaedon Sharpe remains sidelined following right meniscus surgery.

Even without Morant, the Blazers can turn to Lillard, Jrue Holiday and Scoot Henderson to initiate their offense. Avdija and Toumani Camara provide size on the perimeter, while Clingan gives Portland the kind of interior presence that has occasionally troubled the Sixers.

Anfernee Simons and Jabari Walker know the Portland organization better than any other Sixers.

The two shared the floor for 128 games with the Trail Blazers. Portland won 43 of them.

Their responsibilities have changed in Philadelphia. So have the expectations.

Simons scored 18 points in each of the Sixers' last two games and made seven three-pointers. He started in place of Tyrese Maxey against Orlando and hit the clinching three in his hometown. Three nights later, he supplied four more threes off the bench in the Sixers' 132-129 win over Milwaukee.

Walker has also found steady work during the Sixers' recent frontcourt injuries. He recorded nine points, seven rebounds and four assists against the Bucks after scoring 11 against Indiana and hitting a go-ahead three late in Orlando.

Both players recently discussed how their difficult seasons in Portland changed their perspective on filling smaller roles for a winning team.

"You feel appreciative of the times where you go into a situation where your role might be a little bit less, but you're winning," Simons said. "That's something that you can't take for granted, for sure, because it's hard to win in the NBA. We've seen it firsthand."

Their former team will now see them operating within a deeper rotation than the one Philadelphia carried through much of the past week.

Brown, Dean Wade and Adem Bona were all listed as probable on the Sixers' initial injury report after missing time.

Brown and Wade have each missed the last two games. Bona has been sidelined since Nov. 4 because of a cervical spine sprain. Dominick Barlow returned Saturday and scored 12 points on 5-for-6 shooting in his season debut.

Joel Embiid was added to the injury report Monday morning as questionable because of an illness. His availability will determine how the Sixers approach Clingan and Robert Williams III inside.

The Sixers have leaned on smaller lineups and reserve contributors while Nurse has managed injuries across the roster. Monday could give him more options, even if Embiid cannot play.

FanDuel Sportsbook listed the Sixers as 3.5-point favorites Monday afternoon. Philadelphia was -152 on the moneyline, Portland was +128 and the over-under was 229.5.

The Blazers are 7-4 on the road. The Sixers are 7-2 at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

After 17 games within their own conference, the Sixers will finally see what their early success looks like against the other side.

#2720. Consumer confidence shoots up after Democrats' midterm victories — though inflation worries persist

Consumers grew significantly more optimistic in November in the wake of the midterm elections, with a growing number of Americans now seeing improvement in the labor market and expecting inflation to cool.

The Conference Board survey released Tuesday showed improvement across the board, with the headline confidence index jumping to 103.3, up 11.4 points from October and much better than the Dow Jones consensus forecast for 92.2.

Confidence among Democrats and independent voters improved sharply, the Conference Board said, while confidence among Republican respondents fell slightly. Still, confidence among Republicans remained the highest among the three groups.

While respondents "continued to express frustration with high prices and rising costs," they also "cited hope for the general economy," said Fergus McCormick, the board's senior economist for global indicators.

The survey comes with the Federal Reserve continuing to try to bring down inflation, which has run above the central bank's 2% target for some 5½ years. The Fed is expected to raise its benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point when it meets again in two weeks.

Despite the lingering worries about the cost of living — a centerpiece issue during the midterms — the survey's present situation and expectations indexes both posted strong gains. Inflation expectations for 12 months from now fell for the second straight month but remained high at 5.7%.

The survey's closely watched gap between jobs considered "plentiful" versus "hard to get" widened to 12.4 percentage points. The "plentiful" side rose to 30.8% from 26.2% while "hard to get" fell to 18.4%, down 3 percentage points.

The survey results are the second in the past week to reveal that Americans are growing more optimistic about the economy. The University of Michigan's November survey, released Friday, showed a 7.3% increase since October, with a similar partisan split.

#2719. Tiger Woods’ Sun Day Red dealt setback in trademark fight over leaping tiger logo

A divided federal appeals court on Tuesday ordered the dismissal of a trademark lawsuit by Tiger Woods' golf apparel company, which sought approval to use its "leaping tiger" logo after another company with a similar logo objected.

Reversing a lower court ruling, the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals in Pasadena, California, said courts in that state lacked jurisdiction to consider claims by Woods' Sun Day Red against Tigeraire, a Louisiana company that makes cooling fans attachable to athletes' headgear.

The 2-1 majority said this was because Tigeraire, which is affiliated with the Louisiana State University Tigers, had no physical presence in California and did little business there.

More: What your golf fit says about you: Sun Day Red

Tuesday's decision does not affect Tigeraire's trademark infringement lawsuit against Sunday Red, which has been on hold.

Lawyers for both companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Sunday Red, based in San Clemente, California, is part of TaylorMade Golf, which is a subsidiary of South Korean private equity firm Centroid Investment Partners.

Sun Day Red, as Woods' brand is known, launched in February 2024, paying homage to Woods' wearing red on Sunday during golf tournaments.

Its logo contains 15 stripes, one for each of Woods' major championship titles.

Shortly after Sun Day Red's launch, Tigeraire, which launched in 2020, sent a cease-and-desist letter that said the competing logos were confusing consumers. Settlement talks failed, prompting the dueling lawsuits.

Sunday Red's lawsuit sought a declaration it did nothing wrong, and accused Tigeraire of seeking an "unwarranted financial windfall from a larger and more successful brand." A federal judge refused to dismiss the case, and Tigeraire appealed.

Writing for Tuesday's majority, Circuit Judge Morgan Christen called Tigeraire's sales in California "trivial," totaling just 80 products over eight months and including only one item of apparel, a T-shirt.

She also called the cease-and-desist letter a "garden-variety" attempt to begin settlement talks, which did not support asserting jurisdiction.

Circuit Judge Milan Smith dissented. He said the majority was too quick to dismiss Sunday Red's claim it could face irreparable harm if forced to pull products from stores and rebrand itself while Tigeraire asserted its trademark rights.

Woods, 50, launched Sun Day Red after his 27-year partnership with Nike NKE.N ended.

#2718. LeBron Log No. 6: A Rocky night, a shooting lesson and a fight over ‘Bron'

LeBron Log No. 6: A Rocky night, a shooting lesson and a fight over 'Bron' originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

It was another eventful week for LeBron James.

That's why we started the LeBron Log in the first place.

The King spent his latest week taking his teammates to the movies, fighting over his name in federal court and producing his best three-point shooting performance as a Sixer days after recording a podcast about the craft.

This week also marks 20 years since James faced the Sixers alongside Allen Iverson.

James found an appropriate choice for the Sixers' latest team outing.

He organized a private screening of I Play Rocky on Friday night for players, their families and members of the basketball operations staff. The film follows Sylvester Stallone's fight to get the original Rocky made while insisting that he play the title character.

"I mean, it's Rocky. We in Philly," James said. "I heard it was a great movie, and we had a night off. I've got a few connections, and I was able to bring that to my teammates and this organization for us to watch it. I thought it was a great movie. Unbelievably cast. Everyone looked like exactly who they were portraying. That is Hollywood for you. It was pretty cool."

The Sixers shared photos of James alongside Jaylen Brown, Kentavious Caldwell-Pope, Labaron Philon Jr., Jabari Walker, Tacko Fall and Adem Bona.

"Movie night, courtesy of LeBron," the team wrote.

The nationwide release of I Play Rocky came less than two weeks before Philadelphia celebrates the 50th anniversary of the original film on Dec. 3.

Nick Nurse could not attend because of a previous commitment, but he received positive reviews from his players.

"They went, they said it was very good, they loved it," Nurse said. "The big takeaway was how much Anthony actually looked like Rocky. Or Sylvester Stallone. One in the same."

James' first season in Philadelphia now includes a private Rocky screening. A trip up the Art Museum steps remains available for a future edition.

James and Steve Nash devoted the latest episode of their Mind the Game podcast to the art of shooting.

The two examined shooting form, confidence, repetitions, free throws and some of their favorite jumpers. James also revealed one detail that can affect what he does after catching the ball.

"I'm a guy who don't like shooting against the laces," James said. "So sometimes I'll come up on a quick stop and I'm about to raise and I can feel the laces not fixed. I'll turn that into a pump fake."

The episode was released Nov. 17, while James was experiencing an extended struggle from three-point range. It did not provide an instant fix.

James went 1 for 5 from three against Orlando and missed his lone attempt against Milwaukee. He entered Monday night's meeting with Portland shooting 21.7 percent from deep through his first 13 games.

James made all three of his first-half attempts from three. He ended the second quarter by pump-faking, stepping to his left and beating the buzzer with a corner three that tied the game at 69.

Nobody could see where the laces sat on the catch. The pump fake was clear.

James finished 4 for 5 from three and scored a season-high 23 points on 8-for-13 shooting. It was his third consecutive game with at least 20 points, following 22 against Orlando and 21 against Milwaukee.

The Sixers lost to Portland, 128-111, but James produced his best long-range performance since joining them.

Six days after discussing the art of shooting, he provided a brief demonstration.

James is also attempting to protect one of his most recognizable nicknames.

James and LBJ Trademarks LLC filed a federal lawsuit on Nov. 17 against PlayVision Inc. and its founders over a sports-betting research app initially called "Bron."

The complaint alleges that the company used an AI-generated version of James in an advertisement without his permission. The figure wore a No. 23 jersey with "Bron" across the back and resembled James through its voice, build and tattoos.

It also scrolled through wagers involving NBA players.

The lawsuit alleges that the advertisement falsely created the impression that James endorsed the app and suggested that he considered betting on NBA games. The complaint said the video received roughly 1 million views before it was removed.

"The integrity of NBA competition, and the public's confidence that players are not betting on the games they play, is of paramount importance to the league, its players and its fans," the complaint said. "Any suggestion that an active NBA player is betting on NBA games is therefore far from a trivial matter, and it should not be used for clicks and views."

The app offered odds comparisons, betting trends and tracking tools but did not directly accept wagers, according to its developer.

PlayVision renamed it "Evie" on Nov. 18, one day after James filed the lawsuit. James is seeking an injunction and unspecified damages. The case remains active in the Southern District of New York.

CLEVELAND – NOVEMBER 25: LeBron James #23 of the Cleveland Cavaliers looks to pass off when double teamed by the Philadelphia 76ers November 25, 2006 at The Quicken Loans Arena in Cleveland, Ohio. Copyright 2006 NBAE (Photo by David Liam Kyle/NBAE via Getty Images)

James spent Thanksgiving weekend in 2006 on the other side of the Sixers-Cavaliers matchup.

On Nov. 25, 2006, a 21-year-old James recorded 25 points, 11 assists, four rebounds and one block in Cleveland's 108-95 win over Philadelphia.

Donning the Cavs' old-school orange threads, he played nearly 41 minutes.

Iverson led the Sixers with 31 points. Andre Iguodala added 17 points and eight rebounds, while Kyle Korver made three three-pointers off the bench.

James recorded 11 assists that night. Nearly 20 years later, another 11-assist performance against Indiana moved him past Jason Kidd for third place in NBA history.

The 2006 meeting also came near the end of Iverson's original run with Philadelphia. The Sixers traded him to Denver less than a month later.

James was 21. Iverson was nearing his departure.

Twenty years later, James is wearing a Sixers uniform and Iverson's No. 3 hangs above his home floor.

#2717. Gold is doing something strange. Here's one way to play it

Gold has stopped trading like a haven and started trading more like a market index this year. The past week has underscored it. Fears around AI, a hawkish Fed, and a stronger dollar sent many investors rushing to raise cash, and gold was sold along with stocks. GLD (SPDR Gold Shares) and the S&P 500 both slid around 9%. Gold then shared in the market's Monday rebound, with GLD up about 3% as the S&P 500 jumped nearly 5%.

Over long timeframes, gold's returns tend to move independently of the S&P 500's. From 2004 to 2025, the correlation between their daily returns has been just 0.05 (+1 means the two move in lockstep and -1 means they move in opposite directions). That relationship fluctuates, and 2026 has seen an unusually strong link. The correlation has been about 0.41 so far in 2026. Its rolling three-month reading peaked near 0.80 in June and now sits at 0.54, still higher than about 95% of rolling three-month readings since 2005. Since the end of August, GLD has fallen on 77% of the S&P 500's down days, compared with roughly half historically.

The options market is also behaving unusually. Gold options typically price calls richer than puts (call skew). Like other commodities, gold is prone to sharp rallies, and investors use calls to bet on them or hedge against macroeconomic risks. However, gold options have mostly shown the reverse this year, with puts currently trading richer than calls (put skew). It's a sign investors are paying a premium for protection against further declines, which is unusual for gold and more typical of stock options.

Those richer puts come as uncertainty around gold runs high heading into December. The PCE inflation report arrives Wednesday, followed by the jobs report next week and the Fed's decision and CPI the week after. GLD's implied volatility, a measure of how much the options market expects the fund to move, is now higher than on about 80% of days over the past year. Options are pricing in an expected move of about 6%, or roughly $20, by Dec. 18. With gold options pricier than usual and puts unusually rich, that presents an interesting setup for traders willing to sell premium.

Based on Monday's close, I'm selling the Dec. 18 310/300 put spread and 360/370 call spread in GLD for a credit of roughly $2.24.

This is a directionally neutral trade. Gold has been swinging with the market and is down about 33% from its January high. With the Fed and inflation data ahead, it's hard to say whether gold has bottomed or has further to fall into mid-December. A neutral position can collect the elevated premium without picking a direction, and the richer put side adds more.

The short strikes sit just outside the range the options market is pricing for Dec. 18, roughly 7% to 8% from Monday's close. That leaves room for a continued selloff or an extended rebound. The trade reaches its maximum profit of $224 if GLD closes between $310 and $360 on Dec. 18. It carries a 62% theoretical probability of profit and can show a gain before expiration if GLD remains relatively rangebound.

The maximum loss is capped by the long options and reaches $776 if GLD closes below $300 or above $370, 10% to 11% from Monday's close. Defining risk is especially important with the upcoming catalysts and recent price volatility in gold. GLD has had 30 daily moves of more than 3% this year, including a 10.3% drop on Jan. 30. The trade breaks even at $307.76 on the downside and $362.24 on the upside.

A close between $360 and $370 can assign the short call and leave a short position in the fund, so investors looking to avoid that should consider managing the trade before expiration. If GLD finishes between $300 and $310, the short put can be assigned, creating an obligation to buy 100 shares per spread at $310. After the credit, that's a cost basis of about $307.76, roughly 8% below Monday's close.

#2715. Cathie Wood’s Ark Invest was a big buyer of Anthropic as she tells CNBC she’s ‘quite optimistic’

Cathie Wood was a major buyer of Anthropic following its debut Thursday on the Nasdaq, adding shares in all her major funds.

Wood's firm, which already owned private shares of the artificial intelligence company in its Ark Venture Fund leading up to the initial public offering, bought $90.8 million worth of Anthropic in six funds, according to a trade notification from the firm.

"We've owned Anthropic since early '23," Wood told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Friday. "It's our best performing equity by far in ARKVX, our venture fund. ... Our confidence has grown with time as it really took over the enterprise" AI business.

Anthropic shares jumped 17% in their first day, but closed well off the highs of the session and were headed for sizable losses Friday. The Nasdaq, which was expected to get a boost from a major IPO reviving enthusiasm about the technology trade, fell by 2% on Thursday.

"We're climbing a wall of worry," said Wood. "Everybody is worried about AI hype and the political situation after the election, but I think we'll look back and say, OK this is more like the '80s and '90s, climbing a wall of worry you know with bricks much like what we have today: inflation, interest rates, wars, new technologies and so forth so quite optimistic here."

The Anthropic stakes are relatively small across the funds, but Wood typically will buy shares in companies she likes steadily during long stretches. Wood said she is "averaging down" with her purchases of Anthropic.

In her $6.1 billion Ark Innovation ETF, Anthropic is a 0.3% stake. The biggest holdings in that fund are Tesla and SpaceX, representing more than 21% of the fund together.

Ark Innovation, which retail investors piled into during the pandemic as it gained about 150% in 2020, tumbled the subsequent next two years, losing 67% in 2022 alone. Wood's following was dented after the big losses.

The fund had a comeback stretch as the bull market revved back up from 2023 to 2025, but has fallen on hard times again this year, down more than 10% in 2026. The S&P 500 is up 4.8% this year.

Wood dismissed comparisons of today's environment to the dot-com bubble.

"Back then if an Anthropic had gone public, it probably would have gone up threefold the first day," she said. "That's how crazy things were."

#2714. Saudi national charged in OpenAI bugging to be released on $1 million bond

Abdulrahman Alfozan, the Saudi national accused of bugging an OpenAI executive conference room, will be allowed to be released from jail on a $1 million bond, a San Francisco federal court judge ruled Tuesday.

Alfozan, 35, is expected to be released on Wednesday and be fitted with an ankle monitor, according to his attorney, David Rizk.

"We are simply grateful that the Court made the right decision to release Mr. Alfozan and now we look forward to defending the case," Rizk said in a text message after a hearing before U.S. District Court Magistrate Judge Alex Tse.

Tse's ruled in favor of a release motion by Rizk filed last week that said prosecutors had admitted they had "found no new evidence to support the theory that Mr. Alfozan was stealing trade secrets, or to support the speculation that he was acting as an unregistered foreign agent for Saudi Arabia."

The San Francisco U.S. Attorney's Office opposed the former OpenAI engineer's release, saying in its response that he remains a flight risk due to his "considerable resources and ties to Saudi Arabia."

Alfozan's release request "blithely dismisses the seriousness" of the charge he faces, and "appears to presume, without support, that the government's investigation is complete," prosecutors wrote.

Alfozan, who was arrested Oct. 9, is accused of concealing a recording device in the artificial intelligence company's conference room to secretly record discussions. The device was found in a USB port in a television in the room on Sept. 30, prosecutors have said.

Prosecutors said they have found hundreds of audio files on Alfozan's personal computer, "includingdozens of recordings of meetings or conversations that occurred at OpenAI throughout September 2026, many of which involve discussions of what may be trade secrets."

Jury selection for Alfozan's trial is scheduled to begin Jan. 20.

Alfozan is a venture partner in a Saudi Arabian venture capital firm that lists Prince Khalid Bin Bader Al Saud, a member of that nation's ruling royal family, as a fellow partner.

OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Alfozan's planned release.

— CNBC's Ashley Capoot contributed to this article.

#2713. Rams vs. Green Bay Packers: How to watch, start time, odds and prediction

Rams star Myles Garrett knows how to aid a fellow All-Pro edge rusher.

Garrett helped Micah Parsons of the Green Bay Packers secure some tickets for Wednesday night's game at SoFi Stadium.

"The dialogue was, 'Hey, big bro, you got any extra tickets,'" Garrett said. "I hooked him up."

Parsons, a three-time All-Pro, is listed as questionable but he is on track to play for the first time since he suffered a major knee injury last December.

"Just looking forward to him being out there and doing his thing, feeling healthy," said Garrett, a five-time All-Pro and two-time NFL defensive player of the year. "I know he had to take some extra time but the game is better when Micah Parsons is on the field."

Maybe for fans, but not for Rams offensive linemen.

With center Coleman Shelton and guard Steve Avila sidelined because of hamstring injuries, Parsons is capable of wrecking the Rams offense.

Rams defensive lineman Aaron Donald knows a game-wrecker when he sees one.

"I wish he would stay out one more week," Donald joked, adding, "Micah, if you want to take one more week to get yourself 100%, make sure everything is where it needs to be, I'd like to see you on TV.

"I know they're going to be happy to have him back, a hell of a football player."

Parsons, 27, played against the Rams twice as a member of the Dallas Cowboys.

Read more: Healthy Rams pass rushing unit targeting 'Fearsome' performance vs. Packers

In 2022 at SoFi Stadium, he sacked Matthew Stafford twice, hit him three times and forced a fumble en route to sending the Rams to a 22-10 defeat.

In 2023, he had a sack and three quarterback hits in a 43-20 rout over the Rams.

Garrett amassed an NFL season-record 23 sacks last season for the Cleveland Browns. He has three in three games this season.

"It's similar to me," Garrett said, "in which you can line me up pretty much anywhere and expect a win."

Rams: OL Steve Avila (hamstring, out); TE Terrance Ferguson (hamstring, out); C Coleman Shelton (hamstring, out).

Packers: Edge Micah Parsons (knee, questionable); LB Zaire Franklin (shin, questionable); RB Josh Jacobs (finger, questionable); WR Bo Melton (thigh, questionable); WR Skyy Moore (ankle, questionable); OL Sean Rhyan (ankle, questionable); G Kevin Zeitler (triceps, questionable); OL Travis Glover (shoulder, questionable).

#2712. James sees a lot to like — and improve — for East-leading Sixers

James sees a lot to like — and improve — for East-leading Sixers originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

LeBron James likes to refer to the NBA season as a "marathon."

A few miles in, the Sixers lead the Eastern Conference pack.

With 17 regular-season contests down of 82, the team sits at 14-3, which is 2.5 games ahead of the second-seeded Celtics. The Sixers squeaked out their latest win, a 132-129 decision Saturday over the cellar-dwelling Bucks, but the bottom line is they've become accustomed to finding many routes to victory.

"We want to build habits," James said. "We want to try to take steps forward every game that we get the opportunity. I know sometimes it doesn't happen that way, but we want to do it.

"We want to strive to be as great as we can offensively, defensively and on special teams. A win is a win, but there's ways to win and ways to try to continue to build habits over the course of a marathon."

All sorts of Sixers games have gone down to the wire and they've won every single one.

The team is an incredible 12-0 in clutch situations, defined as games with a point differential of five or under in the final five minutes. The Sixers rank third in the NBA in clutch offensive rating (140.3) and third in clutch net rating (plus-42.0).

"It's good to build that part of our game," James said. "Obviously, we wanted to close the game out a lot better. But a team like that, we know they're going to be scrappy. They're going to play as hard as they can for 48 minutes. … We can learn from that."

James was the centerpiece of the Sixers' fourth-quarter offense Saturday. He scored 13 of his 21 points between the 7:46 and 3:13 mark of the fourth.

The four-time MVP got two buckets on no-nonsense drives and another on an after-timeout isolation hoop over rookie Brayden Burries. James also scored three times on a designed Horns action where he brought the ball up, used Tyrese Maxey's back screen at the elbow and caused serious problems for Milwaukee in the paint.

"We continue to add things to the half-court offense and also to the late-game package," Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said. "That's something we added a few game ago. It's one of those things where, especially if we're in the bonus, we've got some big bodies that can cut down the lane and have feel for timing. It was working. Just keep going to it."

James has grown in comfort with Nurse's coaching style. He knows the Sixers expect him to be a de facto coach on the floor, too.

"I'm just trying to be there for the team in any capacity they want," he said. "Just trying to be an extension of his calls and his commands out there on the floor. Trying to make his life and his job a little bit easier as well.

"But it's been great, not only with him but the whole coaching staff. They've welcomed me with open arms and allowed me to kind of be the voice for the team every day, and take that responsibility."

After a tremendous first impression defensively and some subpar offensive nights, the Sixers' numbers have recently evened out.

The team is 12th in offensive rating outside of garbage time and 12th in defensive rating, per Cleaning the Glass. In essence, the Sixers have been a bit above average on both ends of the floor and downright brilliant in the closing minutes.

It's all added up to an early lead in a very long race.

"I think we've bought into the pass," James said. "We have so many guys that can score the ball at elite levels. … In order for us to be a super-complete team, I think the power of the pass is very infectious. And it's also key for our other guys, to make sure they feel in a rhythm and they feel confident. We've done that from Day 1 and I think it's gotten better and better. … And I think our defense has been really good for the majority of the season.

"(Today) it wasn't so great, but we've been very good defensively throughout the course of the season. … I don't want to say there's anything bad. There's so many things for us to do better for sure. There's games where we can defensive rebound a lot better and there's games where we can not turn the ball over (as much). And there's games where we can be a little more phsyical defensively at the point of attack like (today).

"I wouldn't say anything has been bad, though. That's a good thing. We want to continue to have room for improvement and we don't want to be great in November. That would be weird."

#2710. Drugmaker Insmed shares rally 14% after Sanofi agrees to buy it in pharma’s biggest deal in three years

Insmed shares rallied 14% on Tuesday after Sanofi announced it would buy the smaller drugmaker for $41 billion, marking the largest pharma deal since 2023.

The proposed acquisition includes Insmed's portfolio of two commercialized respiratory drugs as well as its pipeline of experimental candidates. Sanofi will pay $175 per share in cash.

It's a big bet by new Sanofi CEO Belen Garijo, who took up the role in May to steer the company through its upcoming patent cliff, when its blockbuster immunology drug Dupixent will face generic competition as patents expire.

If closed, the transaction will be the biggest one the industry has seen since Pfizer bought Seagen for $43 billion in December 2023.

Insmed shares closed up 14.1% at $170.15 on Tuesday, while Sanofi stock closed up 10.9% in Paris.

Barclays analysts called the deal a "breath of fresh air," significantly improving Sanofi's Dupixent patent expiry outlook by adding Insmed's established respiratory assets Brinsupri and Arikayce, plus a late-stage pipeline offering further potential upside.

The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027 and be accretive to earnings by the end of 2028, Sanofi said.

Like much of the industry, Sanofi faces a revenue drop toward the end of the decade as top-selling drugs lose exclusivity and open up for generic drugmakers to compete.

Global biopharma has experienced a sharp uptick in deals in 2026, as the sector is driven by looming patent cliffs, newly buoyant public markets and a race to beef up pipelines. Following a post-pandemic trough in 2022, M&A activity surged in 2025 and has accelerated into 2026.

While companies develop new medicines in-house, acquiring them is often faster and has become the go-to strategy for large biopharma companies with strong cash flows and financial firepower. Investors are also calling for sustainable revenue growth as major drugs lose exclusivity.

"Sanofi could offer a far more attractive investment opportunity given the significantly improved growth outlook," Barclays said in a note early Tuesday.

Formerly CEO at Merck KGaA, Garijo is facing pressure to find Sanofi's next growth driver. Her predecessor Paul Hudson stepped down earlier this year after the board chose not to renew his mandate, following a six-year reign during which his costly emphasis on R&D failed to deliver speedy results.

The Insmed deal is a good strategic fit that will help soften the blow from Dupixent's expected 2031–32 loss of exclusivity, said Jefferies analysts.

Insmed's medicines Brinsupri and Arikayce could add significant long-term revenue, with forecasts of $6.8 billion and $1.3 billion, respectively, in 2035, the analysts said. They see further potential upside if a settlement delays Dupixent's patent cliff, or if Brinsupri is included in Sanofi's alliance with Regeneron and positioned alongside Dupixent in respiratory diseases.

"The deal does not fix Sanofi's R&D/pipeline questions, but it buys time," the analysts said, adding that one potential wrinkle is future competition from AstraZeneca's tozorakimab, which is being studied for treatment in bronchiectasis, a chronic lung condition.

"Insmed builds on our already successful presence in respiratory diseases through its highly differentiated portfolio, strong science and proven commercial success," CEO Garijo said in a statement.

Sanofi shares fell 2.9%, and Insmed rose 24% on Nov. 19 after Bloomberg reported that a deal was underway.

#2709. As Anthropic shares tank, investors scramble to hedge. It could be very expensive

As Anthropic shares tumble toward their IPO price of $83, investors are looking for ways to hedge. Unfortunately, they may have to wait until Monday, when options on the AI giant are expected to list.

If Anthropic breaks its IPO price, it will represent a 27% decline from Thursday's intraday high of $113. The wild price swings offer clues on how expensive it might be to buy protection on the new tech giant once options begin trading.A 20% intraday move points to an implied volatility somewhere between 100 and 150 for Anthropic options, according to estimates from single-stock market-makers on the Cboe trading floor in Chicago.

Options traders are also looking at how SpaceX traded in the days following its offering for clues on how options might price.

Implied volatility in SpaceX started at 116, but that didn't deter options traders big and small from piling into the contracts tracking the stock, with about 1.7 million contracts traded on the first day for a total options premium of about $2.5 billion. Far out-of-the-money call contracts were some of the most popular trades as the stock soared 40% in its first three sessions.One key difference between now and then? Anthropic is trading against the backdrop of S&P 500 volatility close to 30, compared to 17.3 when SpaceX debuted. "I expect ANT options to be super active," said Tom Sosnoff, co-founder of the trading platforms ThinkOrSwim and TastyTrade. "I expect heavy options volume."One thing Anthropic and SpaceX have in common is heavy retail involvement in both IPOs, with retail brokerages receiving a 20% allocation from SpaceX and reports pointing to between a 15-20% allocation from Anthropic on Thursday. "Round one of the Anthropic IPO easily goes to the individual investor," Sosnoff added. "Retail participants bailed early at the best prices of the day while institutional investors paid up to top off their underwhelming allocations. I believe retail was aggressively reloading in the mid-90s."Further signs of retail demand will become evident when options likely begin trading on Monday. One thing to watch: the spread between out-of-the-money call and put contracts, which was heavily skewed toward calls in the case of SpaceX. "I would be careful comparing Anthropic to SpaceX," said Dennis Davitt, CIO and Co-Founder of Millbank Dartmoor Portsmouth. "From a market-structure perspective, the two are dramatically different. The availability and cost of borrowing will be different, the companies are at very different stages of maturity, and SpaceX has allowed employees to monetize portions of their holdings over time. All of those factors matter when pricing options."

#2708. Dell earnings beat on AI strength, company authorizes $25 billion buyback

Dell reported third-quarter earnings on Tuesday that topped Wall Street expectations for earnings and sales, and provided a strong guide for the fourth quarter.

Here's how the chipmaker did versus LSEG consensus estimates:

Dell said that it expected earnings of $8.40 per share on revenue of about $56.3 billion in the current quarter. Analysts polled by LSEG were looking for $7.50 per share on $53.61 billion in revenue.

The company's overall sales more than doubled on an annual basis during the third quarter, driven by AI server demand.

The company's largest line is its infrastructure solutions group, or ISG, which makes AI servers and systems, often based around AI chips from companies like Nvidia and AMD.

ISG sales during the quarter were $41.97 billion, topping an LSEG estimate of $35.27 billion. Of that, $22 billion was for AI-optimized servers, up 291% on an annual basis. ISG now accounts for 85% of Dell's total revenue.

"We are now a different company, with Infrastructure Solutions Group driving the vast majority of our profit and growth," said Jeff Clarke, Dell's vice chairman and COO, in a statement. He said that Dell has 7,500 customers buying AI servers.

In prepared remarks, Clarke said that Dell has a competitive advantage over other computer equipment makers because it allows customers to get their computers working within hours of delivery.

"That allows customers to convert backlog into revenue sooner and more reliably," Clarke said in the prepared remarks published by Dell.

The company also raised its forecast for AI-servers in the coming fiscal year to $78 billion, versus $74 billion expected. The company says it has a backlog of $132.3 billion in AI server orders it is working through.

"Every AI order is vetted for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance and access to land and power," Clarke said on an earnings call with analysts.

The company also sells laptops and PCs, in a group it calls CSG, or client services group. It reported $12.89 billion in sales, which was below LSEG expectations of $14.33 billion.

The overall PC market has been getting whacked of late, with some estimates calling the lull the worst ever, as memory prices have led to higher device prices and consumers are choosing to hang on to their old laptops longer.

Dell said that it had authorized $25 billion in share repurchases, and that it had spent $4.9 billion in the third quarter on share repurchases and dividends.

Dell shares are up over 135% so far in 2026.

Brian Kelly has been a central figure in Maryland's coaching search almost since the dismissal of Mike Locksley.

The former Central Michigan, Cincinnati, Notre Dame and LSU coach, however, isn't the only candidate.

Multiple individuals with direct knowledge of the search told USA TODAY Sports this week Maryland officials have spoken in recent days with Western Michigan coach Lance Taylor and New Mexico coach Jason Eck. UNLV coach Dan Mullen also was vetted for the position.

"They've talked to a lot of people, lot of candidates," an individual with knowledge of the process said.

IN-DEPTH: Maryland football has ambitious coaching targets. Here's the reality

TOPPMEYER: Why Brian Kelly to Maryland football isn't as crazy as you'd think

Three separate people told USA TODAY Sports that Maryland's search party met in person with Eck, whose second New Mexico team became the first in school history to earn top-25 rankings in the AP and US LBM Coaches polls.

Taylor's Western Michigan team faces Miami (Ohio) on Tuesday, Nov. 24, in a game that could propel the program to a second consecutive MAC championship game with a win.

A former walk-on tailback at Alabama under Mike Shula, Taylor launched his coaching career at his alma mater under Nick Saban in 2007-08. He also has coached in the NFL and was named FootballScoop's Running Backs Coach of the Year in 2015 for his work with Stanford's running backs. Taylor later became a top assistant at Notre Dame before leaving to become Louisville's offensive coordinator and eventually landing the Western Michigan job.

Eck is likely among the most sought-after coaches in this cycle and is a top target for multiple jobs, both those already open and others that could develop.

A former Wisconsin offensive lineman, Eck has a larger-than-life personality, a unique story and, most importantly, a proven track record of rebuilding programs. He took over a moribund Idaho program at the FCS level and led the Vandals to five FCS playoff games.

From there, he has won 18 of his first 24 games at New Mexico, including a victory against UCLA last season, while producing one of the nation's stingiest defenses in 2026 under coordinator Spence Nowinsky.

Multiple people with direct connections to the Maryland program also stressed that Aazar Abdul-Rahim has impressed during his stint as interim coach. The Terps have been more competitive, scored an upset victory against Wisconsin and played with greater unity under Abdul-Rahim, one individual noted.

Maryland concludes its season at home Saturday, Nov. 28, against Penn State.

Multiple people indicated Maryland is expected to conclude its search by the end of the week.

The NCAA's early signing period for 2027 football prospects begins Wednesday, Dec. 2, and runs through Dec. 4. The transfer portal opens Jan. 4-13, 2027, but numerous industry insiders and general managers told USA TODAY Sports the timing of these hires is crucial for both high school and transfer-portal signings.

#2704. Trump wanted Jensen Huang back. Now, the president is all alone in Washington

President Donald Trump wanted Jensen Huang back at the helm of Nvidia. Now that the chip mogul is reinstated, Trump is cheering alone in Washington.

Trump celebrated and claimed credit after Huang was reinstated by the Nvidia board on Monday, a stunning return to power for the embattled CEO. In a nearly hourlong phone call with CNBC, the president went as far as saying he "made the deal" to bring Huang back.

But Trump's jubilation stands in stark contrast to the reaction from even his staunchest allies on Capitol Hill, who recoiled after the reinstatement and vowed to continue their investigations into Huang — whose relationship with a potential Chinese intelligence asset they fear may have jeopardized U.S. national security.

"The risk remains that there could be information that a Chinese spy knows about a key individual in the supply chain, and that's not worth the risk," Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said Tuesday on CNBC's "Squawk Box." "We might even have to put a babysitter on Jensen Huang for crying out loud ... just to make sure that he doesn't do something that's going to risk the United States."

Trump's rare isolation from his party over Huang comes after the GOP was throttled in the midterm elections, as Democrats rode a blue tsunami to capture the Senate and the largest House majority this century. And it suggests Republicans, who have spent a decade in lockstep with the president, may have found an issue on which they can't bring themselves to take Trump's side.

"I can accept what the president has done," Cramer said. "But we have to put guardrails around to protect the United States of America."

Many midterm voters identified Silicon Valley's most visible outputs, artificial intelligence and data centers, as top concerns motivating them to cast ballots for Democrats. The CNBC All-America Economic Survey in October found 63% of registered voters oppose an AI data center within 10 miles of their home, while just 13% support one.

By timing his extraordinary intervention in Nvidia so soon after the GOP's historic losses, Trump could spark a national debate about corporate governance and responsibility, former Under Secretary of State Richard Stengel said.

"With the repudiation of Trumpism in the midterms and voter revulsion with corruption, I think there will be a turn back to a more value-based duty of care for boards of directors and away from the current maximization of shareholder value," Stengel told CNBC in an email.

"Directors are citizens first, shareholders second. The idea that you put profit above national security should disgust shareholders, not please them," Stengel, who worked in the Obama administration, wrote.

Bipartisan lawmakers are now racing to pass a series of export control bills before the year ends, a call that has only grown louder since Huang was reinstated.

There's "not just frustration or political worry, but actual, substantive national security concern here from Democrats and Republicans," Chris McGuire, senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations, told CNBC.

"This has historically been a bipartisan issue," McGuire said. "Democrats and Republicans generally pretty much agree that we shouldn't be sending our most advanced chips to China."

"If it happened in massive quantities, people want to know why, how, and they want to make sure that it doesn't happen again," he said. "And putting your thumb on the scale in this clear of a way seems like it could undercut those efforts."

The White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on the political dynamics of Trump's involvement in reinstating Huang.

Republicans will have the first crack at investigating Huang next week before ceding power to Democrats in January. Democrats have vowed their own investigations into the Nvidia CEO and his ties to the president and his Cabinet. The Democrats who will lead those investigations are now hopeful that Republicans will join them.

"I've been seeing a lot of Republicans outraged and scandalized by what has just happened," House Judiciary Committee ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., said Tuesday on "Squawk Box," when asked if Republicans may support a bipartisan investigation of Nvidia.

"When else in American history can you think of a time when a president of the United States called up a corporate board of directors meeting and then essentially dictated to them who was going to be their new CEO right after they had fired the guy?"

Trump throughout his second term has stated repeatedly that achieving AI dominance is required for the U.S. to maintain global superiority. His administration has championed the rapid growth of the country's tech giants and forged close ties with its leaders, especially Huang, while removing constraints on the industry and opposing some new regulatory efforts.

At the same time, Trump has defended Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick against accusations of slow-walking export controls on China, the fiercest competitor in the AI race. And while Trump recently discussed AI during an in-person meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, he appeared to deliver few demands and achieved few assurances about Beijing's efforts to acquire U.S. chips.

"To say we can't do AI safety because of China, and then also be actively loosening the controls on China, makes no sense," McGuire said.

Some of Trump's fiercest allies have raised similar qualms.

"Reinstating Jensen Huang is going to blow back on our national security," MAGA activist Laura Loomer wrote in an X post Monday. "Eventually there has to be accountability for jeopardizing US national security. China didn't just get access to Nvidia chips by accident."

Newt Gingrich, the influential former Republican speaker of the House, in an X post after Huang's reinstatement, wrote, "Congress should really dig into this as a national security issue of enormous proportions and also a significant failure in the federal bureaucracy."

Their criticisms sharply contrast with the praise coming from Silicon Valley and some of the Trump-friendly voices within it, such as Elon Musk, who wrote Monday, "The mistake has been corrected."

But that's a shrinking political constituency, McGuire said.

"The tech-right perspective is very out of touch with where most of the Republican Party is on these issues, to say nothing of the Democratic Party," he said.

"Those positions are just not going to be sustainable for much longer," he added. "I think they're already becoming unsustainable."

#2703. Jensen Huang tells staff that Nvidia doesn't need a succession plan

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Tuesday struck a conciliatory and remorseful tone while leading his first employee meeting since being reinstated, and said how sorry he was for what he had done.

Huang told employees that he let them down and promised to do a better job the second time around, according to people inside the room, who asked not to be named in order to share details. "I hurt all of you," Huang said, according to one of the people.

The CEO also addressed succession planning during the event, the people said. He told staff that Nvidia has built a team that doesn't require succession planning the way a normal organization does, because the company operates a unique business model where there are multiple capable leaders at Nvidia that are leading different parts of the organization.

A succession plan would create unnecessary hierarchy, Huang said, according to one of the people present.

Investors and analysts were left to speculate about the company's future leadership in the wake of Huang's resignation on Nov. 12.

On Monday, Huang was reinstated as CEO of the chipmaker by Nvidia's board of directors. Eleven days before, Huang had resigned from Nvidia after multiple reported affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who is alleged to be a spy for Beijing.

Harvey Jones, Nvidia's newly appointed board chair, said last week that Huang resigned after "disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms."

Huang started the meeting by thanking CFO Colette Kress for her leadership as interim CEO.

Huang told staff that Tuesday's company meeting was the second hardest meeting of his life, the first one being with his wife. He said he is in therapy, according to one of the people present.

In a press release announcing Huang's return on Monday, the company said the board "received input" from senior officials in the federal government about any potential national security risk around the CEO. President Donald Trump told CNBC that he gave the board assurances and "made the deal" to restore Huang to his post.

After the company had its worst week in the stock market since 2008, the stock surged more than 30% the day his return was announced. Shares fell on Tuesday, however.

An Nvidia representative didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.

Following a disappointing defeat against Fenerbahçe in their last Champions League outing, Liverpool return to European action with a trip to Belgium to face Club Brugge.

Andoni Iraola's side will be keen to put that result behind them and get their European campaign back on track. Despite the setback in Turkey, Liverpool have made an encouraging start to the league phase, winning their opening three fixtures before suffering that first defeat.

The Reds will now be looking to respond with a performance that demonstrates the quality and depth available within the squad. With a busy domestic schedule continuing, this is also an opportunity for Iraola to rotate his starting eleven while maintaining the standards expected in Europe.

Club Brugge will provide a difficult test on home soil. The Belgian side are capable of making life uncomfortable for visiting teams, and Liverpool will need to be disciplined, particularly during the opening stages.

I expect Iraola to make changes for this fixture, balancing the need to maintain Liverpool's European momentum with the demands of a busy schedule.

Giorgi Mamardashvili should come into the side, while Joe Gomez and Kostas Tsimikas offer opportunities to rotate the full-back positions. Ronald Araújo and Virgil van Dijk would provide experience and physical presence at the heart of the defence.

In midfield, Trey Nyoni could partner Dominic Szoboszlai, with James McConnell operating further forward as the combative number 10. It would be an interesting selection, particularly given the ongoing questions surrounding Liverpool's midfield balance and the personnel required to make the double pivot work effectively.

The attacking positions could provide opportunities for some of the younger players. Bradley Barcola offers genuine pace and direct running from the right, while Víctor Muñoz could provide a similar threat on the opposite flank. #2698. Unconventional Racing Rebrands With Pratt Miller And Nielsen For 2027

Entrepreneur Naveen Rao has officially launched Unconventional Racing to unite his North American and European programs under one global brand. The new identity will debut on 10 December at the IMSA-sanctioned test at Daytona International Speedway. This move merges the expertise of Pratt Miller Motorsports in the US with Nielsen Racing in Europe to field cars in LMP2 and LMP3 classes starting in 2027.

Rao aims to build a single entity that operates across both sides of the Atlantic while keeping local operations intact. The team will run an ORECA 07-Gibson LMP2 car in the WeatherTech Championship through Pratt Miller. Before adopting a new identity for the 2027 European Le Mans Series season, Nielsen Racing in Europe will conclude its ongoing Asian Le Mans Series campaign.

The strategy relies on using existing infrastructure rather than building from scratch. Nielsen Racing will provide the personnel and operations for the European endurance program, allowing the team to enter multiple categories immediately without hiring new staff or buying new equipment.

"Unconventional Racing is about building something with genuine international ambition," said Rao, the CEO of Unconventional Racing, according to Sportscar365. He believes this structure lets each program draw on expertise that already exists within the organizations while presenting a unified front to sponsors and fans.

Rao plans to drive in both the ELMS and IMSA LMP2 programs himself. He brings experience from Ferrari Challenge North America and has secured podium finishes in IMSA LMP2 at Watkins Glen and Road Atlanta this past season.

Pratt Miller's partnership represents the American company's third LMP2 season following its 2025 return to prototype racing. This partnership gives Unconventional Racing a strong platform in North American sports car racing. According to reports, Pratt Miller's Director of Motorsport Operations said the move signifies an advancement for the group.

"Pratt Miller Motorsports are very excited to partner with Unconventional Racing working together to build a strong foundation for a global programme," said Maurini, according to DailySportsCar. The collaboration involves sharing engineering and mechanical expertise between the US and European teams to prepare for the 2027 season.

Team Principal Ron Hartvelt joined Nielsen Racing in 2025 and took his current role in March 2026. He will remain with the team as it transitions to the new brand. Hartvelt highlighted that an important Asian Le Mans Series campaign remains to be finished by the team prior to the full rebrand becoming active.

"Unconventional Racing represents an exciting evolution for Nielsen Racing," said Hartvelt. He stressed that the group plans to uphold the Nielsen name's ethos during this new phase while collaborating closely with Pratt Miller staff.

Driver lineups and further details on the North American and European programs will be announced in due course. The team expects to have a clear long-term vision in place as they move toward the 2027 European Le Mans Series and the Michelin Le Mans Cup. Rao's focus remains on creating a stable foundation for global competition.

The new identity reflects growing business opportunities within the sector, aligning the race team with Unconventional AI.

#2697. Tee Higgins touchdown highlights inconsistency of replay review

Just when we thought we were out when it comes to not knowing what a catch is, they pull us back in.

The past two days have included three examples of plays that make more confusing the question of whether a player has completed the act of catching the ball — and whether replay review was properly used to correct rulings made on the field.

It started on Sunday afternoon, when an apparent touchdown catch by Jaguars receiver Parker Washington was ruled not a catch on the field, with replay review not overturning the ruling. Even though the visual evidence seemed to provide clear and obvious proof that the ball was caught.

On Sunday night, 49ers receiver Mike Evans bobbled his way to a touchdown catch. He quite possibly didn’t get two feet in bounds after finally securing control of the ball. The play wasn’t even reviewed.

On Monday night, Bengals receiver Tee Higgins made a touchdown catch even though the ball was moving as he landed on the ground and out of bounds. There was no replay review.

The common denominator in these plays (beyond the fact that they involved potential touchdown catches) is the shadowy, uncertain replay process. As one head coach explained it to PFT on Monday (before the Bengals-Commanders game), it’s still not known who is making the decisions in New York as to what will be reviewed and what the outcome of the review will be.

It’s another reason for the NFL to embrace full transparency when it comes to replay review. We need to know who is making the decisions. We need to know their names. We need to hear their voices.

And we also need to know why — as happened in the case of the Evans and Higgins touchdowns — there was no full-blown review.

#2694. Clock operator robbed Bengals of one final play

The Bengals-Commanders game carries a small but not insignificant asterisk.

As ESPN rules analyst Russell Yurk explained in the postgame show, the clock operator incorrectly ran the remaining four seconds off the clock during the game-winning field goal from Washington.

What would have happened if the Bengals had gotten one last chance? We’ll never know, because the person hired to keep track of the time handled it incorrectly.

Or, depending on that person’s rooting interests, he handled it perfectly.

In the NHL, he's now a backup goaltender.

That's because of the emergence of Joel Hofer, who has become the No. 1 guy for the Blues. Hofer ranks second with a .919 save percentage and fifth with a 2.35 goals-against average among goalies who have started at least 15 games.

"He's been awesome the last couple years, and I think people are finally starting to realize how good he is," captain Robert Thomas said. The shift to Hofer, now 26, began last season when he started 43 games to Binnington's 39. That was a tandem approach, and it got St. Louis within reach of a playoff spot before just missing out.

Through the first 24 games this fall, Hofer has started 17 to Binnington's seven. The net is clearly his.

"I'm just trying to go a game at a time and give my team the best chance to win every night," Hofer said. "I'm just trying to have fun doing it. It's a privilege to play in this league and as a goalie to play games in a row. I'm just trying to make the most of it."

And I know that, myself, any time I talk to him, it's an easy conversation and that speaks volumes about him because we're talking about how he's doing and how we're working through things and he's just a consummate professional. He has high-level leadership."

Thomas, who is wearing the "C" for the first time after taking over that role from Brayden Schenn, called Binnington the greatest to play the position in franchise history. Binnington certainly has had his moments to earn that praise, including a 32-save performance to beat Boston in Game 7 of the Cup final in 2019.

Binnington was excellent at the Milan-Cortina Olympics, but his numbers with St. Louis show he is past his prime. Only Chicago's Arvid Soderblom and Vancouver's Kevin Lankinen have a lower save percentage than Binnington's .847 among goalies who have appeared in at least five games.

His teammates still think very highly of Binnington, especially given how he has handled being shuffled into a secondary spot.

"We believe he's one of the best goalies in the league, still," Thomas said. "It's a tough situation for him to be in, but he's a big part of our leadership group and he's really taken that to heart. He's been the ultimate teammate and person. It would be really easy to be frustrated in his situation. He's got a lot of things going on — a contract year, different things — but he's put the team first."

Hofer called Binnington supportive throughout the process of succeeding him.

"I guess this is my fourth year now, so it's been a good journey," Hofer said. "It's been fun with this group. Just trying to build every day. I think we're all going for the same goal here, and when we're all doing that and going in the same direction, it makes things fun."

#2692. The Nasdaq is in freefall. Here's one stock to look at

I asked Claude after Friday's close what I should do about the tanking stock market. Its advice was surprisingly useful: avoid panic selling and look for opportunities. A 40 VIX, which it touched Friday, might provide those opportunities. Specifically, a higher VIX (higher options premiums) signals fear, but it also creates an opportunity to sell elevated premium in some premium stocks, like Amazon.

Amazon's cloud business is growing at its fastest pace in nearly five years. AWS revenue rose 39.3% YoY in the third quarter, and management reported a $578 billion backlog. Trailing 12-month operating cash flow rose 29% to $168.3 billion. However, infrastructure investment accelerated, resulting in more than $42 billion in negative cash flow. The competing forces of accelerating growth and the cost of supplying it could keep the stock in its range over the next four weeks. Its shares are only off 14% from its recent highs, comparatively better than the Nasdaq Composite's near 19% decline.

AWS demand supports the lower end of the range. The backlog gives Amazon a basis for adding capacity even as investors scrutinize the cash cost. Cash spending could temper an upside rerating.

The next leg higher may require evidence that new capacity can earn attractive returns at this scale, and that evidence may be in short supply over the next couple of months.

Breakevens at expiration — $229.10 and $290.90.

Max risk — Unlimited on the uncovered call, but one should think of the trade as risking getting short at a net price above $290, a nearly 13% premium to today's closing price. Buying in bear markets, as the Nasdaq just touched, is never easy. But those opportunities don't present themselves too often. What are you going to do with it?

#2689. Cause of death revealed for ex-NFLer Alphonso Smith Jr. as heartbreaking new details emerge

Former NFL cornerback Alphonso Smith Jr. was crying and praying during an incident where he fatally shot himself in front of two women at a home in Pahokee, Florida, on Sept. 2, according to a police report by the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office obtained by TMZ.

One of the women was inside the home and heard Smith crying, praying aloud and speaking to several people on a conference call, per the report.

He asked her to go upstairs when she tried to comfort him — and then the mother of Smith's children arrived at the home moments later.

Alphonso Smith #33 of the Denver Broncos runs up the field during the game against the Seattle Seahawks on Aug. 22, 2009 at Qwest Field in Seattle, Washington. Getty Images

Both women, who were not named, witnessed Smith shoot himself while sitting on a living room couch.

The 40-year-old Smith was rushed to a nearby hospital before being airlifted to St. Mary's Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead at 3:19 p.m., the report stated.

Toxicology results also revealed THC, or marijuana, was present in his system.

TMZ previously reported that Smith died by suicide at a Florida housing community on Sept. 2.

Hours before his death, Smith shared a troubling Facebook post, in which he called himself a "coward" and said "this is a demon in me."

Ted Ginn Jr. #19 of the San Francisco 49ers runs for a long gain during a second quarter kick return as Alphonso Smith #27 of the Detroit Lions attempts to make the stop during the NFL game at Ford Field on Oct. 16, 2011 in Detroit, Michigan. Getty Images

Smith played four seasons in the NFL with the Broncos and Lions after Denver selected him in the second round of the 2009 draft.

He recorded eight interceptions, two defensive touchdowns, 88 tackles, two fumble recoveries/forced and 19 pass deflections.

A standout at Wake Forest, Smith earned All-American honors and he set an ACC record with 21 career interceptions, which still stands today.

Smith was inducted into the Wake Forest Sports Hall of Fame in 2022.

NICEVILLE, Fla. — Kennedy Blair's career-best scoring game was not enough to help the Michigan State women's basketball team capture the title at the Emerald Coast Classic.

Blair finished with 33 points for the Spartans, who were edged by Virginia Tech, 69-68, in the tournament title game Tuesday, Nov. 24.

Blair helped the Spartans overcome a 13-point second half deficit to take the lead in the fourth quarter. She hit the go-ahead 3-pointer with 1:10 to play to give MSU a 68-65 lead before Virginia Tech scored the final four points. Samyha Suffren hit the game-tying and go-ahead free throws with 4 seconds left to vault Virginia Tech (7-0).

Blair, who opened the Emerald Coast Classic by recording the fourth triple-double in MSU women's basketball history in a Nov. 23 win over Alcorn State, was 11-of-22 from the field and 9-of-11 from the free-throw line in her career-best scoring performance. She was one of two players in double figures scoring for MSU (6-1).

Theryn Hallock contributed 17 points for the Spartans on 7-of-11 shooting from the floor and added seven rebounds.

Suffren led three players in double figures with 19 points to lead Virginia Tech. Leila Wells, a Chelsea native, contributed 10 points for the Hokies.

At Detroit, Buffalo, at Green Bay, 49ers in Mexico City.

#2686. The Lakers are ‘optimistic’ Austin Reaves will return from injury against Spurs

After suffering a bruised heel on Nov. 11 against the Milwaukee Bucks, Austin Reaves has missed the Los Angeles Lakers' past five games. But according to head coach JJ Redick, it sounds like Reaves is progressing well and nearing a return as soon as the Lakers' next game against the San Antonio Spurs on Friday.

"We want to be consistent with our [return to play] stuff," Redick told reporters prior to Monday's win over the Utah Jazz. "I think today was a big step just in terms of getting a stay ready game in and he played great, moved great. We're optimistic for the rest of this week."

Although the Lakers have won four of five without Reaves in the lineup, they'll certainly welcome him back as quickly as possible. Three of those four wins occurred against the Jazz, Sacramento Kings and Charlotte Hornets, which own a combined 9-43 record this season. Their one loss during that stretch came to Utah on the second leg of a back-to-back as well. Even with those four wins against lottery-bound opponents, their play has suffered since Reaves became sidelined.

Through the first 13 games of the year — Reaves played in 12 of them — they were 11-2 with a plus-9.0 net rating (fifth league-wide) and the top-ranked offense (122.5 points per 100 possession). Over the past five contests, they're 4-1 with a plus-4.3 net rating (10th) and the 17th-ranked offense (114.0 points per 100).

Much of that offensive downswing stems from Luka Dončić's five-game slump (53.2% true shooting, 5.2 turnovers per game since Reaves went down). But it's entirely plausible Reaves' absence is creating too hefty of a workload for Dončić to endure. His return should better balance and diversify Los Angeles' offense by easing some of Dončić's burden for the betterment of everyone.

The timing is ideal, too. The Lakers' schedule significantly ramps up over the next five weeks. Across a 13-game stretch spanning from Friday through Dec. 29, the Lakers face the Spurs, Rockets (x2), Timberwolves (x2), Denver Nuggets (x2), Memphis Grizzlies (x2), Philadelphia 76ers and Indiana Pacers, which could have Tyrese Haliburton back by that Dec. 21 matchup.

Los Angeles will certainly need all hands on deck, Reaves included, to prove itself against such a formidable stretch of competition.

#2684. Top Wall Street analysts favor these 3 dividend stocks for strong returns

Investors often favor dividend stocks for their regular income and the promise of potential share price appreciation. But selecting the right dividend stocks from a huge pool of companies can be difficult.

Top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend-paying stocks, as their recommendations are backed by thorough analysis of a company's financials.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Devon Energy (DVN), an independent oil and natural gas exploration and production company, reported better-than-expected third-quarter results. The company announced a quarterly dividend of 32 cents per share for the fourth quarter, payable December 30. Based on the fixed dividends paid over the trailing 12 months, DVN yields 2.85%.

After hosting a virtual investor meeting with management, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on Devon, with a price target of $59. Mehta said that he is now more confident in management's outlook for delivering strong near-term capital returns as well as efforts to drive operational efficiencies and productivity gains.

Devon sees an opportunity to increase share repurchases, driven by solid free cash flow (FCF), contributions from the Eagle Ford divestiture and continued improvement in the balance sheet, Mehta said. Devon expects share buybacks worth more than $1 billion in Q4 2026, up from $414 million in the third quarter, backed by a strong pricing backdrop and improved capital efficiency.

Mehta, a 5-star analyst, said Devon expects about $6.3 billion of excess FCF in 2027, including about $3.5 billion of net proceeds from the Eagle Ford sale. That would enable the company to accelerate buybacks while progressing toward its goal of reducing gross debt to about $9 billion by early 2027. Mehta noted that under DVN's framework to return up to 70% of annual FCF, management favors share buybacks as it believes the stock is discounted compared to large-cap peers.

"Management expects continued capital efficiency gains from merger synergies, extended laterals, surfactant adoption and development of the newly acquired federal acreage," Mehta said.

Mehta ranks No. 876 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 8.1%. See Devon Energy Stock Buybacks on TipRanks.

Energy Transfer (ET), is a limited partnership that operates about 140,000 miles of pipeline and associated energy infrastructure. The company recently announced third-quarter results showing net income per common unit growing about 18% year-over-year, to 33 cents. #2680. Healthy Rams pass rushing unit targeting 'Fearsome' performance vs. Packers

Myles Garrett appreciates football history and, apparently, etymology.

Long before the star edge rusher joined the Rams in June, he studied Deacon Jones, the Rams' Hall of Fame end who was a member of the team's "Fearsome Foursome" defensive line of the 1960s and first dubbed the act of violently tackling a quarterback behind the line of scrimmage a sack.

Garrett, a 10th-year pro, said that when he was in high school he watched programs and interviews that featured Jones.

"Listening to him speak, him coining the term 'sack', how much he's done for this game and how special he was at the time in which he played," said Garrett, who also incorporated Jones' famed head-slap move into his prep pass-rushing repertoire.

On Wednesday, the Rams will honor that era when they don for the first time "Fearsome White" uniforms for their game against the Green Bay Packers at SoFi Stadium.

The new white and blue ensemble pays homage to the Rams' front that featured ends Jones and Lamar Lundy and tackles Merlin Olsen and Rosey Grier.

Grier, 94, will be in attendance along with family members of some of the deceased players that made up the legendary line.

"They set the tone," said Rams defensive lineman Aaron Donald, an eight-time All-Pro. "Obviously, you know how that group played together, the standard they set.

"Coming here as a rookie you heard about it. I always try to live up to their success and everything they were able to do."

Wednesday's game marks the first time this season that the Rams will deploy a front that includes Garrett and edge rusher Byron Young, and linemen Donald, Braden Fiske and Kobie Turner.

Turner is back after sitting out four games because of a groin injury.

"Perfect timing," he said, "Fearsome Foursome week."

Sacks did not become an official NFL statistic until 1982. According to ProFootballReference.com, Jones' 173½ unofficial sacks ranks third all-time behind Bruce Smith (200) and Reggie White (198).

Garrett (128½) is 27th, Donald (112½) 42nd.

The Rams have 21 sacks, which ranks 20th among 32 NFL teams. Young has a team-best 5½ sacks. Garrett, who amassed an NFL season-record 23 sacks for the Cleveland Browns last season, has three in three games. Fiske has 2½, Donald 1½ and Turner is searching for his first.

But to this point, those players were not available at the same time.

Donald, a three-time NFL defensive player of the year, did not play in the season-opener against the San Francisco 49ers in Australia because he was still acclimating after coming out of retirement. Garrett, a two-time NFL defensive player of the year, sat out the next seven games recovering from knee surgery. Then Turner was injured.

Now they are together, along with edge rushers Josaiah Stewart and Wesley Bailey and linemen Tyler Davis, Ty Hamilton and Larrell Murchison.

On a night when the rock band U2 will provide halftime entertainment, members of the Rams' defensive front aim to put on their own show to honor the Fearsome Foursome's legacy.

"They set the standard for what that means," Fiske said, "but for us to be that next generation of pass rushers, it's cool to be part of group that's special."

Rams pass rushers Myles Garrett (95) and Aaron Donald (99) celebrate between Braden Fiske, left, and Byron Young during a win over the Washington Commanders on Nov. 8. (Scott Taetsch / Getty Images)

Young said he was honored to wear a uniform that salutes the past.

"I know we're not there yet — how good they were — but just being in the conversation is pretty cool," he said.

Coach Sean McVay said the Fearsome Foursome set a standard for how the defensive front can impose its will. And the uniforms the Rams will wear to honor them "look pretty swaggy too," he said.

Garrett is looking forward to the opportunity.

"It means a lot to be able to wear that uniform and wear those colors," Garrett said, "and hopefully make them proud."

#2679. Resurfaced clip reveals Michael Jordan link that changed Kobe Bryant’s entire career

Kobe Bryant's career trajectory changed because of Michael Jordan.

In 1996, there were reportedly rumors that the Chicago Bulls superstar was going to retire and Bryant didn't want to pass up a chance to play against him.

Lower Merion's Kobe Bryant goes to the net at the Palestra in a Feb 27, 1996 playoff game against Coatsville. MediaNews Group via Getty Images

In a clip from a 2024 appearance on Byron Scott's "Fast Break" podcast, former NBA player John Salley recalled Bryant explaining why he skipped college and entered the 1996 NBA Draft directly out of high school.

"I said to him, 'Why'd you not go to college?' And he says, 'I heard MJ was going to retire,'" Salley said. "And that was his reason for not going to college."

Bryant was selected 13th overall in the 1996 NBA Draft by the Charlotte Hornets and was immediately traded to the Los Angeles Lakers.

Los Angeles Lakers guard Kobe Bryant(L) and Chicago Bulls guard Michael Jordan(R) talk during a free-throw attempt during the fourth quarter 17 December at the United Center in Chicago. AFP/Getty Images

Lakers #24 Kobe Bryant pumps his fist during the fourth quarter. Anthony J. Causi

Jordan ultimately continued playing for Chicago through 1998. After retiring for a second time, he returned with the Washington Wizards in 2001 and permanently ended his career in 2003.

Bryant and Jordan faced each other eight times during the regular season between 1996 and 2003. They never met in the playoffs or NBA Finals, but their matchups helped connect two of basketball's most celebrated careers.
